Three blank starts - Blank XY table and graph, as before; Blank XY table without a graph, for when you only want to enter and analyse data; Blank column table without a graph, groups side by side for t-tests and ANOVA. A graph can be added at any time. A Samples folder - The sample projects moved from Home into Samples, which opens inside Home with every sample under a heading: curves and regression, comparing groups, survival and reliability, medical tests, signals and thermal analysis, maps and special graphs. - Home now shows only the starts, Samples, Open, Import data, Guide, Roadmap and your recent projects.

heading: Changelog › 0.3.12 — 2026-11-02
text: Changelog › 0.3.12 — 2026-11-02. Dates, second step; median error bars; fixes from testers. Fixes from testers - Pressing Enter in a name box (renaming a data set, a table and so on) now keeps the new name before the window closes. - Right-click an axis › Format Axes opens the page of the axis you clicked (X, Y or the right Y axis), not always X. - One Format Graph window: Format Axes, Format Graph and double-clicks switch the open window to the page asked for instead of opening another. ×, Close and Esc close the window they belong to, not the newest one. - Long data set titles wrap onto up to three lines and the heading grows to fit. Drag the right edge of a heading to widen a column; double-click it to fit. - The date axis's Tick labels choice is now kept in the project (0.3.11 forgot it). Median error bars - Error Bars offer the median with its interquartile range, with its range, or with a 95% confidence interval (from the order statistics), on XY, column, grouped and nested graphs. The point or bar shows the median. Dates, second step - Pasting or importing text that looks like dates into a number X column offers to treat the column as dates.

heading: Changelog › 0.3.12 — 2026-11-02
text: Changelog › 0.3.12 — 2026-11-02. - Format Graph › X Axis › Major ticks every day, week, 2 weeks, month, 3 months or year; minor ticks one step finer. - Format Graph › Notes › Line at a date: a dashed line across the graph at a date you type, with a label. - Column formulas know dates: date(2026, 11, 5), today(), year(X), month(X), day(X), days(B, A), hours(B, A). - Straight-line fits on dates give the X-intercept and interpolated X values as dates, and the fitted value at the first date. - Product and file-format names are trademarks of their owners and are used only to describe file compatibility; code and documents name file types by extension, checked by a test.

heading: Changelog › 0.3.11 — 2026-11-01
text: Changelog › 0.3.11 — 2026-11-01. Dates and times. Dates in tables - The X column of an XY table can hold dates or dates and times: right-click its heading and choose how they are shown (5 Nov 2026, 05-Nov-26, 2026-11-05, 05/11/2026 or Nov 2026). Nothing changes for tables you leave as numbers, and older files open as before. - Type or paste dates in many forms: 2026-11-05, 2026-11-05 14:30, 5-Nov-26, 5 Nov 2026, Nov 5, 2026, 05/11/2026; impossible dates (31 Feb) are refused. File › Options › Dates sets whether 05/11/2026 is day first or month first (the first time, from your system's language). - Dates are kept as numbers, days since 1 January 1970, so everything else works on them unchanged. Dates on graphs - A date X axis with automatic ticks (the year once, then months or days), or day and month, month and year, ISO or week numbers (Format Graph › X Axis), with the range typed as dates. Hovering shows the date, and every export keeps the date ticks. Analyses and exports - Straight-line fits on dates give the slope per day. Workbook exports (.xlsx, .ods) write real dates. From Datum Plan

heading: Changelog › 0.3.11 — 2026-11-01
text: Changelog › 0.3.11 — 2026-11-01. - Datum Plot 0.3.11 is the first version that opens Datum Plan's time charts with dates (xFormat: "date", days since 1970): they open on a date axis with no questions asked. - Readings over time: weekly dissolved oxygen at two river sites, on a date axis, with the fall per day.

heading: Changelog › 0.3.10 — 2026-11-01
text: Changelog › 0.3.10 — 2026-11-01. Control charts and design of experiments. Control charts (Analyze › Quality › Control Chart) - Individuals and moving range for one value per row, X̄ and R or X̄ and S for subgroups (each row a subgroup in its sub-columns), and the p chart for defectives out of the number inspected. - 3σ limits, points beyond them and runs of 8 on one side of the centre line are flagged; give the specification limits for Cp and Cpk. Design of experiments - New Design makes a two-level factorial design as a table: 2 to 7 factors, full factorial or half fraction, replicates and centre points, the factors coded −1/+1 and the runs in a random order (row titles). Type each result in the Response column. - Factorial Analysis gives each factor's and interaction's effect with its test (Lenth's method when there are no replicates), a Pareto chart of the effects and the main-effect plot. Checked: the control limits equal the textbook constants (A2, D4, A3, B4, 2.66, 3.267) and the binomial limits of the p chart; known effects are recovered from a simulated design; designs are balanced and orthogonal.

heading: Changelog › 0.3.9 — 2026-11-01
text: Changelog › 0.3.9 — 2026-11-01. More statistics: three-way ANOVA, ANCOVA, agreement, bootstrap confidence intervals and spline fits. - Three-way ANOVA: a grouped table whose rows are the first factor and whose data sets are named by two levels with a slash ("Young / Drug", "Old / Placebo"…). Main effects and every interaction, with effect sizes. - ANCOVA: an XY table with the covariate in X and one data set per group. Checks that the slopes are parallel, then compares the groups' adjusted means (with Šidák comparisons) and draws the parallel lines on the graph. - Agreement: a contingency table of paired ratings (the first rating in the rows, the second in the data sets). Cohen's kappa with its 95% CI and strength, weighted for ordered categories, and McNemar's test (2 × 2) or Bowker's test (larger tables) for a systematic difference. Statistics and fitting - Bootstrap confidence intervals of each data set's mean, median or SD, and of the difference between the first two, without assuming a distribution (BCa, repeatable). - Spline fit: Smooth has a smoothing spline whose smoothness is chosen automatically; it is drawn on the graph. - Double-clicking an item in the Analyze or Graph gallery now closes the gallery behind the window it opens.

heading: Changelog › 0.3.8 — 2026-10-31
text: Changelog › 0.3.8 — 2026-10-31. Vector fields and 3D scatter graphs. New graph styles for tables of many variables (Graph › Graph Style, or Format Graph › Graph) - 3D scatter: the first three variables as X, Y and Z, coloured by a fourth when there is one. Tilt and turn the view in Format Graph. - Vector field: an arrow at each X, Y with its two components from the next two variables, coloured by its length. Arrows are scaled so the longest is about the distance between neighbouring arrows.

heading: Changelog › 0.3.7 — 2026-10-31
text: Changelog › 0.3.7 — 2026-10-31. Ternary, waterfall, radar and bubble graphs. New graph styles (Graph › Graph Style, or Format Graph › Graph) - Waterfall (XY tables): each data set's curve is lifted above the last and labelled at its end, for spectra, runs or temperatures. The lift is automatic, or set it in Format Graph. - Ternary (tables of many variables): the first three variables of each row as shares of 100 % on a triangle, for compositions. - Bubble (tables of many variables): X, Y, bubble size from the third variable, and colour from a fourth if there is one, with a size key and a colour bar. - Radar (grouped tables): the rows are the spokes and each data set is an outline through its means, for comparing profiles. - A graph style a table cannot make says why (a radar needs at least three rows, a ternary three variables). - Composition triangle: copper, nickel and zinc in 18 alloys on a ternary graph; switch to Bubble to see hardness as bubble size.

heading: Changelog › 0.3.6 — 2026-10-31
text: Changelog › 0.3.6 — 2026-10-31. Multiple t-tests and volcano plots. - Analyze › Multiple t-tests (in Compare Groups): a grouped table with one row per gene, protein or compound and two data sets (for example Control and Treated) with their replicates. Each row gets its own test: Welch's or ordinary unpaired t-test, paired t-test, or the Mann-Whitney test. - The P values are corrected for the number of rows by the false discovery rate (Benjamini-Hochberg, or the two-stage method of Benjamini, Krieger and Yekutieli) or by Holm-Šidák or Bonferroni. Rows below the threshold (q < 0.05 by default) are discoveries, and the answer says how many went up and down. - The results list every row by P value with the means, the difference, the log₂ fold change, t, P and q. - The result shows a volcano plot: log₂ fold change (or the difference) against −log₁₀ P, discoveries coloured and the strongest labelled by their row names. - New table from result turns it into an editable graph, with every row's name kept. - Each row's test equals SciPy's, and the false discovery rates equal the Benjamini-Hochberg step-up worked by hand.

heading: Changelog › 0.3.5 — 2026-10-31
text: Changelog › 0.3.5 — 2026-10-31. Repeated measures and mixed-effects two-way ANOVA; Copy Linked is removed again. - Two-way ANOVA has a new Repeated measures option for grouped tables where the same subjects are measured again (one sub-column per subject): in every row (for example at each time point), in every data set, or in both. - With complete data it is a repeated measures ANOVA with the right error term for each effect and the Geisser-Greenhouse correction for sphericity. When values are missing it fits a mixed-effects model instead, so no subject is thrown away. - Multiple comparisons within each row or each data set, with stars on the graph, come from the fitted model. The results show the variance between subjects and the sphericity estimates. - Checked against independent calculations: the fully repeated design matches a reference repeated measures ANOVA exactly, and the classic and mixed-model tests agree for complete data. - Copy Linked (0.3.4) is gone: it depended on other programs' linking steps and was too awkward to use. Copy Picture, Export, Slides, Document and Workbook remain. Projects saved with 0.3.4 open as before.

heading: Changelog › 0.3.4 — 2026-10-31
text: Changelog › 0.3.4 — 2026-10-31. Copy Linked: slides and documents follow your graph. - Graph › Copy Linked (also on the graph's right-click menu) keeps the graph as a picture in a folder beside the project, and redraws it every time you save. Insert that picture into your slides or document *as a link* once: from then on they show the new graph whenever their links are updated, in any program. The Linked Picture window gives the steps; its path is already on the clipboard. - Tools › Update Linked Pictures redraws every linked picture at once; Stop Linking ends it for one graph. - A project file can only name pictures inside its own pictures folder. - The next releases are planned in Help › Roadmap: repeated measures and mixed-effects ANOVA, multiple t-tests and volcano plots, ternary, waterfall, radar, bubble, vector and 3D scatter graphs, more statistics, control charts and design of experiments, wavelets, a graph digitizer, Bayesian tests, and then Mac and Linux versions. - The roadmap now says plainly that two-way ANOVA is ordinary only for now; repeated measures and mixed models for two and three factors come next.

heading: Changelog › 0.3.3 — 2026-10-30
text: Changelog › 0.3.3 — 2026-10-30. Testers' requests: colour schemes beside the graph, OpenDocument export, and plain names for file types. - Graph › Colour Schemes now sits beside the graph, so each scheme you click shows on the graph at once. Its table is compact again (the colour columns were far too wide). - Schemes whose colours stay easy to tell apart for colour-blind readers carry a small colour-blind safe label: Okabe-Ito (the default), Bright, Muted and Cividis. We checked them by simulating the three common kinds of colour-blindness. - Format Graph › Data Sets shows each data set's colour as it is drawn in the chosen scheme, and its quick colours are that scheme's colours. - Every window can be moved by dragging its title bar. - Tools › Workbook saves .xlsx or .ods, Tools › Slides .pptx or .odp, and Tools › Document .docx or .odt: choose the type in the Save dialog. Datum Plot writes the OpenDocument files itself. - Buttons and texts name the file type, not another company's product: Workbook, Slides and Document; texts say "a spreadsheet", "a document" or "slides". The "Classic" colour scheme and the "Open axes" and "Framed box" graph styles have plain names too.

heading: Changelog › 0.3.2 — 2026-10-30
text: Changelog › 0.3.2 — 2026-10-30. The Datum Plot Guide in English, Chinese and French, and five new samples. - Help › Guide (and the Guide tile on the File page): a step-by-step guide with numbered pictures, from your first table to analyses, graphs, layouts, export and the Python console, with a "which test when" table, a glossary and shortcuts. Choose English, 中文 or Français: the PDF downloads from this release, is checked against its checksum, is saved in your Downloads folder and opens. The installer stays the same size. - Survival study: months to relapse on two treatments, with Kaplan-Meier curves, the log-rank test and the hazard ratio. - Method comparison: a bedside glucose meter against the lab, with Bland-Altman bias and limits of agreement. - Diagnostic test: a biomarker in healthy people and patients, with the ROC curve, its AUC and the best cut-off. - Response surface: process yield over temperature and time, with a contour map and a quadratic surface fit that finds the best settings. - Polar pattern: the radiation pattern of two antennas on a polar graph. - An installation in a folder of your own choosing is updated in place after last version's publisher change.

heading: Changelog › 0.3.1 — 2026-10-29
text: Changelog › 0.3.1 — 2026-10-29. The family publisher name. - Windows now lists the publisher as Datum.

heading: Changelog › 0.3.0 — 2026-10-29
text: Changelog › 0.3.0 — 2026-10-29. A full check of the whole application: security, robustness, reliability and speed. No new features; everything that was there works more safely. Nothing is lost - Saving a project, the options and every export (pictures, pages, .xlsx, .pptx, .docx, notebooks) now writes a temporary file first and swaps it in only when it is complete: a crash, a full disk or a power cut never leaves a half-written file. - If something unexpected goes wrong inside the app during an edit, that one step is refused, your project stays exactly as it was, and the details go to crash.log in the app's data folder instead of closing the app. - A project whose internal numbers were damaged (repeated or impossible identifiers) is repaired on opening, with every graph, result and layout still linked to its data. - Graph settings out of range in a project file (sizes, fonts, angles, contour levels, marker sizes) are brought back within limits when it opens. - Damaged or unreadable data files (broken workbooks, garbled text, cut-off .pzfx files) give a clear message instead of an engine error.

heading: Changelog › 0.3.0 — 2026-10-29
text: Changelog › 0.3.0 — 2026-10-29. - Spreadsheet exports never contain live formulas: text that looks like one (starting with =) is written as text. Notebook CSV files mark text starting with =, +, - or @ so a spreadsheet will not run it. Safe updates and window - The updater accepts only an installer with the expected name, requires the release's checksum file, limits the download size and saves it in a new private folder. - The window refuses frames, plug-ins, forms and remote scripts (a stricter content security policy). Tested to break - New robustness tests feed the engine hundreds of random and hostile projects and edit sequences, damaged and truncated files, and impossible values; they found and fixed one crash (pasting at an impossible position). - An engine check runs every sample project through the real Python engine: every analysis, every graph type on every kind of table, every export format, layouts, slides, reports, notebooks and the console (532 requests, no failures). - The checks now also run on Windows and macOS on every change. - Typing a value in a very large table (a million rows) is about seven times quicker (0.05 s instead of 0.4 s): checking whether an edit changed anything no longer compares a million empty row titles one by one.

heading: Changelog › 0.2.23 — 2026-10-28
text: Changelog › 0.2.23 — 2026-10-28. The Python console, your own analyses, templates, batch processing and notebooks; and a full security, robustness and hardening review. - Tools › Python Console: write Python in the box, press ▶ Run (or Ctrl+Enter), and see what you print, the value of the last line and any figure you draw. Your tables are ready as pandas DataFrames (tables, table(0), tables['Name']), with numpy, pandas, SciPy and matplotlib loaded. new_table(...) puts results back into the project and result(...) reads an analysis's numbers. Variables last between runs. - How to use is built in: the ⓘ How to use button in the console and the ? beside it in the ribbon explain where to write, how to run, how to reach your data and how to put results back; Examples ▾ fills in working code to start from. Your own analyses, templates, batches, notebooks - My Analyses: save console code under a name and run it again from Tools › My Analyses on any project. It is kept with the app, never inside projects. - Analysis Template: repeat one table's analyses (with their options) and its graph's look on other tables. - Batch Process: choose a template table and many files; each file becomes a table with those analyses and a graph, and the answers are listed together.

heading: Changelog › 0.2.23 — 2026-10-28
text: Changelog › 0.2.23 — 2026-10-28. - Notebook: save the project as a Jupyter notebook (.ipynb): its tables, each analysis's answer and the Python behind it. - Every command in the ribbon now works: none are left “coming soon”. Security and hardening - Updates are installed only when the release's checksum file is there and matches the download exactly; links open only on this project's own pages. - Project files with impossible sizes, and files larger than 1 GB, are refused or kept within limits (a million rows, 1000 data sets, 50 replicates) instead of exhausting memory; imported files are limited to 300 MB. - Code never runs from a project: the console runs only what you type when you press Run, and My Analyses stay with the app. - Every change is now also checked for known vulnerabilities in the window's packages and the bundled Python packages, as it already was for the Rust ones. - Every analysis was run on awkward data (identical values, a single value, gaps, empty cells, numbers near the limits) on every kind of table: where something cannot be worked out, it now says why in plain words instead of failing. Editing with impossible values (rows beyond the end, columns that do not exist) is refused safely.

heading: Changelog › 0.2.23 — 2026-10-28
text: Changelog › 0.2.23 — 2026-10-28. - Tables can now hold up to a million rows (before: 100 000, and larger imports were cut off). Undo keeps fewer steps for very large projects, so memory stays bounded. - A damaged .pzfx file, or an unexpected number in a result, gives a message instead of stopping the engine.

heading: Changelog › 0.2.22 — 2026-10-28
text: Changelog › 0.2.22 — 2026-10-28. Large data, region statistics, importing projects, plates and many runs, and slides, reports and posters. - Graphs with hundreds of thousands of points stay quick: a line is thinned to what the screen can show, and dense points are drawn as a picture inside SVG and PDF files while the text stays text. 200 000 points draw in about a second (before: over six) and export at 75 kB (before: 21 MB). Analyses of large tables are faster too. Statistics of a region - Right-click a graph › Statistics of a Region (or Graph › Zoom ▾), then drag a box over part of the curves: for each curve, the points inside, mean, SD, range, area, slope and highest point. Copy the table, or open a linear fit limited to that range. - .pzfx projects: File › Import reads every table of a .pzfx file (XY, column, grouped, contingency, survival, parts of whole and nested) with titles, replicates, row titles and excluded values, each with its graph. - Plate readers: a sheet with a 96- or 384-well block (columns 1, 2, 3… and rows A, B, C…) is offered as a plate: a grouped table with rows A–H and columns 1–12, ready for a heat map.

heading: Changelog › 0.2.22 — 2026-10-28
text: Changelog › 0.2.22 — 2026-10-28. - Several files at once: Data › Several Files reads many runs (tensile tests, spectra): one data set per file, in one table when they share their X values. Slides, reports and posters - Tools › Slides: a 16:9 deck with a title slide, every graph on its own slide and a slide per result (.pptx). - Tools › Document: the project's details, every graph with a numbered caption, every result with its answer and main table, and the methods text (.docx). - Layout › Poster (A0) and Slide (16:9): a page with a large title and your graphs in a grid; graph text grows to suit the page. New page sizes: poster A0 and A1, slide 4:3. Behind the scenes - The built-in Python adds two libraries for slides and documents, so the first start after this update unpacks a new Python runtime (about a minute, once).

heading: Changelog › 0.2.21 — 2026-10-28
text: Changelog › 0.2.21 — 2026-10-28. Testers' requests (axis breaks on column graphs, wider columns, empty columns left alone), and matrices with contour maps, 3D surfaces, polar graphs and surface fits. - Axis breaks on column, grouped and nested graphs: Graph › Axis Break now works on dot plots, bars, box plots and grouped bars, not only on XY graphs (Format Graph › Y Axis › Axis break). Where a break cannot apply, the page says why instead of showing nothing. - Wider columns: drag the right edge of any column heading to widen it, or double-click the edge to fit its name and values. Widths are saved with the project. - More room for names: the × that deleted a data set from its heading is gone, so the name has the whole heading. Delete a data set from its right-click menu, or with Data › Remove Data Set. - Empty columns stay out of the way: graphs and analyses already left out data sets without values; now the analysis dialogs leave them unticked and dim them, and Format Graph marks them “(empty)”, so 3 or 20 columns make no difference. Matrices and 3D

heading: Changelog › 0.2.21 — 2026-10-28
text: Changelog › 0.2.21 — 2026-10-28. - File › New Table › Matrix: Z values on an X–Y grid. X runs down the first column, the Y values are the column titles, and each cell is a Z value (Z title in the bar above the table). - Its graph is a contour map (with contour lines), a heat map, a 3D surface or a 3D wireframe (Graph › Column Graph, or Format Graph), with a colour bar, a choice of colour maps, the number of contour levels and the 3D viewing angle. - Polar graphs: Format Graph › Data Sets › Polar draws an XY graph with X as the angle in degrees and Y as the radius. - Analyze › Regression › Surface Fit: fits Z = f(X, Y) to a matrix, or to three columns (X, Y, Z) of a table of many variables or a worksheet: a plane, a quadratic surface (with its maximum, minimum or saddle point), a cubic surface or a 2D Gaussian peak (centre, height and widths). Coefficients with standard errors and 95% CIs, R², and residual plots; on a matrix graph the fit is drawn as dashed contours or a wireframe.

heading: Changelog › 0.2.20 — 2026-10-28
text: Changelog › 0.2.20 — 2026-10-28. Worksheets with free columns, and column formulas. - File › New Table › Worksheet: free columns, one value per row, for raw instrument data. Each column has a role (X, Y, Y error or not plotted), a long name, units and a comment (Format Data Set, or double-click its heading). - The graph uses the X column for X, and each Y column as a data set; a Y error column right after a Y column gives its error bars. Units go into the axis titles. Linear regression, curve fits and the other XY analyses work on worksheets the same way. - A new sample on the Home page, Worksheet: a cooling curve with an error column and a formula column in kelvin. - Data › Transform › Column Formula (or Format Data Set › Formula): fills a data set from the others, for example log10(A), B + 273.15, (B - mean(B)) / sd(B) or if(C > 0, C, 0). A, B, C… are the data sets, X the X column, i the row number, col("title") a data set by its title; with log10, ln, exp, sqrt, abs, sin, mean, sd, sum, min, max, median, cumsum, diff and more. - Works on any table, for data sets with one value per row; a heading marked ƒ has a formula.

heading: Changelog › 0.2.19 — 2026-10-28
text: Changelog › 0.2.19 — 2026-10-28. Thermal analysis (DSC and TGA) and fatigue S–N curves. DSC and TGA - Analyze › More › DSC / TGA, for curves with temperature in X. - DSC (heat flow): for each peak, the extrapolated onset (where the steepest tangent meets the baseline), the peak and endset temperatures, the area and the enthalpy (area ÷ heating rate: J/g when Y is in W/g). Endotherms down or up; a straight or polynomial baseline; a temperature range to look in. - TGA (mass): for each step, the onset, the temperature of fastest loss (the peak of the derivative), the end and the mass lost, plus the residue and the temperature at 5% loss. The derivative curve (DTG) is shown beside the results. - The DSC sample on the Home page now uses it, and a new TGA steps sample shows a filled polymer losing mass in two steps. S–N fatigue curves - Analyze › Materials › S–N Curves: stress amplitude against cycles to failure, fitted with Basquin's law S = A·N^b (or against reversals 2N). Gives A and b with its 95% CI, R², and the fatigue strength at the lives you choose (10⁶ and 10⁷ cycles by default). - Run-outs (specimens that did not fail) are marked with an arrow and left out of the fit.

heading: Changelog › 0.2.18 — 2026-10-28
text: Changelog › 0.2.18 — 2026-10-28. Peaks and signals: find and fit peaks, Fourier spectra and filters. - Analyze › More › Peaks: finds the peaks of each XY data set above a baseline, a straight line from the first to the last point or a polynomial that follows a curved background. For each peak: its position, height, width at half height and area. Dips (endotherms, absorption bands) work too. - Optionally fits all the peaks at once as Gaussian, Lorentzian or Voigt peaks: centres and areas with their standard errors, so overlapping peaks are separated. - The graph shows the baseline (dashed), the fitted curve and a number at each peak. New table from result gives the baseline-corrected data. Noise is not counted as peaks. - A new sample on the Home page, Spectrum peaks: three overlapping bands on a curved background. - Analyze › More › Signal: the Fourier spectrum (which frequencies a signal holds, and the strongest one), low-, high- and band-pass filters (Butterworth, run forwards and backwards so nothing shifts), and resampling onto evenly spaced X. Unevenly spaced data are interpolated first, and the result says so.

heading: Changelog › 0.2.17 — 2026-10-28
text: Changelog › 0.2.17 — 2026-10-28. Nested data: subgroups within groups, the nested t-test and the nested one-way ANOVA. - File › New Table › Nested: for measurements that come in subgroups, such as specimens from batches or cells from animals. Each group is a data set; its sub-columns are its subgroups, with the replicates down the rows. - The graph shows each group's subgroups side by side as small columns of dots with their means, and the group mean with an error bar across the subgroup means (Format Graph › Error bars). - A new sample on the Home page, Batches: specimens from three batches of each of three suppliers. Nested t-test and ANOVA - Analyze › Compare Groups › Nested (or Significance on a nested graph): tests the groups against the spread between subgroups, because replicates from one subgroup are not independent. Two groups give the nested t-test, more give the nested one-way ANOVA. - The full table (between groups, between subgroups within groups, residual), each group's subgroup means, and the variance components from a mixed model: how much of the variation lies between subgroups (intraclass correlation).

heading: Changelog › 0.2.16 — 2026-10-28
text: Changelog › 0.2.16 — 2026-10-28. Survival: time-to-event tables, Kaplan-Meier curves, the log-rank test and hazard ratios. - File › New Table › Survival: one row per subject (a patient, a specimen, a component). Enter the time in X and, in that subject's group column, 1 if the event happened (death, failure) or 0 if it was censored (still going when the study ended, or lost). - A new sample on the Home page, Time to failure: bare and coated steel specimens in a salt-spray test stopped at 1000 hours. - Analyze › More › Survival: the Kaplan-Meier survival of each group, its median survival with a 95% confidence interval, and the full survival table (at risk, events, survival, standard error and 95% CI at each time). - With two or more groups: the log-rank test of whether the curves differ, and hazard ratios against the first group with their 95% CIs (Cox model). Checked against R (survfit, survdiff, coxph). - A survival table's graph draws a staircase per group from 100%, with a tick at each censored subject. Format Graph › Confidence band shades each curve's 95% CI. Hovering shows the survival and the number still at risk.

heading: Changelog › 0.2.15 — 2026-10-28
text: Changelog › 0.2.15 — 2026-10-28. Patterns in many variables: principal component analysis and clustering. - Analyze › More › PCA: finds the few directions that carry most of the variation in many variables. You get each component's eigenvalue and share of the variance, the loadings (which variables make up each component), the scores of every row, how many components are worth keeping, a scree plot and a biplot (rows as points, variables as arrows). - Each variable is scaled to SD 1 by default, so units do not matter; untick it to keep the original scales. Checked against R (prcomp). - Analyze › More › Clusters: groups similar rows. Hierarchical clustering (Ward's, average or complete linkage) with a dendrogram, or k-means (the best of ten starts). You choose the number of clusters and get each cluster's size and means, the cluster of every row, the mean silhouette (how distinct the clusters are) and a picture of the clusters on the first two components. Results become tables - New table from result turns the PC scores, or the data with each row's cluster number, into a table of many variables to graph or analyse further.

heading: Changelog › 0.2.14 — 2026-10-28
text: Changelog › 0.2.14 — 2026-10-28. Many variables: a table with one row per sample, and multiple, logistic and Poisson regression. - File › New Table › Many variables: one row per sample (name the rows), one column per measured property. Its graph puts the first variable on X and the others on Y; every XY analysis (linear regression, curve fits…) works on it the same way. - A new sample on the Home page, Many variables: the hardness of 24 steels from their carbon content and tempering temperature. - Analyze › Regression › Multiple: predict one variable (the outcome) from several others at once. Choose the model: - Linear for a measurement: each predictor's effect with its standard error, P value and 95% CI; R², adjusted R², the F test, AIC, and how much the predictors overlap (VIF). - Logistic for an outcome of 0 or 1 (fail or pass): odds ratios with their 95% CIs, the likelihood ratio test, pseudo R² and how many rows the model classifies correctly. - Poisson for counts: rate ratios, and a check for counts that vary more than the model expects. - Rows with a missing value are left out and counted. Plots of predicted against actual values and of the residuals. Checked against R (lm and glm). How to cite

heading: Changelog › 0.2.13 — 2026-10-28
text: Changelog › 0.2.13 — 2026-10-28. Security: updated the library that unpacks the Python engine. - The library that unpacks the built-in Python engine on the first start (zip) moves from version 2 to 9.1.3, which fixes three reported problems with symbolic links and file permissions (RUSTSEC-2026-0367, 0368 and 0369). Datum Plot only ever unpacks its own bundled file and did not use the affected function, so the risk was low, but it is now gone. - Every change is now checked for security advisories, licences and where libraries come from (cargo deny), as in the other Datum apps. - Multiple variables and regression move to 0.2.14, and the releases after them one number up (Help › Roadmap).

heading: Changelog › 0.2.12 — 2026-10-28
text: Changelog › 0.2.12 — 2026-10-28. Multi-panel figures: lined-up axes, stacked panels sharing one X axis, and insets. - On a layout, graphs in the same column line up their plot frames left and right, and graphs in the same row top and bottom, even when their Y numbers or titles differ in width (Arrange › Line Up the Axes; on by default). - Arrange › Stack, sharing the X axis: the graphs in one column with no gaps; only the bottom one keeps its X axis title and numbers. Any panel can drop them (right-click › Hide X Axis Title and Numbers). - Right-click a graph panel › Add an Inset Here: a small graph on a white card in its top-right corner, with smaller text and no panel letter. Move and resize it like any panel; any panel can be made an inset. - Bring to Front puts a panel over the others.

heading: Changelog › 0.2.11 — 2026-10-27
text: Changelog › 0.2.11 — 2026-10-27. Page layouts: several graphs on one page with panel letters, at a journal's size, exported as one file. - New Layout (Layout tab, or ＋ beside Layouts in the navigator) starts with up to four of the project's graphs, two per row; right-click a graph › New Layout with This Graph for one. - Drag a panel to move it and its corner to resize it (whole millimetres); Delete removes it; double-click opens the graph. ＋ Graph and ＋ Text add more (a caption, a label). - Arrange puts the graphs in one to four columns; Panel Letters: A, a, (a) or none. - The graphs stay linked: change the data and the layout updates. - Journal Figure sets the page to a column width (85, 114, 174 or 183 mm) or a page (A4, Letter, a 16:9 slide); or type the size. - Export Layout: PDF, SVG or EPS (vector, text stays text) or PNG and TIFF at 300–1200 dpi, at the page's real size. TIFF for journals - TIFF for Journals: CMYK, LZW-compressed, 600 dpi. Single graphs can be exported as CMYK TIFF too (Export › TIFF › CMYK).

heading: Changelog › 0.2.10 — 2026-10-27
text: Changelog › 0.2.10 — 2026-10-27. Your requests: new tables open at once, data sets are easy to remove, Significance lets you pick the test, and gaps work on the X axis too. New tables open at once - File › New Table (choose a kind, Create) now closes the File page and shows the new table, instead of staying on the Home page. Remove data sets - Data › Remove Data Set: tick the data sets (columns) to delete. Also on the right-click menu of the table (Delete Data Set) and as a small × on each data set's heading. Undo brings them back. Choose the test for significance stars - Graph › Significance now offers t-test, one-way ANOVA or a nonparametric test, with only the groups that hold values ticked. A column table with two filled groups and empty ones can now use a t-test. - Empty data sets are left out of t-tests, ANOVA, nonparametric tests and other comparisons (the checks say so) instead of stopping them. Gaps in axes - Axis breaks now work on the X axis as well as the Y axis (Format Graph › X Axis or Y Axis › Axis break), and are easier to find: Axis Break on the Graph tab and on the graph's right-click menu.

heading: Changelog › 0.2.9 — 2026-10-27
text: Changelog › 0.2.9 — 2026-10-27. Work directly on the graph: move notes, zoom and pan, exclude points. Select, drag and edit - Click a note to select it, drag it to move it, press Delete to remove it, double-click it to edit its text. Zoom and pan - Format › Zoom and Pan (or right-click the graph): Zoom to a Box (drag around the part you want), Pan (drag the graph until Esc), Zoom Out, Reset Axes. The ranges are saved with the graph, so exports show the same view. Exclude from the graph - Right-click a point: Exclude it (its replicates at that X stay in the table in blue italics, and graphs and analyses leave them out), or format its data set.

heading: Changelog › 0.2.8 — 2026-10-27
text: Changelog › 0.2.8 — 2026-10-27. Notes on graphs: text, arrows, lines and boxes. - Format › Annotate (or Graph › Annotation): Text — click where it goes and type it; Arrow, Line and Box — drag on the graph. An arrow can carry a label at its start, a box a title. - Format Graph › Notes lists every note: change its text, position, colour, size or boldness, or delete it. - Notes sit in the units of the axes, so they stay on their data when the graph is resized, zoomed or exported, and they never change the axis ranges. Copy Look leaves each graph's notes alone.

heading: Changelog › 0.2.7 — 2026-10-27
text: Changelog › 0.2.7 — 2026-10-27. Axis breaks and a second Y axis. Second Y axis - Tick Right Y for a data set (Format Graph › Data Sets, or Format › Second Y Axis): it is drawn against its own axis on the right, with its own title, scale, range and ticks (Format Graph › Right Y Axis). Fitted curves follow their data set's axis; hovering shows the values. - Format Graph › Y Axis › Axis break: leave out a stretch of the Y axis (for example 12 to 95) when one data set sits far above the others. The graph splits into a short top panel and a tall bottom one, with break marks.

heading: Changelog › 0.2.6 — 2026-10-27
text: Changelog › 0.2.6 — 2026-10-27. Do two methods agree, and how good is a test: Bland-Altman and ROC curves. - Analyze › Bland-Altman: two methods measured on the same items (one row each). Gives the bias and the 95% limits of agreement with their confidence intervals, a check for proportional bias, and the Bland-Altman plot. Differences can be plain, as % of the mean, or ratios. - Analyze › ROC Curve: the values of a test in controls and in cases. Gives the area under the curve with its 95% CI and P value, the best cut-off (Youden) with its sensitivity and specificity, every cut-off in a table, and the ROC curve. - Bland-Altman and ROC plots in the results; New table from result turns either into a data table to graph and style. - One-way ANOVA now shows a forest plot of the differences between groups with their 95% CIs.

heading: Changelog › 0.2.5 — 2026-10-27
text: Changelog › 0.2.5 — 2026-10-27. Parts of a whole: pie and donut charts, and each part as a percentage. Parts of whole - File › New Table › Parts of whole: the parts in the rows (such as phases or elements), one whole per data set (such as two heat treatments). - Graphs: pie, donut, or bars stacked to 100%, one per data set, with the percentages on them (Graph › Column Graph). - Analyze › Fractions: each part as a percentage of its whole; when the values are counts, with 95% confidence intervals (Wilson). - A new sample: Phase fractions (point counts of annealed and quenched steel).

heading: Changelog › 0.2.4 — 2026-10-27
text: Changelog › 0.2.4 — 2026-10-27. Counts: contingency tables with the chi-square and Fisher's exact tests. - File › New Table › Contingency: counts of outcomes (data sets, such as passed and failed) in each group (rows, such as two processes). - Graphs as bars, stacked bars or stacked to 100% (Graph › Column Graph). Tests on counts - Analyze › Contingency: the chi-square test (with Yates' correction if you want it), Cramér's V, observed and expected counts, and row percentages. A check warns when expected counts are too small. - For 2 × 2 tables: Fisher's exact test, the relative risk and odds ratio with 95% CIs, and the difference of the proportions; for a diagnostic test also the sensitivity, specificity and predictive values. Checked against R. - A new sample: Pass or fail (two coating processes).

heading: Changelog › 0.2.3 — 2026-10-27
text: Changelog › 0.2.3 — 2026-10-27. Two factors at once: grouped tables, two-way ANOVA and grouped graphs. - File › New Table › Grouped: one factor in the rows (named by the row titles, such as alloys), the other in the data sets (such as heat treatments), with replicates side by side. - Analyze › Two-way ANOVA: the effect of each factor and their interaction, with SS, DF, MS, F, P and the % of total variation (Type III sums of squares, so unequal numbers of replicates are fine). Checked against R. - Partial η² for each effect, the cell means, and checks of equal SDs and normal residuals. - Comparisons within each row (or within each data set) with Šidák, Holm-Šidák, Bonferroni or no correction, drawn as stars over the bars. - Grouped bars, stacked bars, grouped dots, lines (an interaction plot) and a heat map of the means (Graph › Column Graph). - A new sample: Two factors (three alloys, as received and aged). - Results checks now always show their ✓ or ⚠ mark. - The roadmap is now in small steps: one or two features per release, 0.2.4 to 0.2.24, then 1.0 (Help › Roadmap).

heading: Changelog › 0.2.2 — 2026-10-25
text: Changelog › 0.2.2 — 2026-10-25. A big update: comparing groups, materials testing, data tools, graph styles and exporting everything at once (28 features). - Column tables (New Table › Column): one group per column, values down the rows, or entered as mean, SD and N. - Column graphs: scatter dots (bee swarm) with mean and error bars, bars, box and whiskers, violins, mean ± error, and before–after lines (Graph › Column Graph). - t-tests: unpaired (Welch or Student), paired, ratio paired and one-sample, with the difference and its 95% CI. Works from entered means, SDs and Ns too. - One-way ANOVA: ordinary, Welch, Brown-Forsythe and repeated measures (Geisser-Greenhouse), with multiple comparisons (Tukey, Dunnett, Holm-Šidák, Šidák, Bonferroni, Fisher LSD) and a test for linear trend. - Nonparametric tests: Mann-Whitney, Wilcoxon, Kolmogorov-Smirnov, Kruskal-Wallis with Dunn's test, Friedman. - Effect sizes: Cohen's d and Hedges' g with 95% CIs; η² and ω² for ANOVA. - Significance brackets: stars (or P values) over the groups, kept up to date from the analysis (Graph › Significance). - Correlation (Pearson with 95% CI, Spearman, Kendall, correlation matrix) and power and sample size (t-tests, ANOVA, proportions). - Tensile test: Young's modulus, 0.2% offset yield, UTS, strain at UTS, elongation at break and toughness for every specimen, with mean ± SD; the offset line is drawn on the graph.

heading: Changelog › 0.2.2 — 2026-10-25
text: Changelog › 0.2.2 — 2026-10-25. - Weibull analysis: Weibull modulus and characteristic strength by maximum likelihood (with 95% CIs) or regression, the Weibull plot, and strengths at 1% and 10% failure probability. - Global fit: share parameters across data sets and test whether they differ (extra sum-of-squares F test). - Compare two models for each data set (F test and AICc, with the probability each is right). - Area under the curve with peaks above a baseline (zero, a value, or a straight line from the first to the last point), shaded on the graph. - Smoothing (Savitzky-Golay, LOWESS, moving average), derivatives and cumulative integrals. - Transform: log, ln, 1/X, square root, powers, °C ↔ K, scale or shift, subtract a baseline, normalise to 0–100%, replicates to mean, SD and N. - New table from result: transforms, histograms and smoothed curves become data tables you can graph and analyse. - Sort, Find (Ctrl+F), Exclude rows by a rule, and Check Data (missing X, missing N, typing mistakes, values a log axis cannot show). - Frequency distributions: histograms with a normal curve, cumulative distributions and QQ plots. Graphs and export - Styles: open axes, framed box, Nature, Science, ACS, IEEE, presentation and greyscale; save your own.

heading: Changelog › 0.2.2 — 2026-10-25
text: Changelog › 0.2.2 — 2026-10-25. - Colour schemes: Okabe-Ito, Tol bright and muted, classic, viridis, cividis, magma, greyscale or your own colours, each previewed as people with colour-blindness see it. - Copy Look gives other graphs a graph's fonts, sizes, colours and symbols. - Thumbnails of the graphs in the navigator (View › Thumbnails). - Export All Graphs into a folder, and a spreadsheet workbook (.xlsx) with every data table and result (Tools tab). Help and samples - Test Chooser: a few questions open the right analysis. Statistics Guide: which test when, P values, confidence intervals, SD or SEM, common mistakes. - New samples: Compare groups (ANOVA with brackets), Weibull strength, DSC peak (area = enthalpy); the Tensile sample has a tensile analysis. - A second Python engine calculates results, so a long fit never holds up the graphs. - Two factors and counts are next (0.2.3), then interactive graphs and layouts (0.2.4) (Help › Roadmap).

heading: Changelog › 0.2.1 — 2026-10-25
text: Changelog › 0.2.1 — 2026-10-25. A small "?" beside the tools: click it to see what the tool is for and how to use it. Help beside every tool - Every ribbon group with working tools has a small ? next to its name. A click opens a short card: what the tool does, how to use it, and a tip where one helps. - The navigator (Data tables, Results, Graphs), the Info sheet, the data table, the graph, the results sheet, Format Graph, Export, Import, the analysis options and the New Data Table, Analyze Data and Graph Type galleries have one too. - Help › What Is This Tool? lists every card, so you can read about a tool before you look for it. - The data tools and the releases after them each move up one number: data tools are now 0.2.2 (Help › Roadmap).

heading: Changelog › 0.2.0 — 2026-10-25
text: Changelog › 0.2.0 — 2026-10-25. Statistics, linear regression and curve fitting, with results that stay linked to your data and explain themselves. - Analyze… (or the Analyze tab) adds an analysis to the project. It appears under Results in the navigator, linked to its table: change a value and the result updates. - Each results sheet has tabs (Summary, Details, Interpolated) with tables you can copy straight into a spreadsheet or a document, and small plots (residuals, QQ plots, Arrhenius plots). - The panel on the right gives the answer in one sentence, checks of the assumptions (✓, ⚠), methods text and a figure legend to paste into a report, and Python code that reproduces the calculation. - P values are exact (or < 0.0001) with APA stars. - Descriptive statistics: n, mean, SD, SEM, 95% CI, quartiles, median, range, CV, geometric mean and SD, skewness, kurtosis. - Normality tests: Shapiro-Wilk, D'Agostino-Pearson, Anderson-Darling and Kolmogorov-Smirnov (Lilliefors), with QQ plots. - Outliers: Grubbs' test; one click excludes the outliers (they stay in the table in blue). - Slope, intercept, X-intercept, R², adjusted R², Sy.x, ANOVA table, runs test, with standard errors and 95% confidence intervals. - Fit only part of the data (Fit X from … to …), for example the elastic region of a stress–strain curve.

heading: Changelog › 0.2.0 — 2026-10-25
text: Changelog › 0.2.0 — 2026-10-25. - Through the origin, polynomials (order 2–6), Deming regression (errors in X and Y), weighting by 1/Y², every replicate or only the means. - Compare lines: are the slopes (then the intercepts) of the data sets different? - Interpolate: read X for unknown Y values off the line. - A model library: exponential decay and growth, two-phase decay, power law, logarithmic, logistic, Gompertz, dose-response, Gaussian, Lorentzian, Michaelis-Menten, Langmuir, Freundlich, Arrhenius and Avrami. - Your own equation, such as Y = A*exp(-k*X) + C, with starting values and fixed parameters. - Best-fit values with standard errors and 95% CIs, R², AICc, parameter correlations, residuals, convergence checks. - Rates at several temperatures (°C or K) give the activation energy (kJ/mol, eV, kcal/mol) and the pre-exponential factor, with confidence intervals and the Arrhenius plot. On the graph - Fits are drawn on the table's graphs with their 95% confidence band (or prediction band) and the equation and R², placed where they do not cover the data. Each result can be shown or hidden per graph. - Tensile test (elastic modulus of two alloys from the elastic region) and Arrhenius (activation energies of two catalysts), each with its analysis ready.

heading: Changelog › 0.1.1 — 2026-10-24
text: Changelog › 0.1.1 — 2026-10-24. Copy Picture works, updates are small, data import, and the whole app laid out: every planned feature has its place and says when it arrives. Small, fast updates - Python and its libraries are now a separate "runtime pack". Update now downloads only Datum Plot itself (a few MB); the runtime is downloaded again only when its libraries change. - The first start after installing unpacks the Python engine once (a short wait, shown in the status bar). Later starts are as fast as before. - The copy of Python that 0.1.0 kept in the program folder is removed. Copy Picture works - Copy Picture (and Ctrl+C on a graph) now puts the graph on the Windows clipboard as a picture, so it pastes into documents, slides and email. Paste Special and the Print page's codes use the Windows clipboard too. - File › Import, Data › Import or Home › Import data: CSV, TSV, TXT and spreadsheet (.xlsx) files. - A preview shows the file. Choose the sheet, whether the first row holds titles, the X column, and how many replicates make one data set (guessed from the titles, such as "Sample 1, , Sample 2, ,"). - Semicolon files with decimal commas (1,5) are read correctly. Everything laid out

heading: Changelog › 0.1.1 — 2026-10-24
text: Changelog › 0.1.1 — 2026-10-24. - Help › Roadmap (also on the File page and Home): all 99 features (ready and planned), what each does, the Python library behind it and the release it arrives in. Search it or filter by release. - Planned commands already sit in the ribbon, dimmed with an amber dot. Clicking one tells you what it will do and when. - New ribbon tabs: Layout (layouts, journal figures, posters) and Tools (Python console, your own analyses, batch processing, slide and document export, Restart Engine). - Analyze… opens a gallery of every analysis by family: statistics, regression and fitting, comparing groups, relationships, survival, signals and spectra, planning. - New Table opens a gallery of every kind of data table; Graph Type a gallery of every kind of graph. - If the Python engine ever takes longer than a minute, it is restarted instead of freezing the app. Tools › Restart Engine does it by hand. What comes next - 0.2: statistics and regression: descriptive statistics, normality, outliers, linear and polynomial regression, nonlinear curve fitting with a model library, interpolation, results sheets with explanations.

heading: Changelog › 0.1.0 — 2026-10-24
text: Changelog › 0.1.0 — 2026-10-24. The first version of Datum Plot: the application, automatic updates, an XY data table and publication-quality graphs drawn by a built-in Python engine. Install and update - A Windows installer for your user account, with no administrator rights needed. It brings its own Python with numpy, SciPy and matplotlib, so there is nothing else to install. - The Home page shows your version and checks GitHub for new releases. Update now downloads the new version, checks its SHA-256 checksum, installs it and restarts. - An Update available badge appears in the title bar when a new version is out. Beta versions can be turned on in Options. - A project holds an Info sheet, data tables and graphs, listed in the navigator next to the sidebar (Info, Data, Results, Graphs, Layouts). - Save and open .dplot files (Ctrl+S, Ctrl+O). Double-clicking a .dplot file opens it. Recent projects are on the Home page. - Undo and redo (Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+Y), up to 200 steps. A recovery copy is kept while you work, and Datum Plot asks before closing with unsaved changes. - Samples on the Home page: a growth curve, a standard curve (entered as mean, SD and N) and a dose-response experiment on a log axis. XY data table

heading: Changelog › 0.1.0 — 2026-10-24
text: Changelog › 0.1.0 — 2026-10-24. - An X column, then data sets A, B, C… Each data set has replicate columns (Y1, Y2, …), or takes a mean with its SD or SEM and N. - Titles and units for X and Y become the axis titles. Row titles for samples or animals. - Works like a spreadsheet: select ranges with the mouse, Shift and Ctrl; copy and paste with spreadsheets (a first row of headings becomes the titles, and the table grows to fit); fill handle with series; Paste Special; bold, italic, colours and alignment. - Exclude a value with Ctrl+E: it stays in the table, shown in blue and struck through, and graphs leave it out. - Sum, Average and Count of the selected cells above the grid. - Every table comes with a graph; add more with New Graph. - Means with error bars (SD, SEM, 95% confidence interval or range, above, below or both), or every replicate. Points can be joined by lines. - Linear or logarithmic axes, automatic or fixed ranges, tick spacing, minor ticks and gridlines. - Open axes with outward ticks or a framed box, Okabe-Ito colours that people with colour-blindness can tell apart, eight symbols, a legend, and the graph's size in millimetres with journal presets (single, 1.5 and double column).

heading: Changelog › 0.1.0 — 2026-10-24
text: Changelog › 0.1.0 — 2026-10-24. - Format Graph opens beside the graph and every change shows at once. Double-click an axis, the legend or the data to open the right page. - Hover over a point to see its mean, n, SD and SEM; elsewhere the crosshair shows the X and Y values. Export and print - Export as PNG or TIFF at 150 to 1200 dpi, or as SVG, PDF or EPS with the text kept as text (editable in drawing programs). Transparent backgrounds too. - Copy a graph (Ctrl+C on the graph) and paste it into a document, a slide or an email. - File › Print with a live preview: the graph at its real size or fitted to the page, a caption saying what the points show, headers and footers with your logo, page numbers and Info fields. Choose "Save as PDF" to make a PDF. Data tables and the Info sheet print too. Known limits in 0.1 - No analyses yet: column statistics arrive in 0.1.1, t-tests, ANOVA and curve fitting in 0.2.0. The Analyze tab says what comes when. - Only XY tables. Column, grouped, contingency and survival tables come later. - No CSV or spreadsheet import yet: copy the cells in a spreadsheet and paste them into a table. - No page layouts with several graphs yet (0.3).

heading: Datum Plot: notes for Claude
text: Datum Plot: notes for Claude. Read docs/MEMORY.md first. It is the project's memory: architecture, decisions, roadmap, and a log of every session. Datum Plot is the second app of the Datum family. Follow docs/FAMILY.md in Edgar-Mendonca/Datum-Plan exactly (add that repo read-only); Datum Plan's code is the reference implementation: copy from it rather than reinventing anything. At the end of every session that changes anything, update docs/MEMORY.md: - tick the roadmap - add a session-log entry - record any new decisions - refresh the architecture section if files moved - Rust and Tauri 2 for the shell and the project engine, SolidJS for the window, Python (numpy, SciPy, matplotlib) inside the app for every calculation and graph (the user's decision; it overrides FAMILY §2 for Datum Plot). Small, efficient, robust code. Windows first; the installer bundles embeddable CPython 3.13. - Ship in consecutive releases (0.2.0, 0.2.1, 0.2.2 … no jumped numbers), always three numbers; every release appears in the in-app updater. Since session 8 the user wants small steps again (one to four features per release, to save tokens and finish quickly); the order is in docs/PLAN-0.2.md §12 and the MEMORY roadmap. Check git fetch before releasing: another session may have shipped the next number. - The family look with the Teal accent (FAMILY §3): a ribbon, Cairn-style sidebar, IBM Plex, square controls, light/dark/auto themes.

heading: Datum Plot: notes for Claude
text: Datum Plot: notes for Claude. - A linked chain (data table → analysis → results → graph → layout) with advanced analysis and graphing. - Keep code compact and match the surrounding style. The project model, edit ops, undo and files belong in crates/core (Rust, unit-tested). Statistics, fitting and drawing belong in py/datum (Python, unit-tested against NIST/R values). Never in the UI. - The UI is SolidJS + Vite in ui/src/*.tsx (built to ui/dist). State lives in ui/src/store.ts; the engine computes all values, the window only shows them. - Big asks get a docs/PLAN-x.y.md with questions first; build after the answers. Report in plain language. - The feature catalogue lives in docs/PLAN-0.2.md (IDs A1–J5; release order in §12) and in the app in ui/src/features.ts (Help › Roadmap; planned commands open their card). When a feature ships: set its release in features.ts to the shipping version (and VERSION_NOW), replace its planned command with the real one, tick it in PLAN-0.2 and the MEMORY roadmap. New ideas get an ID in both. - When py/requirements.txt changes, bump py/runtime.txt so installed apps download the new Python runtime pack. Identity: "Datum Plot", .dplot, com.edgarmendonca.datumplot, REPO = "Edgar-Mendonca/Datum-Plot" in src-tauri/src/update.rs, installer DatumPlot-x.y.z-setup.exe. Checks before pushing: - python -m unittest discover -s py/tests (needs pip install -r py/requirements.txt) - cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings - cargo test --workspace

heading: Datum Plot: notes for Claude
text: Datum Plot: notes for Claude. Releasing: 1. Bump the version in src-tauri/Cargo.toml and crates/core/Cargo.toml. 2. Add a CHANGELOG section (## x.y.z — date, a one-line summary, bold sections in plain language). Update docs/site.json (FAMILY §10: about, steps, highlights, roadmap with Next/Soon/Later/Goal) together with the MEMORY roadmap. Public text (CHANGELOG, README, site.json) never names, compares with or claims to copy a commercial product (FAMILY §13); name file formats by extension. Since 0.3.3 (the user's rule) the window and the guide do the same: no other company's product names anywhere users read them (buttons, help cards, toasts, guide); say Workbook, Slides, Document, "a spreadsheet", "a document", "slides", and give extensions (.xlsx/.ods, .pptx/.odp, .docx/.odt). A UI test checks the ribbon. Bump version and date-released in CITATION.cff. The guide (docs/guide/{en,zh,fr}.md): when a release changes what the window shows, update all three texts (UI names stay in English in bold, with the meaning beside them in zh and fr), then npm run build:ui && cargo run -q -p datum-core --example dump guide > tests_ui/guide_fixture.json && NODE_PATH=$(npm root -g) npm run guide to retake the screenshots and rebuild the PDFs (the cover shows the version, so rebuild them for every release). 3. Push the tag vX.Y.Z, or run release.yml with workflow_dispatch when tag pushes are blocked. The workflow creates the tag and publishes one installer (DatumPlot-x.y.z-setup.exe, Python inside) and SHA256SUMS.txt. No

heading: Datum Plot: notes for Claude

heading: Contributing
text: Contributing. Thank you for helping. Datum Plot is MIT-licensed; by contributing you agree your work is shared under the same licence.

heading: Contributing › Layout
text: Contributing › Layout. - crates/core: the project model, edits, undo and files (Rust, unit-tested; src/hardening.rs holds the robustness tests). - py/datum: every calculation, fit and graph (Python with numpy, SciPy and matplotlib; tested against NIST and R values). - src-tauri: the Windows shell (Tauri 2) that joins the two and runs the Python engine. - ui/src: the window (SolidJS + Vite). It only shows what the engines compute.

heading: Contributing › Style
text: Contributing › Style. Small, compact code that matches what is around it. New statistics go in py/datum with a test against a published reference value; new edits go in crates/core as an Op with a test, so they are undoable. Report security problems privately, as SECURITY.md explains.

heading: Datum Plot › What it does
text: Datum Plot › What it does. Datum Plot is part of Datum; see its page: Datum Plot keeps a project as a chain: data tables → analyses → results → graphs → layouts. Everything stays linked, so changing a value redraws its graphs. - Data tables that work like a spreadsheet: XY tables (an X column and data sets with replicates, or a mean with SD or SEM and N) and column tables (one group per column). Paste from a spreadsheet, fill series, exclude a value without deleting it. Worksheets with free columns (X, Y, Y error), units and comments, and column formulas such as log10(A) or (B - mean(B)) / sd(B) that update as the data change. - Publication-quality graphs drawn with matplotlib: means with SD, SEM, 95% CI or range, linear or log axes, colour-blind-safe colours, sizes in millimetres for journal columns. - Export as PNG or TIFF at any dpi, or as SVG, PDF and EPS with editable text; every graph as slides (.pptx) or a report with graphs, results and methods (.docx); posters and slides as page layouts. Copy into documents and slides. Print with headers, footers and captions.

heading: Datum Plot › What it does
text: Datum Plot › What it does. - Import CSV, TXT and .xlsx files, the tables of .pzfx projects, 96- and 384-well plates, and many runs at once. Large data sets (hundreds of thousands of points) stay quick, and a region tool gives the statistics of any part of a curve. - Statistics and regression on the built-in Python engine (numpy, SciPy, statsmodels, lmfit): descriptive statistics, normality, outliers, t-tests, one-way ANOVA with multiple comparisons, nonparametric tests, effect sizes, correlation, power; linear regression (fit ranges, Deming, comparing lines), curve fitting with a model library or your own equation, global fits and model comparison, area under the curve and smoothing; multiple, logistic and Poisson regression, principal components and clustering on tables of many variables; survival analysis (Kaplan-Meier curves, median survival, log-rank test, hazard ratios); nested t-tests and ANOVA for subgroups within groups. Results stay linked to the data, explain themselves and give methods text. - Matrices and 3D: Z values on an X–Y grid as contour maps, heat maps or 3D surfaces; surface fits (plane, quadratic with its maximum or minimum, cubic, 2D Gaussian peak); polar graphs of XY data. - Peaks and signals: find peaks above a straight or polynomial baseline (positions, heights, widths, areas), fit them as Gaussian, Lorentzian or Voigt peaks; Fourier spectra, low-, high- and band-pass filters, resampling.

heading: Datum Plot › What it does
text: Datum Plot › What it does. - Materials testing: tensile tests (modulus, yield, UTS, elongation, toughness), Weibull strength, Arrhenius activation energies, S–N fatigue curves (Basquin, with run-outs), DSC peaks (onset, peak temperature, enthalpy) and TGA steps (onset, mass lost, residue). - Column graphs (dots, bars, box plots, violins) with significance stars, journal styles and colour-blind-safe schemes. Export every graph at once, or the whole project to a spreadsheet (.xlsx). More arrives in releases: see the roadmap. Everything stays on your computer. The only network call is the update check to GitHub.

heading: Datum Plot › Install
text: Datum Plot › Install. Download DatumPlot-x.y.z-setup.exe from Releases and run it. It installs for your user account, with its own Python, and updates itself from the Home page.

heading: Datum Plot › The Python console
text: Datum Plot › The Python console. Tools › Python Console runs your own Python on the project's data, inside the app (nothing else to install): 1. Write code in the box at the top. Your tables are ready as pandas DataFrames: tables lists them, table(0) is the first, tables['Name'] one by its name. Columns are named after the data sets (replicates as Control 1, Control 2), X first. 2. Run it with ▶ Run or Ctrl+Enter. What you print, the value of the last line and any plt figure appear underneath; an error names the line. 3. Keep going: variables last between runs (Reset clears them). np, pd, stats (scipy.stats), scipy and plt are ready. 4. Put results back: new_table('Name', data) adds a table to the project; result('Analysis name') gives an analysis's numbers. 5. Save code you reuse with Save As My Analysis, and run it again from Tools › My Analyses. The ⓘ How to use button in the console and the ? beside it in the ribbon show the same guide. Code runs only when you press Run; projects never contain code, so opening someone else's project never runs anything.

heading: Datum Plot › How to cite
text: Datum Plot › How to cite. If Datum Plot helped your work, please cite it with the version you used (File › Updates shows it): Mendonca, E. (2026). *Datum Plot* (Version 0.3.19) [Computer software]. GitHub's Cite this repository button (from CITATION.cff) gives the same in APA and BibTeX. Every result's methods text already names Datum Plot and the Python library behind the calculation (for example SciPy or statsmodels); cite those too if your journal asks for it.

heading: Datum Plot: project memory › 1. Architecture
text: Datum Plot: project memory › 1. Architecture. - The window never calculates. Every edit is an Op that the Rust core applies to a copy, normalises and keeps only if it changed something (undo/redo of whole projects, 200 steps). Statistics and drawing are done in Python. - Live chain: graphs store only settings and their table's id; the shell sends {table, graph settings} to Python on every render (cached by request in py.rs), so editing a value redraws its graphs. .dplot stores data and settings, never results. - Graphs: matplotlib draws the SVG the window shows (svg.fonttype = none, so text stays text) and every export. Python returns the plot area, axis limits, log flags, legend box and the points so the window can show values under the mouse and open the right Format Graph page on a double-click. Print uses the same SVG. - JSON keys are camelCase everywhere (Rust serde(rename_all = "camelCase"), TypeScript, Python). - Every statistic has a unit test against a value from R (later NIST StRD for regressions).

heading: Datum Plot: project memory › 1. Architecture › How we work (from Datum Plan, FAMILY §11)
text: Datum Plot: project memory › 1. Architecture › How we work (from Datum Plan, FAMILY §11). 1. The user reviews the last release in the app and sends screenshots with bugs and wishes. 2. Diagnose first. Reproduce the problem in the test harness or the real app before changing code. Small fixes go straight to a release. 3. Bigger asks get a plan file (docs/PLAN-x.y.md): feedback, diagnosis, proposal, size, questions. Logged here and pushed. Build only after the user answers. 4. Build in small steps: the model and its op in crates/core (Rust test), the numbers or drawing in py/datum (Python test against R/NIST values), then the UI. Compact code in the surrounding style. 5. heading: Datum Plot 0.1: brainstorm, comparison and release plan
text: Datum Plot 0.1: brainstorm, comparison and release plan. Status: answered and built as 0.1.0. The user approved the plan, icon and colours, asked to see the app before answering the detailed questions, and decided that Python is built in (see §9, which replaces the engine parts of §3). Goal: a small, fast Windows app for scientific graphs, statistics and curve fitting. It joins a guided, "pick the right test and get a publication graph" way of working with an open workbook, many graph types and advanced analysis. It is the second app in the Datum family, so it looks, feels and ships like Datum Plan (FAMILY.md): teal accent, .dplot files, com.edgarmendonca.datumplot, releases and updates from Edgar-Mendonca/Datum-Plot. This file follows the family pattern: two ways of working → what we build → proposal → release plan → size → questions.

text: Datum Plot 0.1: brainstorm, comparison and release plan › 1. Two ways of working. Guided analysis ; Open workbook ; Who needs it ; Biologists, pharmacologists, medical researchers. People who need the right test and a clean graph, not programming. ; Physicists, chemists, engineers, materials science. People with large instrument data, spectra and many curves. ; Core idea ; A project is a chain: data table → analysis → results → graph → layout. The table *type* decides which analyses and graphs make sense. Everything stays linked: edit a value and every result and graph updates. ; A project is a folder of workbooks (free spreadsheets with column roles X, Y, Z, error), matrices, graphs and notes. You pick columns and plot or analyse anything. Analyses can recalculate automatically or on request. ; Strength ; Guidance: the table type, the "which test?" dialogs, analysis checklists, plain-language results ("P < 0.05, significant"), asterisk brackets. A huge built-in curve library with dose-response, binding and kinetics. ; Breadth: 100+ graph types (3D, contour, polar, ternary, waterfall, multi-panel), layers, insets, double Y, peak analysis, signal processing, batch processing, scripting. ; Weakness ; Limited graph types, rigid tables, little signal or spectral analysis, no scripting. ; Steep learning curve, dense dialogs, statistics are less guided. ; Files ; .pzfx (XML, open, documented enough to import). ; Closed binary projects. ;

heading: Datum Plot 0.1: brainstorm, comparison and release plan › 3. Architecture (same stack as Datum Plan)
text: Datum Plot 0.1: brainstorm, comparison and release plan › 3. Architecture (same stack as Datum Plan). Rules (as in Plan): - The window never computes a statistic, a tick or an error bar. Every edit is an Op; the engine applies it, recomputes what depends on it and returns what the window shows. - Live chain: analyses and graphs store only their *settings* and the id of their input. Results are computed when asked (cached by revision), so editing a value updates every result and graph. The .dplot file stores data and settings, never stale results. - Graphs: the engine turns a graph's settings + data into a GraphOut scene (axis ranges, ticks and labels, points, error bar segments, lines, legend entries, all in data and mm units). The window draws it as SVG, so screen, print, SVG/PNG export and later PDF/EMF all come from one scene. Chart.js stays for the small Home/preview charts only, if at all (question 8.4). - Numbers we can trust: every statistic is checked in a unit test against a published value: NIST StRD reference datasets (Norris, Longley for linear regression; Misra1a, Thurber, MGH09, Eckerle4 for nonlinear; ANOVA sets SiRstv, AtmWtAg), plus worked examples from R output. A "validation" page in the docs lists them.

heading: Datum Plot 0.1: brainstorm, comparison and release plan › 3. Architecture (same stack as Datum Plan)
text: Datum Plot 0.1: brainstorm, comparison and release plan › 3. Architecture (same stack as Datum Plan). - Libraries: statrs (MIT, pure Rust) for distributions (t, F, χ², normal, gamma, beta) so P values are correct; our own small Levenberg-Marquardt and QR (parameters are few, a few hundred lines) rather than nalgebra; GridCraft (pinned, as in Plan) for column formulas later. No Python. File .dplot: JSON (format 1), with a format number and migration as in Plan. Later it can be zipped if graphs embed pictures. Window layout (FAMILY §6, adapted): - Title bar, quick access, Tell Me (Ctrl+K), Theme, as in Plan. - Ribbon tabs (proposal): File · Data (clipboard, font, insert rows/columns, exclude, sort, transform) · Analyze (Analyze…, column statistics, quick tests, fit a curve) · Graph (new graph, graph type gallery, change data sets) · Format (Graph Tools, contextual: axes, data sets, colours, size, copy look) · Layout · View · Help. - Left sidebar: the family icon rail with Info first (Plan's Setup), then Data, Results, Graphs, Layouts. Next to it a narrow navigator list with every item of that kind, its family links (data → its results → its graphs), and right-click New/Duplicate/Rename/Delete. - Status bar: Ready, selection N/Mean/SD/Sum (Plot's version of Plan's Sum/Average/Count), item type, zoom.

heading: Datum Plot 0.1: brainstorm, comparison and release plan › 4. Ideas of our own
text: Datum Plot 0.1: brainstorm, comparison and release plan › 4. Ideas of our own. 1. Explain panel for every result: what the test asked, the answer in one sentence ("The means differ, P = 0.003"), the assumptions it checked (normality, equal variance, pairing) with ✓/⚠, and what to try if one failed. The checklists sit next to the numbers. 2. Test chooser: three or four questions (how many groups? paired? normal? what do you want to know?) that open the right analysis with the right options. Starts from the table type. 3. Methods text: every analysis writes a ready-to-paste sentence for a paper's methods and figure legend ("Data are mean ± SD, n = 6. Groups were compared by one-way ANOVA with Tukey's multiple comparisons test."), with the software version. 4. Effect sizes and CIs by default (difference of means with 95 % CI, Cohen's d, Hedges' g, η²) and optional estimation plots, so results are more than a P value. 5. Reproducible check: "Show as R code" for each analysis, so a reviewer can verify the numbers outside the app. No R needed inside the app; it is just text. 6. Journal presets for graphs: Nature, Science, Cell, ACS, IEEE, a thesis: column width in mm, font, line widths, symbol sizes. One click and the graph fits the column. 7. Colour-blind safe palettes by default (Okabe-Ito, from the family), with a greyscale preview.

heading: Datum Plot 0.1: brainstorm, comparison and release plan › 4. Ideas of our own
text: Datum Plot 0.1: brainstorm, comparison and release plan › 4. Ideas of our own. 8. Units-aware columns: units travel with the data into axis titles, results and the methods text. 9. Data lineage: the navigator shows each table → its analyses → its graphs → the layouts that use them (its "family"), and warns before you delete something a graph needs. 10. Region-of-interest tools on graphs: drag a box on an XY graph to get statistics, area under the curve, a quick fit or peak data for just that region. 11. Sample-size and power calculator, built in. 12. Templates for common experiments on Home: dose-response (IC50/EC50), standard curve with unknowns (ELISA, BCA, qPCR), growth curve, enzyme kinetics, Kaplan-Meier study, two-group comparison. Each opens a filled example with its analysis and graph. 13. Import .pzfx files (open XML): a big help for people bringing existing projects. 14. Instrument and plate import later: plate-reader CSVs (96/384 wells) mapped to tables by a layout of samples, standards and blanks. 15. Pairs with Datum Plan: the same file habits, Options, updater and printing, so a user of one app knows the other.

text: Datum Plot 0.1: brainstorm, comparison and release plan › 5. Release 0.1.0: the first publishable version. Purpose: the updater works from day one, the family shell is in place, and one real workflow works end to end: type or paste XY data → see a publication-style graph → format it → print or export it → save and reopen. - Install and update: NSIS per-user installer DatumPlot-0.1.0-setup.exe + SHA256SUMS.txt; update.rs with REPO = "Edgar-Mendonca/Datum-Plot"; badge "Update available"; Home updates card with Check again (spinner and time), What's new (CHANGELOG), GitHub/Releases/Report an Issue; beta channel option. - Shell (copied from Plan, teal accent): title bar with quick access, Tell Me (Ctrl+K), Theme (Auto/Light/Dark); ribbon (File, Data, Graph, Format, View, Help; Analyze shown with "coming in 0.1.1–0.2" empty state); icon rail + navigator; status bar; toasts; dialogs; menus; keyboard shortcuts. - File page: Home (greeting, template tiles, recent files, updates card), New, Open, Save, Save As, Export, Print, Options, Updates. .dplot files, double-click opens, recovery copy, ask before closing with unsaved changes, undo/redo (200 steps). - Info sheet (first in the sidebar): project title, experiment, researcher, date, notes. Its fields can go into page headers and footers. - XY data table: - an X column and data sets A, B, C… (up to 26 in 0.1), each with 1–10 replicate sub-columns, or entered Mean + SD + N / Mean + SEM + N;
