text: Datum Plot 0.1: brainstorm, comparison and release plan › 5. Release 0.1.0: the first publishable version. - column titles and units; row titles; table title; - family grid engine: ranges, Ctrl/Shift, whole rows/columns, TSV paste from a spreadsheet, fill handle with series, Paste Special, Ctrl+B/I/U, N/Mean/SD/Sum in the status bar; - exclude/include values (blue italic, skipped by the graph); - insert/delete rows and data sets. - XY graph (created with the table; more than one graph per table allowed): - each data set as points (8 symbol shapes, Okabe-Ito colours), optional connecting line, mean of replicates or every replicate; - error bars: SD, SEM, 95 % CI, range; both directions or one; cap width; - axes: linear or log10, auto or fixed range, major ticks with "nice" steps, minor ticks, title (with units from the table), number format; frame or open (L-shaped) axes; - legend (on/off, position), graph title; - size in mm (default 80 × 60, journal single column), one font (IBM Plex Sans, Arial, Helvetica, Times) and size; - Format Graph dialog (Data sets · Axes · Graph) and double-click on an axis, a data set or the legend to open its page; - zoom on screen; crosshair tooltip with the values.

heading: Datum Plot 0.1: brainstorm, comparison and release plan › 5. Release 0.1.0: the first publishable version
text: Datum Plot 0.1: brainstorm, comparison and release plan › 5. Release 0.1.0: the first publishable version. - Export and print: SVG and PNG (150/300/600 dpi, transparent or white) from File › Export or right-click; copy the graph to the clipboard as PNG; File › Print with live preview (one graph per page, size as set or fit, header/footer codes and logos from Plan's print.tsx), "Save as PDF" through the WebView dialog. - Templates on Home: Blank XY table, "Growth curve" (time course, 3 replicates), "Calibration curve" (standards with SD), "Dose-response" (log X; data only, the fit comes in 0.2.0). - Options: General (theme, number format, decimal places), Start-up and saving (open last, recovery minutes), New tables (replicates, error bar type), Graphs (size, font, symbol size, export DPI), Printing and branding (paper, company, logo), Updates (beta). - Help tab: Getting Started (written for people coming from other graphing and statistics apps), Glossary (SD vs SEM vs CI, replicate, data set, log axis…), Shortcuts, Tell Me, GitHub links. - Engine: crates/core with model, ops + undo, .dplot read/write, descriptive statistics for error bars (mean, SD, SEM, CI with the t distribution, range), plot.rs (scales, nice ticks, log ticks, error bar geometry). Unit tests (≈15) including CI values against R.

heading: Datum Plot 0.1: brainstorm, comparison and release plan › 5. Release 0.1.0: the first publishable version
text: Datum Plot 0.1: brainstorm, comparison and release plan › 5. Release 0.1.0: the first publishable version. - Quality: CI (clippy -D warnings, cargo test, npm run check:ui, Playwright UI tests with a fixture from cargo run -p datum-core --example dump), release workflow, checked in the real app under Xvfb with screenshots. - Repo: README per FAMILY §5 with badges and a screenshot, CHANGELOG ## 0.1.0, NOTICE, MIT licence, logo in ui/public/logo.svg and Windows icons from it. Not in 0.1.0 (said plainly in the CHANGELOG's "Known limits"): analyses and results, other table types, curve fitting, layouts, CSV/XLSX import (paste works), PDF/EMF export apart from Print › Save as PDF. Size estimate: about 5,000–6,000 lines. Roughly 60 % is reused from Plan (shell, updater, ribbon, backstage, options, print frame, grid engine, styles, sprite, workflows, test harness); the new parts are the XY model, the grid renderer for sub-columns, plot.rs and the SVG graph with its Format dialog. One working session.

text: Datum Plot 0.1: brainstorm, comparison and release plan › 8. Questions for you. Scope of 0.1.0 1. Is §5 the right first version (XY table + XY graph, no analyses)? text: Datum Plot 0.1: brainstorm, comparison and release plan › 8. Questions for you. Engine and numbers 8. heading: Datum Plot 0.1: brainstorm, comparison and release plan › 9. Decision after the review: Python inside the app (24 Oct 2026)
text: Datum Plot 0.1: brainstorm, comparison and release plan › 9. Decision after the review: Python inside the app (24 Oct 2026). The user's answer: use Python and its libraries (numpy, SciPy, matplotlib and more) inside Datum Plot. Rust stays the shell that holds everything together and SolidJS stays the window, in the same style as Datum Plan. A 200–300 MB app is acceptable (the Compressor Engineering Suite already ships Python with FEA and CadQuery). Questions 1–14 wait until the user has seen the app. What changes from §3: ; §3 proposal ; Built in 0.1.0 ; Statistics ; statrs + our own Levenberg-Marquardt in Rust ; numpy + SciPy in a Python worker (py/datum/stats.py); curve fitting later with scipy.optimize ; Graphs ; Our own SVG engine fed by a Rust GraphOut scene ; matplotlib draws the SVG the window shows and every export (PNG, TIFF, SVG, PDF, EPS) — one renderer for screen, print and files ; Rust core ; Model, ops, stats, fitting, scales ; Model, edit ops, undo, .dplot, templates, validation (crates/core) — no numerics ; Tests ; NIST/R values in Rust tests ; NIST/R values in Python unittest (py/tests), run in CI ; How it fits together: - One worker process, started when the app starts (so the first graph is quick) and kept running. Requests and answers are single JSON lines on stdin/stdout; a crash restarts it once and the window shows why if Python cannot start.

heading: Datum Plot 0.1: brainstorm, comparison and release plan › 9. Decision after the review: Python inside the app (24 Oct 2026)
text: Datum Plot 0.1: brainstorm, comparison and release plan › 9. Decision after the review: Python inside the app (24 Oct 2026). - The window never calculates. Rust validates and stores every edit; Python computes statistics and draws; the SVG comes back with the plot area, axis limits and legend box so the window can show values under the mouse and open the right page of Format Graph on a double-click. - The shell caches the last renders, so switching between graphs costs nothing when the data did not change. A render takes about 15 ms after warm-up. - Bundled runtime: the release workflow puts the official embeddable CPython 3.13 into the installer with py/requirements.txt (numpy, SciPy, matplotlib), removes test suites and precompiles everything. Development builds use the Python on the PATH (or DATUM_PYTHON). - Size (0.1.0): a 55 MB installer; the Python folder is 229 MB installed. Every update downloads the whole installer for now; a later release can ship the Python runtime separately so updates are small again (see MEMORY › next steps).

heading: Datum Plot 0.1: brainstorm, comparison and release plan › 9. Decision after the review: Python inside the app (24 Oct 2026)
text: Datum Plot 0.1: brainstorm, comparison and release plan › 9. Decision after the review: Python inside the app (24 Oct 2026). What Python makes easier in the next releases: scipy.stats for every test in §2.2 (t, Welch, Mann-Whitney, ANOVA via scipy.stats.f_oneway, Tukey via scipy.stats.tukey_hsd, Shapiro-Wilk, Kruskal-Wallis, Fisher, log-rank via scipy.stats.logrank), scipy.optimize.curve_fit/least_squares for nonlinear regression with bounds and weights, scipy.signal for peaks, smoothing and FFT (the signal features of 0.5), and matplotlib for 3D, contour, polar and multi-panel graphs. Candidates to add when needed: statsmodels (mixed models, Cox regression), lifelines (survival), pandas (import).

text: Datum Plot 0.2: statistics and regression — what we build next › 1. Your feedback on 0.1.1 (25 Oct 2026). 1. You updated from inside the app: about 87 MB, quick to install, opened fast. heading: Datum Plot 0.2: statistics and regression — what we build next › 4. How it is built (short)
text: Datum Plot 0.2: statistics and regression — what we build next › 4. How it is built (short). - Rust core: a new item Analysis { id, kind, table, data sets, options } with ops to add, change and delete it (settings only, with undo); graphs get "overlays" (a fitted line from an analysis). - Python: py/datum/analyses/ with one module per family (describe.py, normality.py, outliers.py, linear.py, fit.py + models.py), each returning the same result shape: tables, a one-sentence answer, checks, methods text, Python code, and curves for the graph. A results cache by revision, and a second Python worker for long fits so graphs never wait (I3). - Window: a Results view (tabs + Explain panel), an options dialog per analysis, the Analyze gallery's buttons become real. - Tests: every statistic against R; regression against the NIST StRD sets (Norris, Pontius, Longley; Misra1a, Thurber, MGH09 for nonlinear). - Libraries: statsmodels and lmfit are added to the Python pack (about +45 MB unpacked); py/runtime.txt goes to 2 so it is unpacked once more.

heading: Datum Plot after 0.1.0: the full feature catalogue, Python, fast updates › 2. How a graph is made today (in plain words)
text: Datum Plot after 0.1.0: the full feature catalogue, Python, fast updates › 2. How a graph is made today (in plain words). - matplotlib draws every graph, on screen and in every export (PNG, TIFF, SVG, PDF, EPS). What you see is exactly what you export. - Python runs inside the app: a small Python program (py/worker.py) starts with Datum Plot and waits for requests. Nothing is installed on your PC apart from the app. - Rust keeps the project: tables, graphs, undo, files. It never calculates statistics. - A redraw takes about 15 ms after start-up, which is why typing a value updates the graph almost at once.

heading: Datum Plot after 0.1.0: the full feature catalogue, Python, fast updates › 3. Diagnosis › 3.1 Copy Picture
text: Datum Plot after 0.1.0: the full feature catalogue, Python, fast updates › 3. Diagnosis › 3.1 Copy Picture. graph.tsx uses the browser clipboard (navigator.clipboard.write). On Windows, Tauri 2 serves the window from That is not a "secure" address, so WebView2 switches the clipboard API off and the copy fails (it worked in the Linux test browser, which is why the tests did not catch it). The same problem affects Paste Special's fallback and the header-code copy on the Print page. Fix (0.1.1): Rust puts the picture on the Windows clipboard itself (tauri-plugin-clipboard-manager, image + text), so it no longer depends on the browser. Documents and slides then paste it as a picture. Add an in-app test for the command, and you check it in a document.

heading: Datum Plot after 0.1.0: the full feature catalogue, Python, fast updates › 3. Diagnosis › 3.2 Slow updates
text: Datum Plot after 0.1.0: the full feature catalogue, Python, fast updates › 3. Diagnosis › 3.2 Slow updates. The 0.1.0 installer is 55 MB because 50 MB of it is Python and its libraries, and every update repeats that download even when Python did not change. The app itself (Rust + window + our Python code) is about 4 MB. Fix (0.1.1): ship Python separately ("runtime pack"). ; Today ; Proposed ; First install ; DatumPlot-0.1.0-setup.exe, 55 MB ; DatumPlot-x.y.z-setup.exe with the runtime inside (same as today, about 55–80 MB) ; Update when only Datum Plot changed ; 55 MB ; about 4 MB (DatumPlot-x.y.z-update.exe, app only) ; Update when Python libraries changed (rare: new library, new versions) ; 55 MB ; the small update + DatumPlot-runtime-N.zip once ; - The runtime lives in %LOCALAPPDATA%\com.edgarmendonca.datumplot\runtime\N\ (outside the program folder, so app updates never touch it). N is a runtime number that only changes when py/requirements.txt changes. - Each release publishes runtime.json (number, size, SHA-256). The updater downloads the runtime zip only when the number is new, checks its SHA-256, unpacks it beside the old one, switches, then deletes the old one. If anything fails the old runtime stays. - Our own Python code (py/datum) stays inside the small app update, because it changes with every release. - Update now shows both steps with progress ("Downloading Datum Plot 4 MB… Downloading the Python runtime 62 MB (only this time)…").

heading: Datum Plot after 0.1.0: the full feature catalogue, Python, fast updates › 6. Architecture changes
text: Datum Plot after 0.1.0: the full feature catalogue, Python, fast updates › 6. Architecture changes. - Results become a third kind of item: Analysis { id, kind, input table, data sets, options } in crates/core (Rust stores settings only), computed by py/datum/analyses/*.py and cached by revision. Graphs can draw from a table or from a result (fitted curves, brackets). - Python package layout grows into modules: stats.py, tests_group.py (t-tests, ANOVA, post hoc), fit.py + models.py (lmfit), survival.py, signal.py, io.py (CSV/XLSX/pzfx), graph/ (one module per graph family), explain.py (plain-language text), each with tests against R values. - Element geometry (for E2–E4): matplotlib returns the bounding box of every artist with an id (axis.x.title, set.1.points, legend), so the window can select, drag and edit. - Runtime pack (I1): runtime.json + the updater change in update.rs; py.rs looks for the runtime in the data folder first.

heading: Datum Plot after 0.1.0: the full feature catalogue, Python, fast updates › 8. Ideas that set Datum Plot apart
text: Datum Plot after 0.1.0: the full feature catalogue, Python, fast updates › 8. Ideas that set Datum Plot apart. 1. One click from data to paper: table → analysis chosen by the test chooser → graph with brackets → methods and legend text → layout → PDF/TIFF at journal size. 2. Explain everything: every result says in plain words what it means and whether its assumptions hold. 3. Reproducible: every result can show the Python code that reproduces it; every statistic is validated against R. 4. Python when you want it: a console and your own analyses, without leaving the app or installing anything. 5. Small updates, fast app: a 4 MB update and a graph redraw in ~15 ms.

heading: Plan 0.3.11: dates and times › 2. Proposed releases (small steps)
text: Plan 0.3.11: dates and times › 2. Proposed releases (small steps). 0.3.11 — dates I (what the Plan hand-off needs): - Core: Table.x_format ("", "date", "datetime"), clamped on loading; Op::XFormat (undoable); doc::date_number(s, day_first) for ISO, d/m/y or m/d/y, month names (5-Nov-26, 5 Nov 2026, Nov 5, 2026), times; impossible dates refused; typing and pasting into a date X column use it. - Options: "Dates are written day first / month first" (default from the system's language). - Table: X column heading › Format › Number / Date / Date and time, with a display format (5 Nov 2026, 05-Nov-26, 2026-11-05, 05/11/2026, Nov 2026, with or without the time). - Graphs: date X axis (AutoDateLocator, ConciseDateFormatter); Format Graph › X Axis: tick labels (Auto, Day month, Month year, ISO, Week), min and max typed as dates; hover shows the date; every export keeps the date ticks. - Analyses: fits and regressions on dates report slopes "per day". - Workbook export (.xlsx/.ods): date columns as real dates. - Plan's sample opens with dates in the table and on the axis, no questions asked. 0.3.12 — dates II: - Detection: pasting or importing date-like text into a number X column offers once "Treat as dates?". - Format Graph: major step (days, weeks, months), minor ticks; annotations at a typed date (a vertical line at a date).

heading: Plan 0.3.11: dates and times › 2. Proposed releases (small steps)
text: Plan 0.3.11: dates and times › 2. Proposed releases (small steps). - Column formulas: DATE, TODAY, YEAR, MONTH, DAY, DAYS (differences in days or hours). - Intercepts and fitted values shown as dates where meaningful. Later (as the brief says): date columns among Y values, durations (h:mm), working-day axes. The roadmap then moves by two: wavelets 0.3.13, digitizer 0.3.14, Bayesian tests 0.3.15, Mac and Linux 0.3.16.

heading: tagline
text: tagline. Analyse data and make publication-ready graphs: statistics, regression, curve fitting and page layouts, in one app for Windows.

heading: about
text: about. Datum Plot keeps data, analyses and graphs linked. Type or paste data into a table, choose an analysis, and the results and the graph follow; change a value and everything updates. It covers the statistics most lab and research work needs, from t-tests and ANOVA to regression and curve fitting, explains each result in plain words with ready methods text, and makes figures ready for a journal: multi-panel layouts at journal sizes, exported as PNG, TIFF, SVG, PDF or EPS. Python runs inside the app, with nothing else to install, and a built-in console lets you run your own code on the data.

heading: steps
text: steps. Choose a table for your kind of data and type, paste or import it (CSV, TXT, .xlsx, .pzfx, plate readers, many runs at once). Pick a test or a fit; the results, P values and methods text open on a results sheet linked to the data, and fits are drawn on the graph. Style the graph, lay out the figure and export it at journal size.

heading: highlights
text: highlights. A linked chain: data tables → analyses → results → graphs → layouts. Change a value and every result and graph updates. Data tables for every kind of experiment (XY, groups, two factors, counts, survival, nested, many variables) and worksheets with units and column formulas that update as the data change; dates and times in the X column, drawn on date axes. Import CSV, TXT, .xlsx and .pzfx files, plate readers and many runs at once; large data sets stay quick. Statistics: descriptive, normality, outliers, t-tests, nonparametric tests, one- and two-way ANOVA with multiple comparisons, repeated measures and mixed-effects models, multiple t-tests with false discovery rates and volcano plots, nested t-tests and ANOVA, contingency tables, correlation, power, Bland-Altman, ROC, and survival analysis (Kaplan-Meier, log-rank, hazard ratios); three-way ANOVA, ANCOVA, agreement (Cohen's kappa, McNemar) and bootstrap confidence intervals. Linear regression and curve fitting with a model library or your own equation, global fits and model comparison, smoothing splines; multiple, logistic and Poisson regression, principal components and clustering on tables of many variables. Matrices and 3D: contour maps, heat maps, 3D surfaces and 3D scatter, vector fields, polar, ternary, bubble, radar and waterfall graphs, and surface fits (plane, quadratic, cubic, 2D Gaussian). Peaks and signals: find peaks above a baseline, fit Gaussian, Lorentzian or Voigt peaks, Fourier spectra and filters. Quality: control

heading: highlights
text: highlights. charts (individuals, X̄–R, X̄–S, p) with capability, and two-level factorial designs with their effects. Materials testing: tensile tests, Weibull strength, Arrhenius activation energies, S–N fatigue curves, and DSC/TGA thermal analysis (onsets, enthalpies, mass loss). Publication graphs: error bars (mean or median), axis breaks (XY and column graphs), a second Y axis, annotations, colour-blind-safe colours, multi-panel figures and insets. Page layouts at journal sizes, posters and slides; graphs pasted into documents, slides and workbooks that open again in Datum Plot with a double-click (Windows); export as PNG or TIFF (with CMYK), SVG, PDF or EPS, every graph as slides (.pptx or .odp), or a document with graphs, results and methods (.docx or .odt); tables and results as a workbook (.xlsx or .ods). Interactive graphs: zoom, pan, drag notes, exclude points with a right-click, and the statistics of any region. A Python console inside the app, with your tables as pandas DataFrames and a built-in guide; your own saved analyses, analysis templates, batch processing and notebook export. Safe and sturdy: projects never run code, saves never leave half-written files, damaged files open or explain why, and updates are checked against their checksums. A step-by-step guide with pictures in English, Chinese and French (Help › Guide), blank starts with or without a graph, and over twenty sample projects to learn from, grouped by

heading: Changelog › 0.3.1 — 2026-11-02
text: Changelog › 0.3.1 — 2026-11-02. Wording only: the project's documents and code describe Datum Atlas on its own terms. Nothing changes in how the app works. - The plans, the project memory, the notes for contributors and the code comments now describe Datum Atlas's own goals and features, without naming or comparing with other products. - The README and NOTICE say that product and file-format names are trademarks of their owners, used only to describe file compatibility. - A new automatic test reads every page, ribbon tab, dialog, tooltip and ? card of the window and fails if another product's name appears.

heading: Changelog › 0.3.0 — 2026-11-01
text: Changelog › 0.3.0 — 2026-11-01. Eco and process: an eco audit of a product's whole life, greener substitutes, and process selection with the cost per part against batch size. - Every material now has its end of life: the energy and CO₂ to make it from recycled material, the recycled share of today's supply, its heat of combustion and the CO₂ from burning it, and whether it can be downcycled, burnt for energy or biodegrade. - Energy and CO₂ of primary production for 60 more materials, from open datasets or a labelled estimate. Four stay gaps because no open source gives a fair figure. - Public factors for transport (sea, rail, road, air), vehicles, electricity in eleven countries and regions, and the energy of the main manufacturing processes, each with its source. - Describe a product as parts (material, mass, number, process, chips machined away, recycled content, end of life), how it travels and how it is used, for how many years. - Energy and CO₂ for each life phase (material, manufacture, transport, use, end of life) as ranges, with a bar chart, the largest phase named and what usually helps. A missing value is listed in the notes, never counted as zero.

heading: Changelog › 0.3.0 — 2026-11-01
text: Changelog › 0.3.0 — 2026-11-01. - Up to four design options side by side; copy one to change one thing. A chart of CO₂ against years of use shows where a lighter but energy-hungrier design pays back. - The audit goes into the selection report and to a spreadsheet. - From a datasheet, the ribbon or a part of the audit: materials that pass the same stages, with an index nearly as good, and less CO₂ for the same job, with what you give up (price, strength, temperature). - Five more low-carbon and low-energy indices in the library (52 in all). - 55 processes: casting, moulding, forming, powder, composite and glass forming, machining, cutting, 3D printing, joining and finishing, each with the materials it suits, part mass, section, shapes, tolerance, roughness, economic batch and indicative costs. - Castability, machinability and weldability for every metal and polymer. - Describe the part (material, mass, thinnest section, shape, tolerance, roughness, batch size): the processes that can make it come first, and every other one says why it cannot. - Cost per part against batch size for each process (material with what is wasted, tooling shared over the batch, running cost), with the cheapest process for each batch size.

heading: Changelog › 0.3.0 — 2026-11-01
text: Changelog › 0.3.0 — 2026-11-01. - Which processes suit each shortlisted material, ways to join it to another material, and finishes for what you need (corrosion, wear, decoration…). - The chosen part and its processes go into the selection report. - Home tiles for the eco audit and process selection, Getting Started step 5, new Glossary terms, and a ? card for every new tool.

text: Changelog › 0.2.0 — 2026-10-28. The big update: sturdier files, several selections and weighted ranking, a library of performance indices and your own formulas, compare and a selection report, about 250 materials, and your own databases with spreadsheet import. - A damaged or unusual project, database or spreadsheet gives a clear message and never crashes the app. A damaged “My materials” file is kept aside under a new name, never emptied. - Files are written safely: a save that is cut off leaves the old file whole. - Over a thousand random and broken inputs are tried by the tests on every change, and the build checks the licences of everything the app is made from. - Several selection lines on one chart, and bands: two facing lines with the materials between them. - Draw a shape around the materials you want, besides lines and boxes. - Goals that need two charts, such as stiff and strong, set up both. - Set a line to pass through an index value you type, and nudge the active line with the arrow keys. - Rank by weighted properties instead of one index: each property scaled from worst to best, with your weights. Indices and formulas

heading: Changelog › 0.2.0 — 2026-10-28
text: Changelog › 0.2.0 — 2026-10-28. - 25 design goals and a library of 47 performance indices, each with its function, constraint, objective and free variable. Plot any of them in one click. - Build an index from properties and powers; the chart and the line follow. - Formula axes and your own formula properties, such as σy/ρ: calculated for every material with its range, usable in charts, limits and tables. Gaps stay gaps. - Up to four charts side by side, with the hovered material shown on all of them. - The best materials labelled, and labels placed so they do not overlap, with leader lines; drag a label to move it. - Chart styles: classic, publication and mono (greys, for black-and-white print). Compare and report - Compare up to six materials in a table, with the highest and lowest of each property marked, and in a radar chart. - A selection report: requirements, design goal, stages, charts, shortlist, comparison and the candidates' datasheets with their sources, ready to print or save as PDF. - Results to a spreadsheet (.xlsx) or CSV.

heading: Changelog › 0.2.0 — 2026-10-28
text: Changelog › 0.2.0 — 2026-10-28. - 252 materials (105 metals, 53 polymers, 16 elastomers, 30 ceramics and glasses, 15 composites, 12 foams, 21 natural materials), compiled from open and public sources only: government handbooks, open datasets, university notes, producers' datasheets and typical textbook ranges. The tests refuse any source that is not open or public. - Durability ratings for every material: water, acids, alkalis, sunlight and fire resistance. Fatigue strength and electrical resistivity for the metals. - 73 values now checked against published datasheets (✓). The other values remain drafts. Your own data - Import materials from a spreadsheet or CSV: the app guesses what each column holds, reads ranges and imperial units, and shows the rows before adding them. - Open a colleague's database beside the built-in data; its materials are marked with its name and can be closed again. - Save your own materials as a database to share, a spreadsheet or CSV. - Help › Roadmap shows what each coming release brings. New ? cards for selections, ranking, formulas, indices, compare, report, import and databases, and new terms in the Glossary.

heading: Changelog › 0.1.1 — 2026-10-25
text: Changelog › 0.1.1 — 2026-10-25. Design goals that set up the chart, the line and the limits in one pick; SI or imperial units; bar charts; a Sources page; ? help beside the tools; and the first values checked against published datasheets. - A Goal list above the chart with 22 goals, grouped: minimum mass (stiff or strong tie, beam and panel; column; stiff shaft), minimum cost and minimum carbon (tie, beam, panel), elastic design (spring, elastic hinge), damage tolerance (yield before fracture, leak before break, tough and light), and thermal (precision parts, insulation, heat sinks, thermal shock). - A goal sets the axes, draws the selection line of the right slope through the best materials (the top fifth pass), adds the limits it needs, and ranks the results by its index. Its limits are marked “from the goal” in Stages; change or remove them freely. Your own limits are never touched. “Explore” removes the goal's line and limits. - “Why E½/ρ?” explains each goal: the function, the constraint, the objective, the free variable, and how the index follows. - Setup lists the goals too, and Tell Me (Ctrl+K) finds them. Values and units

heading: Changelog › 0.1.1 — 2026-10-25
text: Changelog › 0.1.1 — 2026-10-25. - Derived properties, calculated from each material's own values: price, CO₂ and energy per volume, specific stiffness and strength, thermal diffusivity and thermal shock resistance. They work as chart axes and in limits. - SI or imperial units everywhere: chart axes, tables, datasheets and limits (Options, or the status bar). Values are stored in SI, so switching loses nothing. - Index names are written as they are printed: E½/ρ, E⅓/ρ, σy⅔/ρ. - Bar charts: one property for every material, a bar from its low to its high value, grouped by family and sorted. - Copy the chart as a picture, ready to paste into a report. - Family labels move apart when they would overlap; the index value sits where the line is clear. - The chart toolbar is in two rows so it fits on smaller screens. Data and sources - Home: Material Library, Add a material, Sources and Roadmap tiles. - A Sources page: every source, its kind and licence, and a click shows which materials and values cite it. Open and public sources only.

heading: Changelog › 0.1.1 — 2026-10-25
text: Changelog › 0.1.1 — 2026-10-25. - 51 values in 15 metals are now checked against published datasheets from producers and suppliers (aluminium 2024, 5083, 6061, 7075 and A356; steels 1045 and 4340; 17-4PH; ductile iron; copper, brass and copper-nickel; titanium grades 2 and 5; nickel alloy 718). Each checked value cites its datasheet, with a link, and shows ✓ on the datasheet. Where a datasheet was outside our range the range was widened (4340 elongation, A356 strength and elongation, brass density and conductivity, copper-nickel yield strength, 5083 conductivity, 17-4PH tensile strength). The other values remain drafts. - A small ? beside the tools (goal, chart tools, slope, envelopes, bars, stages, limits, results, browse, datasheet, sources, units and more): a click says what the tool is for and how to use it. Help › What Is This Tool? lists them all. - Tell Me also finds materials by name, UNS or EN number and opens their datasheet.

heading: Changelog › 0.1.0 — 2026-10-25
text: Changelog › 0.1.0 — 2026-10-25. The first Datum Atlas: about 100 referenced materials, property charts with family envelopes, and selection with limits and index lines. - About 100 generic materials from every family: metals, polymers, elastomers, ceramics and glasses, composites, foams and natural materials. - Each value is a range with its source. The datasheet numbers the references and lists them at the bottom. - Built-in values are drafts: compiled from the named sources, not yet checked against each table or page. - Browse: a family tree and a table you can sort, select and copy to a spreadsheet (Ctrl+C), with Sum, Average and Count. Your own materials - Add Material explains what is needed: a name, the family, density, at least one more property, low and high values in the unit shown, and where the values come from. - Your materials are saved on this computer and appear in Browse, the datasheets, every chart and the selection. Edit or delete them, or copy a built-in material and change it. - Any two properties on log or linear axes. Each material is an ellipse spanning its ranges; each family has a smooth envelope (one per group where a family is spread out). - Hover for the ranges, click for a short datasheet beside the chart, double-click for the full one.

heading: Changelog › 0.1.0 — 2026-10-25

heading: Datum Atlas: notes for Claude
text: Datum Atlas: notes for Claude. Read docs/MEMORY.md first. It is the project's memory: architecture, decisions, roadmap, and a log of every session. Datum Atlas is the third app of the Datum family (after Datum Plan and Datum Plot). Follow docs/FAMILY.md and docs/briefs/DATUM-ATLAS.md in Edgar-Mendonca/Datum-Plan exactly (add that repo read-only). Datum Plan's code is the reference implementation: copy from it rather than reinventing anything. Datum Plot (Edgar-Mendonca/Datum-Plot) is checked for chart and graph-view patterns, but its renderer is Python and is not reused. At the end of every session that changes anything, update docs/MEMORY.md: - tick the roadmap - add a session-log entry - record any new decisions - refresh the architecture section if files moved - Rust and Tauri 2, small and efficient code, Windows first. No Python inside the app. - Ship in small numbered releases (0.1.0, 0.1.1, …), always three numbers. Every release appears in the in-app updater. - The family look with the Violet accent (FAMILY §3): ribbon with tabs and groups, a sidebar of pages, IBM Plex, square controls, light/dark/auto themes. - Keep code compact and match the surrounding style. Engine logic (units, ranges, geometry, hulls, selection, indices) belongs in crates/core (pure Rust, unit-tested), not in the UI. The window only maps engine geometry to the screen.

heading: Datum Atlas: notes for Claude
text: Datum Atlas: notes for Claude. - The UI is SolidJS + Vite in ui/src/*.tsx (built to ui/dist). State lives in ui/src/store.ts. - Every tool gets a small ? beside it that opens a card saying what it is for and how to use it (ui/src/help.tsx, one HELP table). No separate teaching mode. The user wants this in all Datum apps. - Data: every value is compiled by us from public sources, with a reference in data/sources.json. Never copy a proprietary or licensed database, or an aggregator site, not even to check a value. Missing values are gaps, never zero. - The repository is public, so all of it is public text (README, docs, plans, MEMORY, code comments, the app): Atlas stands on its own. Never name commercial products, never say it copies, combines, replaces or targets one, and never use their trademarks, data or wording (hub FAMILY §13). File-format names appear only where they name a file the app reads or writes. A test fails if a product name appears in the window. - Big asks get a docs/PLAN-x.y.md with questions first; build after the answers. Report in plain language: what changed, what was checked, what is not done. Identity: "Datum Atlas", .datlas (projects) and .datdb (user databases), com.edgarmendonca.datumatlas, REPO = "Edgar-Mendonca/Datum-Atlas" in src-tauri/src/update.rs, installer DatumAtlas-x.y.z-setup.exe. Checks before pushing:

heading: Datum Atlas: notes for Claude
text: Datum Atlas: notes for Claude. - cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings - cargo test --workspace (includes the database checks) - npm run check:ui - UI tests: npm run test:ui (Playwright against ui/dist with the dump fixture) Releasing: 1. Bump the version in src-tauri/Cargo.toml and crates/core/Cargo.toml. 2. Add a CHANGELOG section (## x.y.z — date, a one-line summary, bold sections in plain language). Update docs/site.json (about, steps, highlights and roadmap, each checked against what the app really does; the family site and the Datum network read it) together with the roadmap in docs/MEMORY.md §3. Push the tag vX.Y.Z, or run release.yml with workflow_dispatch when tag pushes are blocked. The workflow creates the tag and publishes the installer and SHA256SUMS.txt.

heading: Contributing
text: Contributing. Ideas, bug reports and data corrections are welcome as issues. Help › Roadmap in the app (and docs/site.json) shows what is planned.

heading: Contributing › Data: open sources only
text: Contributing › Data: open sources only. Every value in data/ names its source in data/sources.json. A value may come only from: - government handbooks and data (public domain); - open datasets; - a producer's or supplier's own datasheet that is free to read, cited value by value with its link; - our own compilation of typical textbook ranges, labelled as ours. Never copy, or check against, a proprietary or licensed materials database or an aggregator site. Never name one in the app or the docs. A correction needs a published source we can cite. Missing values are gaps, never zero. cargo test checks every value, its source and the source's kind.

heading: Contributing › How the code is laid out
text: Contributing › How the code is laid out. - crates/core: the engine in pure Rust (materials, units, chart geometry, selection, goals, files). All logic lives here, with tests. - src-tauri: the desktop shell (commands, files, updater). - ui/src: the window (SolidJS + TypeScript). It shows what the engine computes and sends edits back as operations. - docs/MEMORY.md: architecture, decisions, roadmap and a log of every session. Read it first.

heading: Contributing › Before you send a change
text: Contributing › Before you send a change. Keep code compact and in the style around it. A new engine feature comes with a test, and a new window feature with a UI test where it can. By contributing you agree your work is released under the MIT licence.

heading: Datum Atlas
text: Datum Atlas. Choose the right material: property charts, selection and referenced data, in one app for Windows.

heading: Datum Atlas › What it does
text: Datum Atlas › What it does. Datum Atlas is part of Datum; see its page: Datum Atlas helps engineers, designers and students pick a material and show why it is the right one: 1. Pick a design goal (light stiff beam, cheap strong tie, spring, heat sink…) or write down the requirements: what the part does, what it must meet, what to minimise. 2. See every material on a property chart: two properties on log axes; each material is a bubble spanning its ranges, each family has its envelope. 3. Select: limits (max service temperature ≥ 150 °C, price ≤ 5 USD/kg, recyclable), a selection line for a performance index (E^½/ρ for a light, stiff beam is a line of slope 2), a band, a box, a drawn shape, or whole families left out. 4. Rank, compare and report: the materials that pass, ranked, and the reason every other one fails; the best side by side; a report that documents the choice.

heading: Datum Atlas › Features (0.3.0)
text: Datum Atlas › Features (0.3.0). - About 250 materials from every family: metals, polymers, elastomers, ceramics and glasses, composites, foams and natural materials. Every value has a reference, compiled from open and public sources only (government handbooks, NIST, USGS, the Wood Handbook, open datasets, university notes, producers' datasheets and typical textbook ranges). No proprietary database is used. Gaps stay gaps, never zero. 73 values are checked against published datasheets so far (marked ✓). - Durability ratings for every material (water, acids, alkalis, sunlight, fire), and fatigue strength and resistivity for the metals. - 25 design goals and 52 performance indices, low-carbon and low-energy ones among them. A goal sets the axes, draws the selection line of the right slope through the best materials, adds the limits it needs and ranks the results; goals with two constraints set up two charts. “Why?” explains the function, constraint, objective and free variable. An index builder makes your own. - Formula properties and axes: define σy/ρ or any formula of the properties; it is calculated for every material, with its range, and works in charts, limits and tables.

heading: Datum Atlas › Features (0.3.0)
text: Datum Atlas › Features (0.3.0). - Property charts of any two properties, log or linear; family envelopes; hover for ranges, click for the datasheet; zoom, pan, guide lines; the best materials labelled with labels that keep apart; classic, publication and mono styles; up to four charts side by side. Bar charts of one property. - Selection: limits, several selection lines, bands, boxes, drawn shapes and families left out. Results ranked by an index with “× best”, or by weighted properties; every failure explained. - Eco audit: energy and CO₂ of a product from its materials to the end of its life (material, manufacture, transport, use, end of life), as ranges, for up to four design options, with the largest phase named and the break-even life. Greener substitutes find materials that do the same job with less CO₂. - Process selection from 55 processes (casting, moulding, forming, composites, machining, 3D printing): the ones that can make your part from your material, why the others cannot, the cost per part against batch size, and joins and finishes that suit it. Castability, machinability and weldability for every metal and polymer. - Compare up to six materials in a table and a radar chart, and print a selection report (with the eco audit and the manufacture) with the requirements, charts, shortlist, comparison and datasheets.

heading: Datum Atlas › Features (0.3.0)
text: Datum Atlas › Features (0.3.0). - Your own data: add materials by hand, import from a spreadsheet or CSV, open a colleague's database beside the built-in data, and save yours as a database, a spreadsheet or CSV. Results go to a spreadsheet too. - SI or imperial units everywhere; derived properties such as specific stiffness, cost per volume and thermal diffusivity. - Browse with a family tree and a spreadsheet-like table, datasheets with numbered references, and a Sources page. - ? help beside the tools, a Glossary, and Tell Me (Ctrl+K) for commands, goals and materials. - Print or save as PDF; export charts as SVG or PNG, or copy them as a picture. Light, dark and auto themes; the in-app updater; recovery of unsaved work; damaged files never crash the app.

heading: Datum Atlas › Install
text: Datum Atlas › Install. Download DatumAtlas-x.y.z-setup.exe from the latest release and run it (per-user install, no administrator rights). Windows SmartScreen may warn on the first install because the installer is not signed yet. Updates install from File › Updates.

heading: Datum Atlas › Build
text: Datum Atlas › Build. Rust (stable), Node 22, and on Linux the WebKitGTK development libraries. The engine (crates/core) holds the materials data, units, chart geometry and selection, with unit tests; the window (ui/src, SolidJS) only shows what it computes. npm run test:ui runs the Playwright tests against the real engine.

heading: Datum Atlas › Data
text: Datum Atlas › Data. Values are in data/*.json, one file per family, with their sources in data/sources.json. Each value is [low, high, source]. Built-in values are “draft” until each one is checked against a published source; checked values list the property in the material's checked list and cite that datasheet, and the tests refuse a checked value that cites only our own compilation; corrections with a reference are welcome as issues or pull requests.

heading: Datum Atlas: project memory › 1. Architecture
text: Datum Atlas: project memory › 1. Architecture. - The engine computes every value: ranges, bubbles and envelopes (in axis space: log10 on log axes), pass/fail with reasons, rankings and the index value at each selection line. The window maps engine geometry to pixels (zoom/pan window), draws ticks and labels, and sorts/filters tables for display. - After every change the shell returns Out = project + every chart laid out + results + dbRev; the window reloads the database (database) when dbRev changes. - Every edit is an Op (AddChart, SetChart, DelChart, Select, SetStages, Name, Notes, Ui, Batch, Goal) with undo; Goal is turned into a Batch by goals::apply in the shell and the bridge (it needs the database); the selection line is moved in the window while dragging and sent as one Select on release. - Built-in data: data/*.json (one per family; values [low, high, source], flags [bool, source]), data/sources.json; embedded with include_str!; db::check runs in the tests. User materials: My materials.datdb in the app data folder (ids u-…, sources u-s-…), checked by db::check_user (name, family, density, one more property, a source for each value). - Envelopes: per family (or class), split into groups of nearby bubbles (geometry::clusters, gap 5 % of the axes), each the convex hull of its ellipses grown by a rounded margin; only the biggest group is labelled, at its top edge.

heading: Datum Atlas: project memory › 1. Architecture
text: Datum Atlas: project memory › 1. Architecture. - Limits on ranges pass on the mean (geometric for log properties) or, with rule "all", on the whole range; missing values fail ("no data for …") or are kept and marked. - Index of a line of slope n on log–log axes Y vs X: Y^(1/n)/X (n > 0), Y^(1/ ; n ; )·X (n < 0); ranked descending when "above passes". - Design goals (goals.rs, 22): a goal sets the chart's axes, name and goal, places the line of its slope at the 80th percentile of cy − n·cx through the median x (the top fifth pass), replaces the limits marked goal: true with its own, and sets rank_chart. Empty id = Explore (no line, goal limits removed). - Derived properties (db::derive, source derived): cv = price·ρ, co2v, eev, es = E/ρ, ss = σy/ρ, diff = λ/(ρcp), shock = σts/(Eα); products low·low/high·high, quotients low/high, high/low. - Units: stored SI; db::props_out gives each property imperial: [unit, k, c]; the window converts with conv/toShown/toStored/vtext (store.ts) and computes ticks in shown units. - Checked values: Material.checked lists the properties checked against a published source; db::check refuses a checked value that is missing or cites a textbook-typical or estimate source.

heading: Datum Atlas: project memory › 1. Architecture › How we work (from Datum Plan, FAMILY §11)
text: Datum Atlas: project memory › 1. Architecture › How we work (from Datum Plan, FAMILY §11). 1. The user reviews the last release in the app and sends screenshots with bugs and wishes. 2. Diagnose first. Reproduce the problem in the test harness or the real app before changing code. Small fixes go straight to a release. 3. Bigger asks get a plan file (docs/PLAN-x.y.md): feedback, diagnosis, proposal, size, questions. Logged here and pushed. Build only after the user answers. 4. Build in small steps, engine first (crates/core, with a unit test), then the UI. Compact code in the surrounding style. 5. Check in the real app under Xvfb, with screenshots of each change. Fix what looks wrong. 6. Add a UI test for every reported bug and new feature (tests_ui/run.cjs). Make it fail on the old code where possible. 5b. Real app: scratchpad/app.sh (Xvfb :99 at 1600×1000, target/debug/datum-atlas, kill with pkill -x), drive with xdotool, screenshot with import -window root. 7. Run the checks: clippy -D warnings, cargo test --workspace (with the data checks), npm run check:ui, npm run test:ui. 8. Release: bump, CHANGELOG (becomes the in-app "What's new"), update this file, commit, push, run release.yml, watch CI + Release, confirm the installer and its size. 9. Report to the user in plain language: what changed, what was checked, what is not done, what to check on Windows.

heading: Datum Atlas: project memory › 4. Session log › 2026-10-28: Session 11, continued (0.2.0 stage B: selection)
text: Datum Atlas: project memory › 4. Session log › 2026-10-28: Session 11, continued (0.2.0 stage B: selection). - Chart.sels is a list of selections (Line, Box, new Poly); a material passes a chart when it passes all of them, so facing lines make a band. Old files' select moves into sels and is never written. - Stages.rank_line, ranking ("line" or "weighted") and weights (property, weight, higher better). Weighted scores scale each property so the best passing material scores 1 (a ratio for log properties, min–max for linear ones), then average by weight. - Op::Select { sels }, Op::PassThrough (line through a typed index value, via select::y_for), geometry::in_polygon. - Three two-constraint goals (25 in all): stiff and strong beam, stiff and strong panel, stiff and damage-tolerant tie. Each adds its second chart, marked /2; a new goal removes the old second chart. - every selection drawn, with its own handle and index label; - Shape tool (click corners; Enter or double-click closes; Esc cancels); - + Line, Pass through…, and selection chips (edit, remove, "rank by it", "ranks"); - arrow keys and Delete on the focused chart; - a Ranking section in Stages (line or weighted); - ? help topics sels and ranking; - the second chart in the goal's Why card; printed captions for every line. - 28 engine tests; 9 new UI checks, all passing.

heading: Datum Atlas 0.1.1: plan and menu › 1. Feedback on 0.1.0
text: Datum Atlas 0.1.1: plan and menu › 1. Feedback on 0.1.0. 1. Design goal list (screenshot 1, from the user's earlier attempt): one drop-down that picks the goal and sets up everything for it. The goals are grouped by what you minimise or maximise: - Minimum mass: light stiff tie E/ρ, light stiff beam E½/ρ, light stiff panel E⅓/ρ, light strong tie σy/ρ, light strong beam σy⅔/ρ, light strong panel σy½/ρ. - Minimum cost: cheap stiff beam E½/(Cₘρ), cheap strong tie σy/(Cₘρ). - Minimum carbon: low-carbon stiff beam E½/(CO₂·ρ). - Elastic design: spring σy²/E, elastic hinge σy/E. - Damage tolerance: yield before break KIc/σy, leak before break KIc²/σy. - Thermal: precision part with little thermal distortion λ/α. - "Explore (no goal)" at the top. The user remembers this from the established selection tool and wants it here. 2. Home page tiles: after Roadmap, add Material Library and Sources. The order should be: Material Library → Add a material → Sources → Roadmap. Sources is there to show plainly where every value comes from (open sources only, nothing proprietary). The user says to drop it if it doesn't fit; it fits. 3. Print (screenshot 3) works; no change was asked. 4. Next: update the memory, list what can be built in 0.1.1 and after, so the user can combine and choose.

heading: Datum Atlas 0.1.1: plan and menu › 2. Diagnosis
text: Datum Atlas 0.1.1: plan and menu › 2. Diagnosis. - Goals. 0.1.0 has six of these as *templates* on the File page. Each makes a new selection, and changing goal means starting again. There is no list inside the chart, and only 6 of the 16 goals exist. Four of the missing ones cannot be drawn yet: - cheap beam E½/(Cₘρ), cheap tie σy/(Cₘρ), low-carbon beam E½/(CO₂·ρ): these need cost per volume (Cₘ·ρ) and CO₂ per volume (CO₂·ρ) on an axis, and 0.1.0 has no derived axes; - the other goals only need the right two axes and slope: λ/α is slope 1 on λ–α; KIc²/σy is slope ½ on KIc–σy; σy⅔/ρ is slope 1.5 on σy–ρ. - Index names. The engine writes "E^½/ρ" and "σy^(1/1.5)/ρ". The goal list writes E½/ρ and σy⅔/ρ, which reads better. - Home tiles. The library (Browse) and the sources (Data page) exist but are only reachable from the sidebar. The File page shows design problems, Open, Add a material and Roadmap.

heading: Datum Atlas 0.1.1: plan and menu › 3. Proposal for 0.1.1 › 3.1 Design goal (the drop-down)
text: Datum Atlas 0.1.1: plan and menu › 3. Proposal for 0.1.1 › 3.1 Design goal (the drop-down). - a Goal drop-down at the left of the chart toolbar, and a big Goal button in Home and Select; - Setup gets the same list, with a short "why" text for each goal. - What it does (engine table goals.rs, so the list and the maths live in one place): - sets the chart's axes and log scales; - places the selection line with the right slope through the middle of the materials ("above passes"); - ranks the results by that index; - with "Explore", it removes the line. - Goals never touch your limits or families. - The 16 goals from screenshot 1, plus a few more: stiff column E½/ρ (same line as the beam), light stiff shaft, thermal insulation (minimum λ), heat sink (maximum λ), cheap stiff panel E⅓/(Cₘρ) and low-carbon strong tie σy/(CO₂·ρ). Each has: - its group; - its index in proper notation (E½/ρ); - the function, the constraint, the objective and the free variable, in one line each; - the axes and the slope. - Derived properties needed by the cost and carbon goals, computed by the engine from the ranges (product of lows, product of highs) and shown like any property, marked "derived": - cost per volume Cₘ·ρ (USD/m³); - CO₂ per volume (kg/m³); - embodied energy per volume (MJ/m³);

heading: Datum Atlas 0.1.2 and after: plan › 2. Where we are (diagnosis)
text: Datum Atlas 0.1.2 and after: plan › 2. Where we are (diagnosis). - One selection per chart. Chart.select holds one line *or* one box (Option ). Results rank by the line of one chart (rank_chart). - "Several lines on one chart" needs a closer look. The catalogue's example (C9: "stiffness and strength together") does not fit on one chart. The lines on a chart share its axes: on modulus–density, every line is a stiffness index. Stiffness *and* strength needs two charts (E–ρ and σy–ρ). Atlas already combines selections across charts, but the user has to build the second chart by hand. What one chart with several lines does well: - a band between two lines (e.g. stiff enough but not over-designed); - two indices on the same axes: a tie (slope 1) and a beam (slope 2) made from one material. - The catalogue also lists for 0.1.2: - charts side by side (B13); - labelling the best materials (B14). Together with the four roadmap items, that is more than one small release. - Results leave the app only by print or Ctrl+C from Browse. The results table has no export. A real .xlsx file needs a Rust crate (rust_xlsxwriter); CSV needs nothing new. - Keyboard: the line moves only by dragging or by typing its slope. - 51 values in 15 metals are checked.

heading: Datum Atlas 0.1.2 and after: plan › 2. Where we are (diagnosis)
text: Datum Atlas 0.1.2 and after: plan › 2. Where we are (diagnosis). - 14 metals are still drafts: 1020, 1080, 304, 316, 430, grey iron, 1100, AZ91, 625, CoCr F75, zinc AG40A, lead, tin, tungsten. - All 23 polymers are still drafts. - The 0.1.1 check used datasheet figures quoted by web search: this environment's network policy blocks opening the datasheets themselves (Q5). - The in-app roadmap (ui/src/features.ts) keeps its own release list, and it uses two-number versions ("0.2", "0.3"). - docs/site.json now holds the same roadmap, so the two can drift apart. - Hardening (hub FAMILY §11, added at the user's request). Every Datum app must meet the family's hardening standard, from Datum Plan 0.3.11. Atlas has only part of it: Required ; Atlas today ; hardening test module: failed edits change nothing; random documents never panic; damaged files never panic; speed gate ; Missing ; deny.toml and cargo deny check (advisories, licences, sources) ; Missing ; license = "MIT" in every crate ; Yes (core, shell) ; CI runs cargo test on Windows and macOS as well as Linux ; Linux only ; The shell's state lock recovers from a poisoned mutex ; No: every command calls lock().unwrap(), so one panic makes every later command fail ; SECURITY.md and CONTRIBUTING.md ; Missing ;

heading: Datum Atlas 0.1.2 and after: plan › 2. Where we are (diagnosis)
text: Datum Atlas 0.1.2 and after: plan › 2. Where we are (diagnosis). Data-loss risk found while checking: the shell reads My materials.datdb with .ok(). A damaged file is treated as empty, without a word. The next Add Material then writes that empty list plus the new material, so the user's own materials are lost. Hardening fixes this first. - Not yet confirmed on a real Windows PC: - Copy Picture; - the 0.1.0 → 0.1.1 update through the updater.

heading: Datum Atlas 0.1.2 and after: plan › 3. Proposal
text: Datum Atlas 0.1.2 and after: plan › 3. Proposal. Keep every release small. Split the 0.1.2 theme in two, and the 0.2 theme in three.

heading: Datum Atlas 0.1.2 and after: plan › 3. Proposal › 0.1.2 "Lines and results" (next)
text: Datum Atlas 0.1.2 and after: plan › 3. Proposal › 0.1.2 "Lines and results" (next). 1. Several lines on a chart (C9). A chart keeps a list of selections: lines and at most one box. - Each line has its slope and its side. - Two lines of the same slope with opposite sides make a band. - Results rank by one line, which you choose (marked "ranks" in Stages). - Old .datlas files open unchanged: a single selection becomes a list of one. - Engine first, with tests: a band, two slopes, and ranking by the chosen line. 2. Goals with two constraints. New goals that need two charts add the second chart themselves: - stiff and strong beam; - stiff and strong panel; - light, stiff and tough tie. Selections already combine across charts, so the shortlist is what passes both. 3. Keyboard for the line (C10): - arrow keys move the selected line (Shift for big steps); - Delete removes it;

heading: Datum Atlas 0.1.2 and after: plan › 3. Proposal › 0.1.2 "Lines and results" (next)
text: Datum Atlas 0.1.2 and after: plan › 3. Proposal › 0.1.2 "Lines and results" (next). - "Pass through…" types the index value the line should pass through. 4. Label the best (B14). The five best materials by the index are labelled on the chart (on/off in the toolbar). The labels move apart as the family labels do. 5. Results to a spreadsheet (D5). File › Export › Results: the ranked list with the index, "× best", the stages and the reason each failure failed. Saved as .xlsx and CSV (Q3). 6. Data. Check the 14 remaining metals, then start on the polymers. Same rule as 0.1.1: primary publishers only, ✓ only when the datasheet's figure falls in our range. 7. One roadmap. - Embed docs/site.json in the app, and have Help › Roadmap take its release names, timing and items from it, so the app, the family site and MEMORY show the same plan. - Versions in the app become three numbers. 8. Hardening (FAMILY §11). Copy the standard from Datum Plan 0.3.11 and adapt it to Atlas's files: - Your materials are never lost. - The .datdb reader moves into the engine (db::read_user) and returns a clear error. - A damaged file is kept aside as My materials (damaged ).datdb, and the window says so. - Saving never writes over a file that could not be read.

heading: Datum Atlas 0.1.2 and after: plan › 3. Proposal › 0.1.2 "Lines and results" (next)
text: Datum Atlas 0.1.2 and after: plan › 3. Proposal › 0.1.2 "Lines and results" (next). - Saves go through a temporary file and a rename, so a crash mid-save leaves the old file whole. - hardening tests in crates/core: - a failed edit (Op, including Goal and Batch) leaves the project exactly as it was; - random projects and user databases (a small built-in generator, no extra crate) never panic, and keep their invariants: hulls hold their bubbles, counts add up, no NaN; - damaged .datlas, .datdb, options, recent-files and recovery files (cut short, garbled bytes, wrong types, huge numbers, deep nesting) never panic: each opens or gives a clear error; - a speed gate: a project of 20 charts over 1,000 materials (built-in data repeated) is laid out and selected within a time limit, looser in debug builds. - Shell: the state lock recovers from a poisoned mutex, as in Plan. - Supply chain: - deny.toml and cargo deny check in CI; - license = "MIT" stays in every crate; - CI runs cargo test on Windows and macOS as well as Linux. - Repo: SECURITY.md (how to report a problem; the app's only network call is the update check, to this repo) and CONTRIBUTING.md (the checks; data corrections need a published source, never a proprietary database).

heading: Datum Atlas 0.1.2 and after: plan › 3. Proposal › 0.1.3 "Charts side by side"
text: Datum Atlas 0.1.2 and after: plan › 3. Proposal › 0.1.3 "Charts side by side". - B13: two or four charts at once, one selection shared across them. Hovering a material highlights it on every chart. - Two-constraint goals open their two charts side by side.

heading: Datum Atlas 0.1.2 and after: plan › 3. Proposal › 0.2.0, 0.2.1, 0.2.2 "Indices"
text: Datum Atlas 0.1.2 and after: plan › 3. Proposal › 0.2.0, 0.2.1, 0.2.2 "Indices". - 0.2.0 Index library and builder (C7, C6): - about 40 standard indices with their derivations; - pick function → constraint → objective → free variable, and get the index, its derivation and the chart with the line. - The 22 goals become the first entries of the library. - 0.2.1 Expression axes and formula properties (B8, A13): - an axis such as [Young's modulus]^0.5/[Density]; - your own derived properties as spreadsheet-style formulas. - This needs the family's formula engine. It is its own release because parsing, units and errors need care. - 0.2.2 Weighted ranking (C11, new): rank by any property or a weighted mix (e.g. 60 % mass, 40 % cost), with the trade-off explained.

text: Datum Atlas 0.1.2 and after: plan › 4. Order of work in 0.1.2. 0. Hardening first (it protects the user's data and makes the rest safer to build): - the .datdb fix; - the hardening tests; - the poisoned-lock recovery; - the Windows/macOS CI jobs; - SECURITY.md and CONTRIBUTING.md. 1. Engine (crates/core): - selections as a list (model.rs, with old files loading); - select.rs with bands and the ranking line; - two-chart goals (goals.rs); - results to .xlsx/CSV. - Each comes with tests. 2. Window: - lines list in the toolbar and Stages; - best-material labels; - the Export › Results tile; - the Roadmap page reading site.json; - ? help for every new tool. 3. Data check (metals, then polymers) with checked lists and sources. 4. UI tests for each item; the real app under Xvfb; CHANGELOG, MEMORY, site.json; release.

heading: Datum Atlas 0.1: plan and questions
text: Datum Atlas 0.1: plan and questions. Status: answered (§10); 0.1.0 built and released. §10 overrides the earlier sections where they differ. Goal: a small, fast Windows app for materials selection with property charts (the property-chart method): find the right material for a part, see why it is right, compare candidates and document the decision. Open data with a reference for every value, spreadsheet-style formulas, publication-quality charts. Sources: the brief Datum-Plan/docs/briefs/DATUM-ATLAS.md (followed; this file refines it), FAMILY.md (followed exactly), Datum Plan's code (the reference implementation) and Datum Plot's code (checked for reuse, §3). This file follows the family pattern: brief → what we reuse → proposal → 0.1.0 scope → release plan → size → questions.

heading: Datum Atlas 0.1: plan and questions › 3. What we reuse › From Datum Plot: checked, and what fits
text: Datum Atlas 0.1: plan and questions › 3. What we reuse › From Datum Plot: checked, and what fits. Datum Plot draws every graph with matplotlib in an embedded Python (py/datum/graph.py), and the window shows that SVG. That renderer, the Python worker (py.rs) and the runtime pack (runtime.rs) cannot be reused: Atlas has no Python. So Atlas builds the SVG chart engine the brief allows for (ui/src/chart/, geometry in Rust). What does carry over from Plot: Plot part ; Reused in Atlas ; graph.tsx toData/toPt ; The data ↔ screen mapping for linear and log axes, ported to our own SVG (same maths). ; graph.tsx interaction ; Crosshair, hover tooltip with values, Ctrl+wheel zoom, double-click hit zones (axis → axis settings, legend → families, data → datasheet), right-click menu (Format, Copy Picture, Export). ; graph.py Prism look ; As SVG rules: open or framed axes, ticks out, 1 pt axes, bold axis titles, log axes with decade labels (10², 10³) and minor ticks at 2–9, light optional gridlines. ; format.tsx ; The docked Format panel that applies each change at once (with undo), SIZES (journal widths in mm), FONTS, OKABE_ITO. ; graph.tsx exportGraph ; The Export dialog (format, dpi 150/300/600, transparent), used in 0.1.1. ; Copy Picture through Rust (tauri-plugin-clipboard-manager) ; Lesson from Plot 0.1.0: WebView2 blocks navigator.clipboard on All picture copy and clipboard reads go through Rust from day one. ; Plot's print page for graphs ; Charts

GridCraft (formulas) arrives with expressions in 0.2.1, calamine/rust_xlsxwriter with import in 0.3.x: each dependency comes with the release that needs it.

text: Datum Atlas 0.1: plan and questions › 4. Architecture › Engine modules (brief §5, refined). File ; 0.1.0 contents ; model.rs ; Material (id, name, family path, synonyms, designations, props, notes, uses, refs), PropValue (Range { lo, hi, typical, src }, Rating, Flag, Text), Property (key, name, symbol, group, unit kind, log default, description), Source (id, title, publisher, year, url, licence, kind), Database, Project format 1 (charts, notes, ui). ; units.rs ; Unit kinds with one stored SI unit each (§6.2); formatting with significant figures; the imperial set comes in 0.1.1 but the conversion table and its round-trip test land now. ; db.rs ; Embedded database: parse, validate (the data checks of §8), family tree with counts, lookup by id, plain search by name/synonym/designation (full search UI in 0.1.1). ; geometry.rs ; Bubble = axis-aligned ellipse in log space spanning lo–hi on each axis (minimum size when lo = hi); family hull = convex hull of sampled bubble outlines, then smoothed (rounded offset) so it encloses every bubble; linear axes use the same code without the log. ; chart.rs ; ChartReq { x, y, log_x, log_y, hull_level } → ChartOut { bubbles, hulls, extents, missing }: materials missing a value are listed, never drawn at zero. ; doc.rs ; Op (chart axes, scale, style, notes), undo/redo, .datlas read/write with a format number (as Plan and Plot). ;

heading: Datum Atlas 0.1: plan and questions › 4. Architecture › Engine modules (brief §5, refined)
text: Datum Atlas 0.1: plan and questions › 4. Architecture › Engine modules (brief §5, refined). Later (per the brief): expr.rs (0.2.1), select.rs (0.2.0), index.rs (0.2.1), io.rs (0.3.x), report.rs (0.3.0). Rule: the window never calculates material values, ranges, hulls or pass/fail. It only maps engine geometry to the screen (an affine transform in log space), draws ticks and places labels. This matches Plan's rule and Plot's graph view, and lets pan and zoom run at full speed without a call per frame.

heading: Datum Atlas 0.1: plan and questions › 5. Proposal for the window › 5.1 Layout (family)
text: Datum Atlas 0.1: plan and questions › 5. Proposal for the window › 5.1 Layout (family). - Title bar: QAT (save, undo, redo, print), document name, Tell Me (Ctrl+K), Theme (Auto/Light/Dark). - Ribbon tabs (brief §4): Home (clipboard, find, new chart, units), Select, Chart, Data, Report, View, Help; contextual Chart Tools › Format while a chart is open. "Home" is the brief's word for Atlas; Plan dropped a Home tab because it was crowded, which does not apply here (to confirm, Q11). - Left sidebar: Setup · Browse · Datasheet · Charts ; Stages · Results · Compare · Index builder ; Report · Data. - Main area: the chart canvas on Plan's dotted whiteboard background (white when printed or exported); the stage panel on the right arrives with stages in 0.2.0. - Status bar: Ready · materials shown / total · the database · the units · zoom. - File page, Options, Print, updater, themes: as in Plan.

heading: Datum Atlas 0.1: plan and questions › 5. Proposal for the window › 5.2 Browse
text: Datum Atlas 0.1: plan and questions › 5. Proposal for the window › 5.2 Browse. - Left: the family tree (Metals › Non-ferrous › Aluminium alloys …) with counts; clicking a node filters the table. - Right: the record table on the family grid engine: name, family, and chosen property columns (density, E, σy, K_IC, λ, price…) shown as lo – hi with units in the heading; sort by clicking a heading (by the geometric mean of the range), ranges with Sum/Average/Count, Ctrl+C copies tab-separated text for a spreadsheet. - Double-click a row → Datasheet.

heading: Datum Atlas 0.1: plan and questions › 5. Proposal for the window › 5.3 Datasheet
text: Datum Atlas 0.1: plan and questions › 5. Proposal for the window › 5.3 Datasheet. - Header: name, family path, designations (EN, UNS, ASTM, ISO, JIS), synonyms. - Grouped properties (General, Mechanical, Thermal, Electrical, Optical, Durability, Processing, Eco): a row per property with lo – hi, the typical value when present, the unit, and a superscript reference number; missing values show "–" with "no data", never zero. - References list at the bottom (title, publisher, year, link, licence). Notes and typical uses.

heading: Datum Atlas 0.1: plan and questions › 5. Proposal for the window › 5.4 Property chart (the heart)
text: Datum Atlas 0.1: plan and questions › 5. Proposal for the window › 5.4 Property chart (the heart). - Defaults to Young's modulus vs density, log–log; X and Y pickers list every range property; Linear/Log per axis. - Bubbles: an ellipse per material spanning its ranges, filled with its family colour at about 35 % opacity with a 1 px edge. Hulls: one per family, smoothed, about 12 % opacity, labelled with the family name. - Hover: tooltip with the name, family and both ranges with units; the bubble's edge thickens. Click: opens the Datasheet. Double-click an axis: axis settings. - Zoom (Ctrl+wheel, zoom box, buttons), pan (drag the background), Fit; decade ticks 10⁻¹, 10⁰, 10¹ … with minor ticks at 2–9 and optional light gridlines. - Guide lines for slopes 1, 2, 3 (E/ρ, E^½/ρ, E^⅓/ρ) can be switched on in 0.1.0 as plain guides; draggable index lines and pass/fail come with stages in 0.2.0. - Family legend (click a family to show or hide it). - Family colours (Okabe-Ito, colour-blind safe, to approve, Q12): Metals #0072B2 blue · Polymers #E69F00 orange · Elastomers #CC79A7 pink · Ceramics and glasses #009E73 green · Composites #D55E00 vermilion · Foams #56B4E9 sky · Natural materials #8C6D1F brown (Okabe-Ito yellow is too pale for edges on white). - New icons in the sprite: i-atlas (chart), i-bubble, i-hull, i-index (slope line), i-datasheet, i-tree, i-stage, i-results, i-compare, i-radar, i-units, i-material, i-db.

heading: Datum Atlas 0.1: plan and questions › 5. Proposal for the window › 5.5 Help
text: Datum Atlas 0.1: plan and questions › 5. Proposal for the window › 5.5 Help. Getting Started for newcomers to the property-chart method (what a property chart is, why log axes, what a bubble and a hull are, how an index line selects), a searchable Glossary (bubble, hull, family, class, performance index, selection line, limit stage, range, typical value, log decade…), Shortcuts, Tell Me, GitHub links.

heading: Datum Atlas 0.1: plan and questions › 6. Data › 6.1 Policy (brief §3.5)
text: Datum Atlas 0.1: plan and questions › 6. Data › 6.1 Policy (brief §3.5). - Every value is compiled by us with a reference: src points to a record in data/sources.json (title, publisher or author, year, edition, URL, licence, kind: handbook, government, open-dataset, datasheet, textbook-typical, computed). - Allowed: public-domain US government handbooks and data (MIL-HDBK-5J, MIL-HDBK-17, NIST, USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries for metal prices), open datasets with a compatible licence, named per record (Materials Project, CC-BY 4.0, only for computed properties and marked as computed), manufacturer datasheets (cited with the product and date), and textbook-level typical ranges rewritten as our own compilation and cited. - Never a proprietary or licensed database or an aggregator site, and no product names or wording from them in the app. - Each record carries a checked status (draft → checked), so we can ship honest drafts and tighten references over releases. The Datasheet shows a "draft value" mark until it is checked (Q7). - Prices and CO₂ carry their year and basis (e.g. USD/kg, 2025, bulk) because they change.

heading: Datum Atlas 0.1: plan and questions › 6. Data › 6.2 Stored units (SI, one per kind)
text: Datum Atlas 0.1: plan and questions › 6. Data › 6.2 Stored units (SI, one per kind). density kg/m³ · modulus GPa · strength MPa · toughness MPa·m½ · hardness HV · temperature °C (shown in °C or K, °F in imperial) · conductivity W/(m·K) · expansion µstrain/°C (10⁻⁶/°C) · specific heat J/(kg·K) · resistivity µΩ·cm · price USD/kg · embodied energy MJ/kg · CO₂ kg/kg · loss coefficient (–) · elongation % strain.

heading: Datum Atlas 0.1: plan and questions › 8. Size and quality
text: Datum Atlas 0.1: plan and questions › 8. Size and quality. Size (0.1.0): core ~1,400 lines (+ ~60 records of data JSON, ~25 sources), shell ~450 (most copied), UI ~2,600 TSX/TS + CSS (half copied from Plan), UI tests ~150. Installer expected about 2 MB (Plan 0.1.0 was 1.7 MB; the database adds tens of kB). Engine tests: unit round-trips (for 0.1.1's imperial set too); range maths in log space (geometric mean, decade span); every bubble lies inside its family hull for the default and several other axis pairs; missing values are excluded from charts and listed; the database checks (every value has a source that exists, lo ≤ hi, positive values where a log axis is possible, units consistent with the property, no duplicate ids or designations); .datlas round-trip. UI tests: the chart renders a bubble per material with both values and a hull per family; hover shows the ranges; click opens the datasheet; Browse tree filters the table and Ctrl+C gives TSV; the ribbon fits at 1280 and 1600 px; every view prints; Options lines up; no script errors. Checked in the real app under Xvfb with screenshots before release.

Earlier attempts at this app (repos or files) to reuse or learn from?

heading: Datum Atlas 0.2.0: the big update (plan) › 2. The big update: everything that is possible now › A. Sturdy (hardening, FAMILY §11): built first
text: Datum Atlas 0.2.0: the big update (plan) › 2. The big update: everything that is possible now › A. Sturdy (hardening, FAMILY §11): built first. 1. Your materials are never lost. - A damaged My materials.datdb is kept aside and reported, never written over. - Saves go through a temporary file and a rename. 2. hardening tests: - failed edits change nothing; - random projects and databases never panic and keep their invariants; - damaged .datlas, .datdb, options, recent and recovery files open or give a clear error; - a speed gate on a large project. 3. Shell: the state lock recovers from a poisoned mutex. 4. Supply chain and repo: - deny.toml and cargo deny check; - CI on Windows and macOS as well as Linux; - SECURITY.md, CONTRIBUTING.md.

heading: Datum Atlas 0.2.0: the big update (plan) › 2. The big update: everything that is possible now › B. Selection
text: Datum Atlas 0.2.0: the big update (plan) › 2. The big update: everything that is possible now › B. Selection. 5. Several selection lines on a chart, and a band between two lines. Results rank by the line you choose. 6. Goals with two constraints: - stiff and strong beam; - stiff and strong panel; - light, stiff and tough tie. These goals add their second chart themselves; the shortlist is what passes both. 7. Keyboard: - arrow keys move the selected line (Shift for big steps); - Delete removes it; - "Pass through…" types the index value. 8. Polygon selection (C8): draw any shape on a chart. 9. Weighted ranking (C11): rank by any property, or by a weighted mix (e.g. 60 % mass, 40 % cost), with the trade-off explained.

heading: Datum Atlas 0.2.0: the big update (plan) › 2. The big update: everything that is possible now › C. Indices and formulas
text: Datum Atlas 0.2.0: the big update (plan) › 2. The big update: everything that is possible now › C. Indices and formulas. 10. Index library (C7): about 40 standard performance indices (ties, beams, panels, columns, shafts, springs, hinges, pressure vessels, flywheels, thermal and electrical uses), each with its derivation. The 22 goals become its first entries. 11. Index builder (C6): pick function → constraint → objective → free variable, and get: - the index; - its derivation, step by step; - the chart with the line. 12. Expression axes (B8): an axis such as [Young's modulus]^0.5/[Density], with units, on the formula engine copied from Datum Plan. 13. Formula properties (A13): your own derived properties as spreadsheet-style formulas, usable in charts, limits and ranking.

heading: Datum Atlas 0.2.0: the big update (plan) › 4. Order of work
text: Datum Atlas 0.2.0: the big update (plan) › 4. Order of work. 1. A. Sturdy: it protects your data and makes everything after it safer to build. 2. Engine foundations: - selections as lists (old files load unchanged); - the formula engine copied from Plan; - the index library; - spreadsheet input and output. 3. B and C: selection, indices and formulas. 4. D and E: charts, compare and report. 5. F: data, in batches. The 150 new materials are drafted with sources, then checked as far as published datasheets can be found. 6. G: the app; then the full checks, the real app under Xvfb with screenshots, CHANGELOG, MEMORY, site.json, README. Then release 0.2.0.

heading: Datum Atlas 0.2.0: the big update (plan) › 7. Answers (2026-10-28)
text: Datum Atlas 0.2.0: the big update (plan) › 7. Answers (2026-10-28). 1. The list: all of §2, nothing dropped. Build it. 2. Eco audit: not answered; it stays with process selection in 0.3.0, as proposed. 3. Checking data: network unchanged, so values are checked from search results quoting the datasheets, labelled as such. 4. Data rule (the user, repeated and made strict for the 250 materials): only open, public and free sources: - government handbooks and data (public domain); - open datasets; - producers' and suppliers' own datasheets that are free to read, cited value by value; - our own compilation of typical textbook ranges, labelled as ours. Never a proprietary or licensed database or an aggregator site, not even to check a value, and never named in public text. db::check refuses any source whose kind is not on the open list. CONTRIBUTING.md states the rule.
