heading: Datum Atlas 0.3.0: eco and process, one big update (plan) › 2. The big update › A. Eco data (built first; everything else uses it)
text: Datum Atlas 0.3.0: eco and process, one big update (plan) › 2. The big update › A. Eco data (built first; everything else uses it). 1. CO₂ and embodied energy for every material, from open life-cycle datasets and government reports; the 64 gaps filled where a public source exists, left as gaps where none does. 2. End of life per material: recyclable, downcyclable, combustible (with heat of combustion), landfill, biodegradable; the energy and CO₂ of recycling and the typical recycled fraction in today's supply. 3. Processing energy and CO₂ for the main primary processes (casting, rolling and forging, extrusion, moulding, machining per kg removed), as typical ranges with sources. 4. Factors table (data/eco.json): transport by sea, rail, road and air (MJ and kg CO₂ per tonne·km); electricity CO₂ by region; fuels. Each with its public source and year. 5. Water use where public data exists (gap otherwise).

heading: Datum Atlas 0.3.0: eco and process, one big update (plan) › 2. The big update › B. Eco audit
text: Datum Atlas 0.3.0: eco and process, one big update (plan) › 2. The big update › B. Eco audit. 6. Bill of materials: parts with material, mass, process, and the recycled content used; picked from the database, or from the shortlist in one click. 7. Life phases: material, manufacture, transport (legs with distance and mode), use (energy over the life: electrical, or fuel for moving mass, with the mass-to-fuel factor shown), end of life (one choice per part). 8. Results: energy and CO₂ per phase and per part, as bar charts and a table; the phase that dominates is said in words, with what usually helps for it. 9. Design options side by side: two to four versions of the product (e.g. steel against aluminium against composite), compared phase by phase, with the break-even life where the lines cross. 10. End-of-life credit shown separately, never mixed in silently. 11. The audit is part of the .datlas project, has undo, and goes into the selection report and to a spreadsheet.

heading: Datum Atlas 0.3.0: eco and process, one big update (plan) › 2. The big update › C. Greener substitutes
text: Datum Atlas 0.3.0: eco and process, one big update (plan) › 2. The big update › C. Greener substitutes. 12. "Like this, but greener": for a material, the materials that meet the same limits and index within a chosen tolerance, ranked by CO₂ per unit of function (the index, not per kg), with what you give up shown. 13. Eco goals in the library: minimum CO₂ and energy versions of the tie, beam, panel, column and shaft (some exist; the set completed), and the eco charts (CO₂ against modulus, strength, price).

heading: Datum Atlas 0.3.0: eco and process, one big update (plan) › 2. The big update › D. Process data
text: Datum Atlas 0.3.0: eco and process, one big update (plan) › 2. The big update › D. Process data. 14. A process database (data/processes.json), about 40 processes from public sources (university course notes, government manufacturing guides, open textbooks, producers' own guides): - shaping: sand, die and investment casting; injection, blow and compression moulding; extrusion; forging; rolling; sheet forming; powder methods; composite lay-up and filament winding; - machining: turning, milling, drilling, grinding, EDM, laser and water-jet cutting; - joining: welding (arc, laser, friction), brazing, soldering, adhesives, fasteners; - additive: powder-bed fusion, extrusion (FDM), resin (SLA), binder jetting; - finishing: painting, anodising, plating, polishing. 15. Each process record: the materials it suits (by family and class); part mass and section thickness; shapes it can make (flat, prismatic, 3-D solid, hollow, sheet); tolerance and roughness; economic batch size; relative tooling and equipment cost, rate; energy and CO₂ per kg; notes and sources. 16. Processing ratings for materials: castability, machinability and weldability filled for the metals and polymers (already defined, empty today).

heading: Datum Atlas 0.3.0: eco and process, one big update (plan) › 2. The big update › E. Process selection
text: Datum Atlas 0.3.0: eco and process, one big update (plan) › 2. The big update › E. Process selection. 17. Your part: material (or the shortlist), mass, smallest section, shape, tolerance, roughness, batch size. 18. Stages like material selection: each requirement removes processes that cannot do it, and every failed process says why. Process charts: tolerance against roughness, mass range, section thickness, economic batch size, as bar charts per process. 19. Material–process matrix: which of the shortlisted materials each process can make. 20. Cost model: cost per part against batch size for each process that passes (material, tooling spread over the batch, equipment and labour per hour at its rate), drawn as lines on a log chart, with the cheapest process for each batch size. Every input is shown and can be changed; the default costs are labelled as indicative. 21. Joining and finishing pickers: which joins work for two materials, which finishes for one.

heading: Datum Atlas 0.3.0: eco and process, one big update (plan) › 2. The big update › F. The app

heading: tagline
text: tagline. Choose the right material: property charts, selection and referenced data, in one app for Windows.

heading: about
text: about. Datum Atlas helps you pick a material and show why it is the right one. Choose a design goal, such as a light, stiff beam or a cheap, strong tie, and Atlas sets the property chart, the selection line and the limits for you. Every material is a bubble spanning its range of values, grouped by family. Limits, index lines, bands, boxes, drawn shapes and whole families left out narrow the field; the materials that pass are ranked, and every one that fails says why. Compare the best side by side, add up their energy and CO₂ through a product's life, find the processes that can make the part and what it costs, and print a report. Every value names its source, and you can add, import and share your own materials.

heading: steps
text: steps. Choose a design goal, or set the two properties to chart yourself. Move the selection line, add limits and boxes, and watch the field narrow. Rank, check and report See the materials that pass, ranked. Compare the best, audit their energy and CO₂, choose how to make the part, and print the selection report.

heading: highlights
text: highlights. About 250 materials from every family, compiled from open and public sources. Every value names its source; 73 values are checked against published datasheets so far, and gaps stay gaps, never zero. Property charts of any two properties or of your own formulas, with family envelopes, the best materials labelled and labels kept apart; bar charts; up to four charts side by side. 25 design goals and a library of 52 performance indices, including low-carbon and low-energy ones, with an index builder; a goal sets the axes, the selection line and the limits in one pick, and explains why. Selection by limits, index lines, bands, boxes, drawn shapes and families; results ranked by an index or by weighted properties, with the reason every other material fails. An eco audit: energy and CO₂ of a product from its materials to the end of its life, for up to four design options, with the largest phase named, the break-even life, and greener substitutes for the same job. Process selection from 55 processes: the ones that can make your part from your material, why the others cannot, and the cost per part against batch size; joins and finishes that suit it. Compare up to six materials with a radar chart, and print a selection report with the charts, shortlist, eco audit, manufacture and

heading: Changelog › 0.2.1 — 2026-11-02
text: Changelog › 0.2.1 — 2026-11-02. Automation: run models from the command line and from Python. Command line: datum-sim-cli, installed next to the app. - run a model and write the results as CSV or JSON, or print a summary. Set variables (--set Kp=120), block parameters (--param PID:D=5) and run settings (--stop, --solver …), pick signals, and reduce the points. - sweep a variable and write one file per value; check a model (exit code 1 on errors, for build servers); info lists blocks, parameters, variables and signals; examples. Python: import datum_sim. Open a model or an example, set variables and parameters, run, and get the results as NumPy arrays (or a pandas table). Sweep a variable, check, save. Install with pip install "git+ Help › Automation shows the commands for the open model, ready to copy. The command line and Python use the app's own engine, so their results are the same as the window's.

heading: Changelog › 0.2.0 — 2026-10-29
text: Changelog › 0.2.0 — 2026-10-29. Reusable models: masks and My blocks. - Give a subsystem a mask (Model › Mask, or the Inspector): parameters of its own with labels, units and defaults, a text on the block, its own help card, and typical ratings saved from the block's values. - The blocks inside use the parameters by name; a parameter's value can use the model's variables and the parameters of masks around it. A masked subsystem is set in the Inspector like any block, and errors point at it. - Look under the mask (right-click or the Inspector) to see and change the blocks inside. - Save any subsystem to My blocks; it appears at the top of the Library for every model. Drag it in or double-click it: each model gets its own copy, so changing a saved block later never changes models that already use it. - Options › My blocks chooses the folder, so a team can share one on a network drive. Worked example: a masked DC motor block used for two different motors in one model. Files: models are saved in file format 2 (it can hold masks). Files from earlier versions open as before.

heading: Changelog › 0.1.6 — 2026-10-29
text: Changelog › 0.1.6 — 2026-10-29. Wires and the diagram: easier to draw, read and find your way in. - Drag a wire's middle segment sideways to move it; the bends stay square. - Alt-drag (or Ctrl-drag) from a wire to branch its signal to another input. - Double-click a bend to remove it. - Signal names: double-click a wire (or use the Inspector) to name the signal it carries. The name shows on the wire, on the printed diagram and in scope legends and results, and every wire from the same output carries it. - Notes: text notes on the diagram for explanations, reviews and teaching (Format › Note). Wires run over them and they are printed with the diagram. - Find (Ctrl+F): find a block, or a named signal, anywhere in the model, inside subsystems too; choosing one opens its diagram and selects it. - Block colours: colour blocks to mark the plant, the controller and the sensors (Format › Block Colour, or right-click). - Distribute: space three or more blocks evenly, across or down.

heading: Changelog › 0.1.5 — 2026-10-29
text: Changelog › 0.1.5 — 2026-10-29. Scopes you can measure with, and a probe that reads any wire. - Cursors: two lines, A and B, that you drag across the plot; a table gives every signal at A and at B, the difference, Δt and 1/Δt. - Marks: rise time (10–90 %), overshoot, peak and settling time (2 %) of the first signal, drawn on the plot. - Compare runs: the last five runs are kept; overlay any of them, dashed in the same colours. - Axes: drag up or down to zoom the y axis; a fixed y range; one plot per input (stacked) on a shared time axis. Layout and range are saved in the Scope block. - Pictures: PNG as shown, PNG at three times the size for print, and SVG for papers and reports. - Simulate › Log all signals logs every signal of the model. After the run, hover any wire to read its value at cursor A (or at the end of the run), inside subsystems too. - With every signal logged, the first run no longer opens an empty scope.

heading: Changelog › 0.1.4 — 2026-10-29
text: Changelog › 0.1.4 — 2026-10-29. Discrete control: controllers that run at a sample time, as in a microcontroller, and more motor and drive blocks. - Discrete transfer function and discrete state space. - Discrete integrator (forward Euler, backward Euler or trapezoidal) with limits and a reset input. - Discrete PID with a filtered derivative, output limits and anti-windup (clamping or back-calculation). - Rate transition, to pass a signal between sample times (hold, or a one-sample delay). - Sample-time colours (View › Sample-time colours): every block is coloured by how often its output changes, with a legend: continuous, each sample time, constant, or several rates. - A reset input on the Integrator (rising, falling or either edge), located exactly. - Goto and From: send a signal by name without a wire, within one diagram or across the whole model. - Sources: square wave, triangle wave, chirp (frequency sweep), repeating sequence. - Terminator, to end an output you do not need. Motors and drives - Switched reluctance motor (6/4, 12/8 …) with an asymmetric bridge, and typical ratings. - DC link (with a diode rectifier that only charges it), inverter DC current, and a current sensor with gain, offset, bandwidth and noise.

heading: Changelog › 0.1.4 — 2026-10-29
text: Changelog › 0.1.4 — 2026-10-29. Worked examples: a digital PMSM drive (10 kHz current loop, 1 kHz speed loop) whose DC link rises while the motor brakes; a DC motor with a digital and a continuous PID side by side; switched reluctance motor speed control. Checked: the discrete blocks against their difference equations; power balance for the induction, synchronous, DC and BLDC machines; the switched reluctance motor's torque and energy balance. See the verification record. - A signal resting at exactly zero (such as a reset input between pulses) could make the variable-step solvers take endless tiny steps.

heading: Changelog › 0.1.2 — 2026-10-28
text: Changelog › 0.1.2 — 2026-10-28. The motor library: DC, induction and synchronous motors, BLDC and stepper motors, and the pieces of a drive. - DC motors: separately excited, shunt, series and compound, each with its field circuit. - Induction motors: squirrel-cage, double-cage and wound-rotor (rotor voltages as an input, for starting resistors or a rotor-side drive), fed with three-phase voltages. - Synchronous motors: permanent-magnet with three-phase inputs (surface or interior magnets), synchronous reluctance, and the wound-field salient-pole motor with damper windings used for large medium and high voltage drives. - BLDC motor with ideal six-step commutation and Hall signals; two-phase hybrid stepper motor. - Typical ratings: choose a rating in the Inspector (for example 400 V 11 kW, 3.3 kV 500 kW, 11 kV 5 MW) and every value is filled in at once, as one step you can undo. Replace them with nameplate data when you have it. Drives (a new library group) - Three-phase source, three-phase inverter (average model, or switched with the switching instants located exactly), PWM, encoder. - Clarke and Park transforms and their inverses.

heading: Changelog › 0.1.2 — 2026-10-28
text: Changelog › 0.1.2 — 2026-10-28. Worked examples: induction motor direct-on-line start, induction motor V/f speed control, PMSM field-oriented control with an inverter, BLDC speed control, a 3.3 kV synchronous motor on the grid taking a load step, a DC series motor starting a heavy load, and a stepper motor making full steps. Checked: the induction motors' torque against the exact equivalent circuit at three slips, the DC motors' and the synchronous motor's steady states, the three-phase PMSM against the d–q PMSM, BLDC no-load speed, the stepper's step angle, the inverter's mean voltages and the encoder. See the verification record. - A zero-crossing that fell exactly on zero at the end of a step could be missed; the variable-step solvers now keep its sign and locate it.

heading: Changelog › 0.1.1 — 2026-10-28
text: Changelog › 0.1.1 — 2026-10-28. Dragging blocks from the library works on Windows, and small fixes from first use. - Blocks can be dragged from the Library onto the diagram again on Windows: a ghost of the block follows the pointer and the block lands where you drop it. - A wrong parameter shows its error in the Inspector as soon as you change it, before you press Run. - When the scopes open under the diagram for the first time, the diagram fits itself into the smaller space. - Dots show where a wire splits to several inputs.

heading: Changelog › 0.1.0 — 2026-10-28
text: Changelog › 0.1.0 — 2026-10-28. The first version: draw a model as blocks and wires, press Run and watch the scopes. - A block diagram editor: drag blocks from the library, connect outputs to inputs, and the wires find their own way around the blocks. Move, resize, flip, rename, copy and paste, undo and redo, zoom and pan, a minimap for big diagrams. - About 45 blocks: sources (step, ramp, sine, pulse, clock, table, CSV file, random noise), math (gain, sum, product, divide, min/max, function, saturation), continuous (integrator with limits, derivative, transfer function, zero-pole-gain, state space, PID with anti-windup, transport delay), discontinuities (dead zone, rate limiter, relay, backlash, quantiser), discrete (zero-order hold, unit delay), routing (mux, demux, switch, selector), 1-D and 2-D lookup tables, and sinks (scope, XY graph, display, CSV file). - Motors: a DC motor block and a permanent-magnet synchronous motor block (d–q model). - Subsystems: select blocks and make them one block; open it to see inside; ungroup it again. - Model variables: name a value once (R, L, Kp …) and use it in any parameter. - Five solvers: variable step (Dormand–Prince), stiff (Rosenbrock), and fixed-step RK4, Heun and Euler. Jumps in the inputs are hit exactly; relay switching and integrator limits are located exactly. - Run, stop, pause and single step, with live scopes.

heading: Changelog › 0.1.0 — 2026-10-28
text: Changelog › 0.1.0 — 2026-10-28. - Clear errors that point at the block: unknown names, sizes that do not fit, algebraic loops. - Parameter sweeps: run the model for several values of a variable and compare the runs. Results and analysis - Scopes with cursors, zoom and PNG pictures; results as CSV, ready for Datum Plot. - Bode plot, stability margins, step response and poles and zeros of linear blocks, and the rise time, overshoot and settling time of any signal, from the built-in Python engine. Worked examples: mass–spring–damper, DC motor speed control (the motor built from blocks in a subsystem), DC motor position control, PMSM speed control, pump and tank level control, vehicle cruise control and a room thermostat. And the Datum family window: ribbon, File page, options, print to PDF, a ? card beside every tool, light and dark themes, recovery of unsaved work and updates from inside the app.

heading: Datum Sim: notes for Claude
text: Datum Sim: notes for Claude. Read docs/MEMORY.md first. It is the project's memory: architecture, decisions, roadmap, and a log of every session. The family design guide is FAMILY.md in Edgar-Mendonca/Datum (read-only from here; docs/FAMILY.md links to it). At the end of every session that changes anything, update docs/MEMORY.md: - tick the roadmap - add a session-log entry - record any new decisions - refresh the architecture section if files moved - Rust and Tauri 2, small and efficient code, Windows first. The same look, ribbon, help, printing and updater as every Datum app (FAMILY §2–9); copy from Datum Plan rather than reinventing. - Ship in small numbered releases (0.1.0, 0.1.1, …). Every release appears in the in-app updater. - Engine logic belongs in crates/core (pure Rust, unit-tested), not in the UI. The window never calculates. - The UI is SolidJS + Vite in ui/src/*.tsx (built to ui/dist). State lives in ui/src/store.ts. - Big asks get a docs/PLAN-x.y.md and questions first; build after the answers. - Public words (README, CHANGELOG, site.json, help): never name, compare with, or say the app copies or replaces a commercial product (FAMILY §13). - Licences: check every dependency (MIT/BSD/Apache/MPL only in the app; no GPL, LGPL or AGPL linked in). Record each one in NOTICE. Note evalexpr ≥ 12 is AGPL: do not add it. How we build (see PLAN-0.1 §2):

heading: Datum Sim: notes for Claude
text: Datum Sim: notes for Claude. - Layers point inward: crates/core ← src-tauri ← ui. One owner per meaning (block registry, units, sizes). Expected failures are typed errors, never panics. - Every block and solver has a test against a known answer: solver conformance in crates/core/src/solve.rs, blocks and models in crates/core/src/verify.rs, and a dated record in docs/verification/. - Report only checks that actually ran; say what was not verified. Checks before pushing: - cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings - cargo test --workspace (includes the hardening and verification tests) - python -m unittest discover -s py/tests (needs pip install -r py/requirements.txt; run after cargo test, so the Python API tests find target/debug/datum-sim-cli) - npm run check:ui, then npm run test:ui (dumps the engine fixture, builds the window, runs the Playwright checks) - cargo deny check (licences, advisories, sources; CI runs it) - A change you can see: check it in the real app (cargo build -p datum-sim && tests_ui/realapp.sh steps.sh shots/, see the script) and add a UI check for every bug

heading: Datum Sim: notes for Claude
text: Datum Sim: notes for Claude. Releasing: 1. Bump the version in src-tauri/Cargo.toml and crates/core/Cargo.toml. 2. Add a CHANGELOG section (## x.y.z — date). 3. Push the tag vX.Y.Z, or run release.yml with workflow_dispatch when tag pushes are blocked. The workflow creates the tag and publishes DatumSim-x.y.z-setup.exe and SHA256SUMS.txt. 4. After the first release: tell the user to add Datum Sim to the hub's apps.json and its icon to the hub's brand/ (in the hub chat). 5. A change to py/requirements.txt needs py/runtime.txt bumped, so installed apps unpack the new runtime. 6. Keep docs/site.json true with each release: about and steps (the Overview on the family site's app page, FAMILY §10), highlights and roadmap. Check every sentence against what the app really does; never name or compare with commercial products (FAMILY §13).

heading: Contributing › How the code is laid out
text: Contributing › How the code is laid out. - crates/core: the engine in pure Rust: the model and its edits, the block library, the compiler, the solvers, results, wire routing and sweeps. All calculation lives here, with tests. - src-tauri: the desktop shell (commands, files, the run thread, the Python engine, the updater). - ui/src: the window (SolidJS + TypeScript). It shows what the engine computes and sends edits back as operations. - py: the Python analysis engine (python-control) and its tests. - docs/MEMORY.md: architecture, decisions, roadmap and a log of every session. Read it first.

heading: Contributing › Before you send a change
text: Contributing › Before you send a change. Keep code compact and in the style around it. A new block or solver comes with a test against a known answer; a new window feature with a UI test where it can. Never add GPL, LGPL or AGPL code to the app. By contributing you agree your work is released under the MIT licence.

Model and simulate dynamic systems: block diagrams, control and motors. Draw a model as blocks and wires, press Run, and see how the system behaves over time. Datum Sim is for control, mechanical, electrical, process and mechatronics engineers, researchers and students. It is free and open source (MIT), Windows first, installs in seconds and updates itself.

heading: What it does
text: What it does. - Block diagrams: 84 blocks (sources, math, transfer functions, state space, PID, delays, discontinuities, lookup tables, scopes, discrete control, motors and drives). Wires find their own way around the blocks; move their segments, branch from them and name the signals they carry. Notes, block colours and Find (Ctrl+F) on the diagram. - Discrete control: discrete transfer function, state space, integrator and PID, rate transition; the diagram can colour every block by its sample time. - Motors: DC (permanent-magnet, separately excited, shunt, series, compound), induction (squirrel-cage, double-cage, wound-rotor), synchronous (permanent-magnet, reluctance, wound-field with dampers), switched reluctance, BLDC and stepper motors, with typical values for low, medium and high voltage ratings. - Drives: three-phase source, inverter (average or switched), DC link, PWM, Clarke and Park transforms, encoder, current sensor; worked examples from a direct-on-line start to field-oriented control. - Subsystems: group blocks into one, open them, nest them; give them a mask (parameters of their own, help, typical ratings) and keep them in My blocks, your own library. Goto/From tags send signals without wires. - Five solvers: from fixed-step Euler to variable-step and stiff; the variable-step solvers find switching times exactly.

heading: What it does
text: What it does. - Live scopes with two measuring cursors, step-response marks, comparison of earlier runs, stacked plots and PNG or SVG pictures; a probe reads any wire after a run. Parameter sweeps, and results as CSV for Datum Plot. - Analysis from the built-in Python engine: Bode plots and stability margins, step responses, poles and zeros, rise time, overshoot and settling time. - Checked: the solvers, main blocks and motors are tested against known answers. See the verification records for 0.1.0, the motors and discrete control.

heading: What it does › Automation

heading: Datum Sim: project memory › 1. Architecture
text: Datum Sim: project memory › 1. Architecture. crates/core is the engine (pure Rust, no Tauri): the model and its edits, the block library, the compiler, the solvers, results, wire routing and sweeps. src-tauri is the shell: commands, files, the run thread, the Python engine and the updater. ui is the window: it draws what the engine returns and sends edits as operations. py is the Python analysis engine.

heading: Datum Sim: project memory › 1. Architecture › How a run works
text: Datum Sim: project memory › 1. Architecture › How a run works. 1. compile.rs flattens subsystems (their In and Out blocks become pass-throughs), evaluates every parameter with the model variables, infers signal widths (iterating to a fixed point), and sorts blocks by direct feedthrough (Kahn's algorithm). A cycle without a state is an algebraic loop error naming its blocks. 2. Each block (rt.rs) has out (outputs from state and inputs), deriv (continuous states), update (at accepted steps: discrete states, modes, histories), next_hit (times the solver must land on: jumps and samples) and zc (zero-crossing surfaces). 3. solve::drive steps the system: fixed step (Euler, Heun, RK4) or variable step (Dormand–Prince 5(4) with dense output; Rosenbrock 2(3) for stiff systems). It never steps over a hit, locates zero-crossings by bisection on the dense output, and calls the model at every accepted step (log, update, stop/pause). 4. The shell runs this on a thread and streams new samples to the window (sim-live, about 20 a second); sim-done ends it. Full results stay in Rust; the scopes ask for each zoom level reduced with peaks kept (decimate_multi).

heading: Datum Sim: project memory › 1. Architecture › Release flow
text: Datum Sim: project memory › 1. Architecture › Release flow. release.yml (windows-latest): checks the tag matches the version, builds the newest embeddable CPython 3.13 with py/requirements.txt, runs the Python tests on that runtime, zips it into src-tauri/runtime.zip, builds one NSIS installer with it inside (tauri.release.conf.json), writes SHA256SUMS.txt, takes the notes from CHANGELOG and publishes the GitHub Release. Run it by pushing a tag vX.Y.Z or from the Actions tab. Every update downloads the whole installer (Plot's rule); the runtime is unpacked again only when py/runtime.txt changes.

heading: Datum Sim: project memory › 1. Architecture › How we build (from PLAN-0.1 §2; practices taken from morluto/rea)
text: Datum Sim: project memory › 1. Architecture › How we build (from PLAN-0.1 §2; practices taken from morluto/rea). - Layers point inward: crates/core ← src-tauri ← ui. One owner per meaning: the block library (blocks.rs), port geometry (blocks::port_xy, drawn by the window), widths (the compiler). Expected failures are typed errors with the block's id, never panics. - Test depths: module tests in each file; solver conformance in solve.rs; closed-form verification in verify.rs; boundary tests (file reader, Python protocol); acceptance (UI tests and real-app screenshots). - Goldens come from closed-form answers or published values (Robertson, Hairer & Wanner). - Dated verification records in docs/verification/, listing what was not verified. - Report only checks that ran.

heading: Datum Sim: project memory › 1. Architecture › How we work
text: Datum Sim: project memory › 1. Architecture › How we work. 1. The user reviews a release and sends screenshots. 2. Reproduce first. 3. Big asks get a plan file and questions; build after the answers. 4. Engine first (with a test), then the UI. 5. Check every change in the real app (Xvfb screenshots, tests_ui/realapp.sh). 6. Add a UI test for every bug. 7. Run all checks: clippy -D warnings, cargo test (with the hardening and verification tests), the Python tests, the UI type-check and UI tests, cargo deny check. 8. Release. 9. Report in plain language: what changed, what was checked, what is not done.

heading: Datum Sim: project memory › 5. Known limits and next steps
text: Datum Sim: project memory › 5. Known limits and next steps. - The user ran 0.1.0 on Windows (installer, Python, printing, updater work). The 0.1.2 motor library has not yet been run on a Windows PC; CI builds and tests on Windows and macOS. - The Python engine's large-array path (binary frames instead of JSON) is not needed yet: analyses send small data; step specifications send at most 20 000 points. - A branch is a second wire from the same output (drawn along the first where they run together); a wire's first and last segments stay on their ports. - Algebraic loops are reported, not solved (0.3). Discrete blocks have no sample offset yet, and are not linearised for analysis. - Motors: no saturation, iron losses or BLDC commutation ripple; presets are typical values, not real machines; power-balance checks and switched reluctance are still to do. The switched inverter is slow for long runs (every switching instant is located); the average model is the default. - Linear analysis works on single blocks; linearising whole models arrives in 0.3. - Datum Plot has the same zip 2.x advisories (fix in Plot's chat: zip 9). - After the first release: add Datum Sim to the hub's apps.json and copy docs/brand/datum-sim-icon.svg into the hub's brand/ (in the hub chat), then regenerate the brain.

heading: Datum Sim: plan for 0.1 › 1. The brief in one paragraph
text: Datum Sim: plan for 0.1 › 1. The brief in one paragraph. A free, open-source (MIT) Windows desktop app to model and simulate dynamic systems. You draw a block diagram, press Run and watch scopes fill as the system evolves. Later releases add control design (linearise, Bode, root locus, PID tuning), physical components (mechanical, electrical, hydraulic, thermal), sweeps and Monte Carlo, fitting to measured data and FMU exchange. It is part of the Datum family and follows FAMILY.md for stack, look, docs, updater and releases. The full brief is in briefs/DATUM-SIM.md.

heading: Datum Sim: plan for 0.1 › 2. What we learned before planning
text: Datum Sim: plan for 0.1 › 2. What we learned before planning. heading: Datum Sim: plan for 0.1 › 2. What we learned before planning › Corrections to the brief
text: Datum Sim: plan for 0.1 › 2. What we learned before planning › Corrections to the brief. Brief says ; What we found ; Consequence ; Start the block editor from Plan's Network Diagram ; Plan's diagram (ui/src/views.tsx 13–144, crates/core/src/network.rs) is read-only: automatic col/row layout, fixed 3-segment wires that pass through boxes, click-select only. No dragging, ports, wire drawing, routing or multi-select. ; Reuse its viewport (scroll pan, zoom, minimap, dot grid, arrows, print path). The editing layer is new (about 1–1.5k lines of UI plus a router in Rust). The biggest UI job in 0.1. ; Undo/redo "as ops, like Plan's doc.rs" ; Plan sends ops (enum Op, Batch) but undoes with whole-document snapshots (undo: Vec , limit 200). ; Copy exactly that. A model is small; snapshots are simple and safe (the hardening rule "a failed edit leaves the document exactly as it was" falls out for free). ; evalexpr for block expressions ; evalexpr became AGPL-3.0 from v12 (Oct 2024). meval/fasteval are unmaintained. ; Write our own small expression parser (≈300–400 lines, expr.rs). We need it anyway: units, symbolic derivatives for linearisation (0.3) and equations for physical components (0.4). ; Scopes in the family chart style with Chart.js ; Chart.js struggles with 10⁵–10⁶ points updated live. Datum Plot does not use Chart.js at all (matplotlib SVG). ; Propose uPlot (MIT, ≈50 kB, built for large live time series) for scopes, styled exactly like the

heading: Datum Sim: plan for 0.1 › 2. What we learned before planning › Corrections to the brief
text: Datum Sim: plan for 0.1 › 2. What we learned before planning › Corrections to the brief. family charts (white plot, thin axes, Okabe-Ito, crosshair, PNG button). Chart.js stays for small charts. Question 7. ; Python "as in Datum Plot" ; Plot's worker is one request → one answer over JSON lines: no request ids, no progress, no cancel, 60 s timeout, arrays as JSON/base64. Its installer is 113 MB and every update re-downloads the runtime. ; Reuse Plot's runtime pack and process handling; extend the protocol (ids, progress, cancel, binary arrays) when Python arrives. Question 2 decides when. ; diffsol, SUNDIALS for solvers ; diffsol 0.18 (MIT, pure Rust, active, BDF/SDIRK, mass-matrix DAEs, root finding), but its API still changes between minor versions. sundials-sys is BSD but needs CMake + clang on Windows. ; Hand-write Euler, Heun, RK4 and Dormand–Prince 5(4) (full control of steps, events and streaming); use diffsol for BDF behind our own Solver trait. SUNDIALS (IDA) only if 0.4 needs fully implicit DAEs. ; OpenModelica as an optional compiler ; OpenModelica is OSMC-PL / AGPL-3. The full ModelingToolkit (Julia) is now AGPL too. ; Study ideas, never copy code. External-process use only (0.5, optional). See question 4. ;

heading: Datum Sim: plan for 0.1 › 2. What we learned before planning › What rea teaches us (the way of building)
text: Datum Sim: plan for 0.1 › 2. What we learned before planning › What rea teaches us (the way of building). morluto/rea (MIT) has nothing about simulation, but it is a good model of how to build a hard tool so it stays right. We take these practices; we do not use rea against any other simulator (that would break their licences and FAMILY §13). - Layers that point inward: engine (crates/core) ← app commands (src-tauri) ← window (ui). One owner per meaning: units are parsed once, block definitions live in one registry, sizes are worked out once in the compiler. Expected failures are typed errors, never panics; "unknown" is never treated as "absent". - Test depths, each with a purpose: - *module*: colocated unit tests per block and solver; - *boundary*: one real seam per test (the .dsim reader, a Tauri command, later the Python worker); - *acceptance*: the built UI driving a real model end to end (Plan's tests_ui/run.cjs pattern); - *conformance*: every solver passes one shared contract (order of convergence, Dahlquist, oscillator energy, events), parameterised by what it supports (stiff, events, DAE). - Goldens from real producers: reference trajectories come from closed-form answers or published test sets, stored with tolerances and the source they came from. - Property tests (proptest): save → open is identity; block sorting is a valid order; halving the step shrinks the error by about 2^p.

heading: Datum Sim: plan for 0.1 › 2. What we learned before planning › What rea teaches us (the way of building)
text: Datum Sim: plan for 0.1 › 2. What we learned before planning › What rea teaches us (the way of building). - Mutation testing (cargo-mutants) on the solvers, step control, event location and the compiler, nightly and informational at first: it shows which tests would not notice a broken solver. - Dated verification records: docs/verification/YYYY-MM-DD.md with commit, test counts, accuracy and speed numbers, and what was not verified. These grow into the verification report that ships with the app (§5 of the brief). - Report only checks that ran. Already Datum's habit; written into CLAUDE.md. What we skip from rea: Turbo, the CLI/MCP dual adapter, plugin packaging and its very long testing guide. Cargo, npm scripts and FAMILY §11 are enough.

heading: Datum Sim: plan for 0.1 › 3. Brainstorm › Who uses it and for what
text: Datum Sim: plan for 0.1 › 3. Brainstorm › Who uses it and for what. - Students and lecturers: step and Bode of a second-order system, PID loops, a worked example per lecture. They need clear help, examples and printouts. - Control engineers: tuning loops before commissioning (anti-surge, level, temperature, speed). They need trustworthy solvers, step specifications, sweeps and Datum Plot export. - Mechanical, electrical and process engineers: physical components (0.4) without writing equations. - Researchers: reproducible models, verified solvers, scripting (Python blocks, 0.6), FMUs (0.5).

heading: Datum Sim: plan for 0.1 › 3. Brainstorm › What makes it good (beyond the feature list)
text: Datum Sim: plan for 0.1 › 3. Brainstorm › What makes it good (beyond the feature list). 1. Trust. Every block and solver is tested against a known answer, and the verification report ships in the app. "Is this number right?" always has an answer. 2. Instant feedback. Scopes fill live; editing a parameter and pressing Run again takes under a second for typical models. Later: "live tuning" (drag a gain while it runs). 3. Explains itself. A ? card on every block, with the equation, ports, parameters and a tiny example. Errors in plain words that point at the block: "Algebraic loop: Sum1 → Gain2 → Sum1. Add a delay or an integrator in the loop." 4. Units on every parameter (0.1 shows and checks them; conversion arrives with Calc's units work). 5. Family connections. Results to Datum Plot in one click; materials from Atlas (0.4); the same printing, help and updater as every other app. 6. Files you can read. .dsim is pretty JSON, versioned with migrations, diff-friendly in git.

heading: Datum Sim: plan for 0.1 › 3. Brainstorm › Ideas parked for later (not 0.1)
text: Datum Sim: plan for 0.1 › 3. Brainstorm › Ideas parked for later (not 0.1). Live parameter tuning while running · signal logging to HDF5 · model comparison (diff two .dsim files) · "explain this result" (energy balance, which block saturated) · a command line (datumsim run model.dsim --out results.csv) for batch work and CI · a lecture pack of examples · a model checker (unconnected ports, unused parameters, suspicious step sizes) · code generation (C) for embedded targets · co-simulation with Datum Field later.

heading: Datum Sim: plan for 0.1 › 4. Architecture
text: Datum Sim: plan for 0.1 › 4. Architecture. The block interface (taken from how open simulators are built: Scicos-style job flags, Drake/Collimator-style declarations; ideas only, no code): - Signals are f64 vectors whose width the compiler infers (most are width 1); Mux/Demux change width. - Execution order: a graph with only direct-feedthrough edges, sorted with Tarjan SCC. Integrators, delays and unit delays have no feedthrough, so they break loops. A non-trivial SCC is reported as an algebraic loop in 0.1; it is solved with Newton and tearing in 0.2. - Major and minor steps: the solver calls outputs/derivatives at its stages (minor). Logging, discrete updates and mode changes (saturation, relay) happen only at accepted steps (major), so a variable-step solver never sees a block change its mind mid-step. - Transport delay keeps a history buffer and reads it with interpolation. - Running: src-tauri starts the simulation on a worker thread. Every ~50 ms it sends the new decimated samples to the UI as an event, and the scopes append them. Stop sets an AtomicBool; Step runs one major step. Full-resolution results stay in Rust; CSV and Plot export read them there.

heading: Datum Sim: plan for 0.1 › 4. Architecture
text: Datum Sim: plan for 0.1 › 4. Architecture. - Wires that route around blocks: route.rs in Rust (fast, testable). A* on a sparse orthogonal grid built from block edges and port stubs, penalising bends and crossings, then nudging parallel segments apart. The UI asks for the routes after each move; a user-placed bend point is kept as a waypoint. No LGPL/EPL routing library is needed. - The window never calculates (FAMILY §2): the UI sends ops and draws what the engine returns. Python, when it arrives (question 2): Plot's runtime pack (release.yml runtime step, runtime.rs, runtime.txt) and process handling (py.rs) are copied. The protocol is extended: - request ids; - progress lines before the answer; - cancel messages; - per-command timeouts; - binary arrays: a JSON header followed by raw little-endian f64, or a memory-mapped .npy in the cache folder, never base64. Python starts lazily, on the first analysis. Heavy modules are imported inside their handlers. Results come back as arrays that the UI draws; matplotlib is used only for publication figures, if at all. Dependencies for 0.1 (Rust): serde, serde_json, petgraph (MIT/Apache), diffsol (MIT; the nalgebra backend), nalgebra (Apache-2.0), tauri 2, tauri-plugin-dialog, ureq, sha2 (as Plan). UI: solid-js, @fontsource IBM Plex, uPlot (MIT). All recorded in NOTICE; deny.toml from Plan.

heading: Datum Sim: plan for 0.1 › 5. Scope of 0.1
text: Datum Sim: plan for 0.1 › 5. Scope of 0.1. The brief's 0.1 list is large. To keep the family rule "small, consecutive releases" and have the updater working from day one, 0.1 is split into steps. Each step is a release through the updater. Release ; What ships ; 0.1.0 shell ; FAMILY §12 shell copied from Plan and renamed: installer, updater, title bar, ribbon (Model · Simulate · Analyze · View · Help), File page (Home, New, Open, Save, Save As, Export, Print, Options, Updates, Roadmap), Options, Help with ? cards, Roadmap page reading docs/site.json. The whole UI laid out with planned features dimmed (as Plot did). .dsim open/save with undo. The canvas shows a model (pan, zoom, minimap), with a first working run: Step → Transfer function → Scope with RK4. Hardening tests, deny.toml, CI on Linux, Windows and macOS. ; 0.1.1 editor ; Place blocks from the searchable library, drag with snap, draw wires port to port, orthogonal routing around blocks, multi-select (marquee, Shift/Ctrl), copy/paste, delete, align, inspector with parameters and units, a ? card per block. ; 0.1.2 blocks and solvers ; About 25 core blocks (below). Euler, Heun, RK4, Dormand–Prince with error control, BDF (diffsol). Run bar: start, stop time, solver, step or tolerance, Run/Stop/Step, progress. Algebraic-loop and size errors pointing at the block. Live scopes with cursors and a PNG button; XY graph;

heading: Datum Sim: plan for 0.1 › 5. Scope of 0.1
text: Datum Sim: plan for 0.1 › 5. Scope of 0.1. display. ; 0.1.3 results and examples ; Parameter sweep (scope overlays); export to CSV and Datum Plot; Print to PDF (diagram, scopes, results report); worked examples; the first verification record. ; The ~25 blocks of 0.1: - Sources: Step, Ramp, Sine, Pulse, Constant, Clock, From table, From file (CSV). - Math: Gain, Sum, Product, Divide, Abs, Sign, Min/Max, Function (expression), Saturation. - Continuous: Integrator (with limits; reset arrives with events in 0.2), Derivative, Transfer function, Zero-pole-gain, State-space, PID, Transport delay. - Discontinuities: Dead zone, Rate limiter, Relay, Backlash, Quantiser. These use major-step modes; exact zero-crossing location arrives in 0.2. - Routing: Mux, Demux, Switch, Selector. - Lookup tables: 1-D, 2-D. - Sinks: Scope, XY graph, Display, To file, To Datum Plot. That is a little over 25. The rest of the brief's list follows its own release plan: discrete blocks, goto/from, subsystems and buses in 0.2. Worked examples for 0.1 (question 3): mass–spring–damper; DC motor speed with PID; pump–pipe–tank level (signal-block version); vehicle cruise control. Compressor anti-surge needs a compressor map, valve dynamics and events, so it suits 0.2 (events) or 0.4 (physical). The heat exchanger suits 0.4 (thermal).

heading: Datum Sim: plan for 0.1 › 5. Scope of 0.1
text: Datum Sim: plan for 0.1 › 5. Scope of 0.1. Definition of done for 0.1.x: every block and solver has a test against a known answer; CI is green on three OSes; real-app screenshots (Xvfb) have been checked; and a 500-block model edits smoothly and runs within the measured speed gate.

heading: Datum Sim: plan for 0.1 › 7. Verification plan (grows every release)
text: Datum Sim: plan for 0.1 › 7. Verification plan (grows every release). - Solvers (conformance contract): - Dahlquist y' = λy; - order of convergence (halve h → error / 2^p); - harmonic oscillator (energy and phase); - Van der Pol at μ = 1 and μ = 1000; - Robertson to 1e11 (mass conserved; BDF only); - Lotka–Volterra (invariant); - bouncing ball (0.2: impact times t1 = sqrt(2h/g), later intervals × e). - first-order step 1 − e^(−t/τ); - second-order step (peak exp(−ζπ/√(1−ζ²)), settling ≈ 4/(ζωₙ)); - PID loop against its closed form; - transport delay exactness; - lookup interpolation; - saturation and dead-zone algebra. - Published sets: the Bari *Test Set for IVP Solvers* (Robertson, HIRES and others, with reference solutions); Hairer–Wanner problems. - Cross-checks (once Python is in): SciPy solve_ivp and python-control step_response/step_info. FMI Reference-FMUs in 0.5. - Output: docs/verification/YYYY-MM-DD.md (what ran, numbers, what was not verified) and, from 0.1.3, a printable verification report under Help.

heading: Datum Sim: plan for 0.1 › 9. Questions for the user
text: Datum Sim: plan for 0.1 › 9. Questions for the user. 1. Accent colour. The spares are Amber #A8650F (too close to the amber diamond and the warning colour) and Crimson #B83250 (close to the error red). Proposed: a new Orange #C2410C, which is distinct from Plan's blue, Plot's teal and Atlas's violet, and passes 4.5:1 for text on white. Its accent set would be: --blue #C2410C, --blue2 #A3360A, --sky #F6C3A5, --pale #FCEEE6, --sel #F9E0D1, --sel2 #F0C2A6, dark --blue #F08A5D, sidebar #5C220A. The icon in all four candidates is in docs/brand/accent-options.png. 2. Python. Bundled from 0.1, like Plot: a ~110 MB installer, but analysis is ready from the start. Or (proposed) a Rust-only 0.1 (installer about 8–10 MB) with Python arriving in 0.3 for control design, with the improved protocol. 3. Worked examples for 0.1. Proposed: mass–spring–damper, DC motor PID, pump–tank level, cruise control. Anti-surge and the heat exchanger come later (they need events or physical components). Is that the right order, and do you have real parameters (for example from your anti-surge work) you would like used? 4. Physical modelling (0.4). Proposed: our own equation-based components in Rust. This keeps everything MIT, is fast, and works with our solvers and FMU export. OpenModelica would be an optional external compiler later; it is AGPL/OSMC, so it runs as a separate process only. 5. Priority after 0.1. Proposed: 0.2 (events, subsystems, discrete)

heading: Datum Sim: plan for 0.1 › 9. Questions for the user
text: Datum Sim: plan for 0.1 › 9. Questions for the user. first, because both control design and physical models need it. Then control design (0.3) before physical modelling (0.4), as the brief says. Agree? 6. Ribbon tabs. Model · Simulate · Analyze · View · Help, with a contextual Format tab when blocks or wires are selected. Proposed: yes, with the File button first as in every family app. 7. Scope charts. Use uPlot (MIT, fast with large live data) for scopes, in the family chart style, instead of Chart.js. OK to add it as a family-approved chart library for large time series? 8. Updates with Python (when it arrives). Plot re-downloads its whole runtime (~100 MB) on every update. Keep that simple rule, or allow a small app-only update when the runtime has not changed? 9. Default branch and deployment. The repo is empty. Our first push (claude/dreamy-babbage-dyf9nr) becomes the default branch, as in the other apps. Is that fine, or would you like a main branch? Code signing waits for 1.0, as in the other apps. Agree? 10. 0.1 split. Ship 0.1 as four small releases (0.1.0 shell → 0.1.1 editor → 0.1.2 blocks and solvers → 0.1.3 results and examples), as in §5?

heading: Datum Sim: plan for the 0.1.x releases (and the road to 0.2) › 1. Where 0.1.0 stands
text: Datum Sim: plan for the 0.1.x releases (and the road to 0.2) › 1. Where 0.1.0 stands. - Works and is tested: the editor, 45 blocks, motors, subsystems, five solvers, live scopes, sweeps, Python analyses, the family window. CI green on three systems; installer 85.6 MB. - Not yet seen on a real Windows PC: installer, first Python start, print to PDF, updater. The user's Windows test feeds 0.1.1 first, as in Plan. - Rough edges found while using it under Xvfb (session 2), not fixed yet: - wires: no branch dots when one output feeds several inputs; feedback wires can bunch up; bend points can only be added, not moved; - when the scopes dock opens on the first run, the bottom of the diagram is hidden; - scopes: no measuring cursors, no y-zoom, no auto-scale button; - a bad parameter shows only when you press Run; - the hover tooltip on blocks covers the diagram; - print preview not checked page by page.

heading: Datum Sim: plan for the 0.1.x releases (and the road to 0.2) › 2. Brainstorm › A. Comfort while building (small, high value)
text: Datum Sim: plan for the 0.1.x releases (and the road to 0.2) › 2. Brainstorm › A. Comfort while building (small, high value). 1. Wire branch points: a dot where a wire splits; drag a branch from the middle of a wire to a new input (as people expect). 2. Move wire segments: drag a straight segment sideways; double-click a bend to remove it. 3. Signal names on wires: name a signal once ("speed"); the name shows on the wire and in scope legends. 4. Live parameter checks: the inspector shows "unknown name Kx" under the field as you type, before Run. 5. Text notes on the diagram: a note box for explanations (teaching, reviews). 6. Find a block (Ctrl+F) across subsystems; distribute blocks evenly; align to grid. 7. Block colour (to mark plant, controller, sensors).

heading: Datum Sim: plan for the 0.1.x releases (and the road to 0.2) › 2. Brainstorm › B. Seeing results
text: Datum Sim: plan for the 0.1.x releases (and the road to 0.2) › 2. Brainstorm › B. Seeing results. 1. Scope cursors: two vertical cursors with t, y and Δt, Δy readouts; peak and value markers. 2. Scope settings: y-range or auto-scale, one plot per input (stacked), line styles, legend on or off. 3. Signal probe: after a run, hover any wire to read its value at the cursor time (no scope needed). Needs the engine to log every signal (an option: "log all signals"). 4. Keep and compare runs: the last few runs kept; overlay "run 3 vs run 5" in a scope. 5. Publication export: a scope as SVG or a high-resolution PNG at a chosen size. 6. Step-response lines on the scope: rise time, overshoot and settling marked on the plot.

heading: Datum Sim: plan for the 0.1.x releases (and the road to 0.2) › 2. Brainstorm › C. More blocks (pulled forward from 0.2 where they are small)
text: Datum Sim: plan for the 0.1.x releases (and the road to 0.2) › 2. Brainstorm › C. More blocks (pulled forward from 0.2 where they are small). - Signal sources: square, triangle, chirp (frequency sweep), PWM, repeating sequence. - Discrete: discrete transfer function, discrete integrator, discrete PID, rate transition; sample-time colours on blocks. - Integrator reset (external reset input), dynamic saturation, Coulomb and viscous friction, hit crossing. - Goto / From (send a signal by name without a wire). - Math function (exp, log, sqrt, square, reciprocal) and trigonometry as blocks, not only in Function.

heading: Datum Sim: plan for the 0.1.x releases (and the road to 0.2) › 2. Brainstorm › D. Making subsystems reusable
text: Datum Sim: plan for the 0.1.x releases (and the road to 0.2) › 2. Brainstorm › D. Making subsystems reusable. - Masks: a subsystem gets its own parameters (R, L, Kt …) shown in the inspector, an icon or text on the block, and a ? card. The inside uses the mask parameters. - My blocks (user library): save a subsystem to a library file; it appears in the Library panel for every model. - Linked or copied: decide whether library blocks update when the library changes (linked) or stay as copied.

heading: Datum Sim: plan for the 0.1.x releases (and the road to 0.2) › 2. Brainstorm › E. Motors and drives (the user's interest)
text: Datum Sim: plan for the 0.1.x releases (and the road to 0.2) › 2. Brainstorm › E. Motors and drives (the user's interest). - Clarke and Park transforms (abc ↔ αβ ↔ dq) and their inverses. - Induction motor (d–q model) with a speed or V/f example. - BLDC motor with six-step commutation, and Hall sensors. - Three-phase inverter (average model) and a PWM source; DC link. - Encoder (quantised angle, speed estimate) and a current sensor with noise and delay. - An example pack: FOC of a PMSM with Park/Clarke on real three-phase signals; V/f induction motor; BLDC six-step.

text: Datum Sim: plan for the 0.1.x releases (and the road to 0.2) › 2. Brainstorm › F. text: Datum Sim: plan for the 0.1.x releases (and the road to 0.2) › 4. Questions for the user. 1. Windows test first? Shall 0.1.1 wait for your screenshots from a Windows PC, or start now with the known fixes and add your findings to 0.1.2? 2. Order after 0.1.1: the plan puts wires (0.1.2) and scopes (0.1.3) before new blocks and motors. Would you rather have motors and drives (0.1.5) earlier? 3. Motors: which matter most to you: induction motor, BLDC six-step, the three-phase inverter with PWM, or full FOC with Park/Clarke on three-phase signals? 4. Live tuning (sliders while running): worth it in 0.1.x, or later? 5. Masks and user libraries: should library blocks be linked (change the library, every model updates) or copied (each model keeps its own copy)? Linked is more powerful; copied is simpler and safer. 6. Discrete blocks (0.1.4): do you need them soon for real controller work (sample times, discrete PID), or can they wait for 0.2?

text: Datum Sim: plan for the 0.1.x releases (and the road to 0.2) › 5. Answers (session 4, 2026-10-28) and the new order. Cause of the drag bug: on Windows, Tauri's window catches drag-and-drop for dropping files (dragDropEnabled, on by default), so HTML drag-and-drop from the library never reached the diagram. Linux (where 0.1.0 was checked) does not do this. Fixed both ways: the setting is off, and the library drag now uses plain mouse events with a ghost block, which behaves the same on every system and is covered by a UI test. text: Datum Sim: plan for the 0.1.x releases (and the road to 0.2) › 6. The motor library (0.1.2), first draft (built in session 5; see MEMORY for what differs). heading: Plan 0.2: a bigger build › 1. The idea
text: Plan 0.2: a bigger build › 1. The idea. The roadmap has three small releases next: discrete control (0.1.4), wires and diagram (0.1.5) and scopes (0.1.6). The user asked for "a little bigger build". This plan merges them into one release, 0.2.0, and adds the two features that make models reusable: masks and My blocks. That joins the "Reusable models" item already planned for 0.2. Theme: build real controllers, read the results properly, reuse what you build. Releases stay numbered and small inside the build. Each part is pushed as it is done, and patch releases (0.1.4, 0.1.5, …) can still go out on the way if you want them (question 2).

Left for later (not in 0.2.0). - Buses, solving algebraic loops, live tuning, linearising whole models (0.3). - Switched reluctance motor, DC link and current sensor blocks, motor power-balance checks: these could join 0.2.0 if you want (question 4).

heading: Plan 0.2: a bigger build › 3. Engine changes behind it
text: Plan 0.2: a bigger build › 3. Engine changes behind it. - Sample times: each block gets a rate (continuous, discrete Ts with offset, inherited, constant). Inherited rates are worked out by fixed-point iteration, as the widths are today. The solver already lands on every next_hit; discrete blocks share one timetable instead of each having its own. - Masks: a subsystem's mask parameters are evaluated in its own scope: inner names first, then the model's variables. This needs a scope stack in parameter evaluation. Today there is one flat variable table. - Signal logging: an option to log every signal, decimated with peaks kept, for the probe and for comparing runs. - File format: .dsim gets version 2 (masks, notes, signal names, run history off by default). Version 1 files open and are upgraded; a test keeps every 0.1 example and a damaged file opening.

heading: Plan 0.2: a bigger build › 4. Order of work and size
text: Plan 0.2: a bigger build › 4. Order of work and size. Step ; Part ; Size ; 1 ; Sample times in the engine + discrete blocks + verification ; medium ; 2 ; Integrator reset, Goto/From, sources, discrete examples ; small ; 3 ; Scopes: cursors, y-zoom, stacked, pictures, step marks ; medium ; 4 ; Signal logging, probe, compare runs ; medium ; 5 ; Wires: branch, segments, names, notes, find, distribute, colours ; medium ; 6 ; Masks (engine scopes, Inspector, mask editor, file v2) ; large ; 7 ; My blocks (save, library panel, copy into models) ; medium ; 8 ; Docs, help cards, verification record, site.json, release 0.2.0 ; small ; About three times the size of 0.1.2. Every step keeps the CLAUDE.md checks green, adds UI checks for what you can see, and is checked in the real app.

heading: Plan 0.2: a bigger build › 5. Risks
text: Plan 0.2: a bigger build › 5. Risks. - Masks touch parameter evaluation everywhere: the largest change since 0.1.0. Mitigation: build them last, behind the same tests, with the file upgrade tested on every example. - Logging every signal can use a lot of memory on long runs. Mitigation: it is off by default, decimated, and has a cap (as MAX_POINTS today). - One big release delays everything in it. Mitigation: push each step as it is done, and release patches on the way if you prefer (question 2).

heading: Plan 0.2: a bigger build › 6. Questions for the user
text: Plan 0.2: a bigger build › 6. Questions for the user. 1. Scope: all four parts (A–D) in 0.2.0, or A–C now and masks and My blocks in a following build? 2. Releases on the way: one release at the end (0.2.0), or a patch release after each part (0.1.4 discrete, 0.1.5 scopes, …) and 0.2.0 when masks land? 3. Order: the plan starts with discrete control, then scopes, then wires, then masks. Is any part more urgent for you? 4. Motor extras: add the switched reluctance motor, DC link and current sensor, and the motor power-balance checks to this build? 5. Examples: are there models you want as worked examples, for example a model from your own work, a textbook problem, or a particular drive? 6. My blocks location: keep your library in a folder you choose (it can then be shared on a network drive), or only in the app's own data folder?

heading: Plan 0.3: control design › 1. Where we start
text: Plan 0.3: control design › 1. Where we start. Today the analyses (Bode, step response, poles and zeros, margins) work on one linear block at a time: a transfer function, a state space, a PID, the DC motor, a gain or an integrator. Python-control computes them from that block's A, B, C, D. Step-response figures come from a logged signal. 0.3 takes this to whole models. You mark where to look in the diagram (an input, an output, a loop to open). The engine finds the model's linear behaviour there, at an operating point that it can also search for. From that come Bode, Nyquist, root locus and margins of the real loop, a PID tuner, and parameters you can tune while the model runs.

heading: Plan 0.3: control design › 2. What is in it › A. Linearising whole models
text: Plan 0.3: control design › 2. What is in it › A. Linearising whole models. Item ; What it does ; Analysis points ; Mark a wire as an input (where a test signal goes in), an output (what is measured), or a loop opening (the loop is cut there for open-loop analysis). They are drawn on the wire and saved with the model, and they do not change a run. ; Linearise ; The engine linearises the whole model between the marked points: the system's A, B, C, D around an operating point. It uses central differences on the compiled model, so it works with motors, lookup tables and nonlinear blocks too. Linear blocks come out exact. ; Operating points ; Linearise at the model's initial state, at a time in the last run (the states at t = 2 s, say), or at a trimmed point (B). Operating points can be saved and named in the model. ; Discrete parts ; A loop where every sample time is the same is linearised in z, and the analyses work in z. Mixed rates are converted to one rate (ZOH), and the app says so. ;

heading: Plan 0.3: control design › 2. What is in it › B. Trim: finding operating points
text: Plan 0.3: control design › 2. What is in it › B. Trim: finding operating points. Item ; What it does ; Trim ; Find the states and inputs where the model is at rest (all derivatives zero), with chosen outputs held at chosen values. Examples: the tank at 2 m, the motor at 1500 rpm under its load, the cruise control at 25 m/s. ; How ; Pick which inputs are free and which outputs are fixed, in a dialog. The engine solves with Newton–Levenberg–Marquardt in Rust and reports what it could not meet. ;

heading: Plan 0.3: control design › 2. What is in it › C. Analyses of the linearised model
text: Plan 0.3: control design › 2. What is in it › C. Analyses of the linearised model. Item ; What it does ; Bode and margins ; The loop, not only one block: gain and phase margins with their frequencies, marked on the plot ; Nyquist ; With the −1 point, the number of encirclements, and the stability verdict ; Root locus ; Poles as a gain varies, with the gain read under the pointer, and the damping and natural-frequency grid ; Step, impulse, poles and zeros ; Of the open or the closed loop ; Sensitivity ; S and T over frequency: peak sensitivity Ms as a robustness figure ; The plots use the family chart style. The numbers come from the engine (Rust) and python-control. Each analysis can be saved as CSV and as a picture.

heading: Plan 0.3: control design › 2. What is in it › D. PID tuning
text: Plan 0.3: control design › 2. What is in it › D. PID tuning. Item ; What it does ; Tune a PID ; Select a PID (continuous or discrete) and press Tune. The loop is opened at the PID and the plant it sees is linearised. You choose response speed (bandwidth) and robustness (phase margin) with two sliders, and the gains are designed to meet them. Before and after step responses and the loop's Bode plot update as you move the sliders. ; Classic rules too ; Ziegler–Nichols (from the ultimate gain the engine finds) and SIMC (from a first-order-plus-dead-time fit), for teaching and comparison ; Apply ; One undoable edit sets P, I, D and N. A discrete PID's gains are designed for its sample time. ;

heading: Plan 0.3: control design › 2. What is in it › E. Live tuning
text: Plan 0.3: control design › 2. What is in it › E. Live tuning. Item ; What it does ; Tunable variables ; Mark a model variable as tunable with a range. A slider panel appears while the model runs, and moving a slider changes the running model at once: the scopes show the effect. ; What can change live ; Gains, PID gains, constants, limits, set points, lookup-table values: parameters that do not change the model's structure. A change that would (a transfer function's order, a vector's width) waits for the next run, and the app says so. ; Real time ; An option to slow a run to real time (or ×0.1 to ×10), so tuning by hand is possible. ; Keep the result ; "Keep these values" writes the slider values back to the variables as one undoable edit. ;

heading: Plan 0.3: control design › 2. What is in it › F. From the old 0.3 list (question 1)
text: Plan 0.3: control design › 2. What is in it › F. From the old 0.3 list (question 1). - Buses: group named signals into one wire and pick them out by name. - Algebraic loops solved: a loop with no state is solved by Newton iteration at each step, instead of being reported as an error.

heading: Plan 0.3: control design › 3. Engine changes behind it
text: Plan 0.3: control design › 3. Engine changes behind it. - Linearisation (linearise.rs): perturb each state and each marked input on the compiled model, and read the derivatives and marked outputs. Use central differences with steps scaled to each variable. A loop opening becomes an extra input and output pair at the cut. For discrete parts the same is done on the update map. - Trim (trim.rs): a damped Newton (Levenberg–Marquardt) solve for the derivatives = 0 and outputs = targets, with the Jacobian from the same differences. LU is already in linalg.rs. - Live parameters: runtimes get retune(&Pv) for the blocks whose parameters can change live. The run thread takes slider messages between steps, re-evaluates the affected blocks' parameters and retunes them. States are kept, so nothing jumps except what changed. - Analysis points are a new field on wires (point: in ; out ; open), with a format 3 file. Older files open unchanged. - Python: Nyquist, root locus and margins use python-control as Bode does now. The PID design maths (loop shaping to bandwidth and phase margin, Ziegler–Nichols, SIMC, the fit) live in Rust, so they are fast enough to follow the sliders and can be unit-tested.

heading: Plan 0.3: control design › 4. How it is checked
text: Plan 0.3: control design › 4. How it is checked. - Linearisation against closed forms: the mass–spring–damper's A, B, C, D exactly; the DC motor block's transfer function; a PMSM at an operating point against its d–q equations by hand; a Gain → Integrator loop opened at the gain. - Trim against known equilibria: the tank level (√ law), the cruise force balance, the motor speed under load. - Nyquist, margins and root locus against python-control on textbook loops (and against hand results for a type-1 second-order loop). - PID tuning: after tuning, the margins and crossover the engine computes for the new loop must match the targets within a tolerance; Ziegler–Nichols against the classic table on a known plant. - Live tuning: a run where a gain is changed at t = 1 s must match a run where the same change is made by a Step block at 1 s. - As always: UI checks for everything you can see, the real app under Xvfb, and a dated verification record.

heading: Plan 0.3: control design › 5. Order and releases (my proposal)
text: Plan 0.3: control design › 5. Order and releases (my proposal). Release ; Contents ; Size ; 0.2.1 ; Analysis points, linearising whole models at the initial state or a time in a run, Bode and margins of the loop ; medium ; 0.2.2 ; Nyquist, root locus, sensitivity, step and impulse of the loop ; medium ; 0.2.3 ; Trim and saved operating points ; medium ; 0.2.4 ; PID tuning ; medium ; 0.2.5 ; Live tuning and real-time pacing ; medium ; 0.3.0 ; Buses and algebraic loops (if wanted, question 1), docs and the 0.3 verification record ; medium ; About the size of the 0.2 build. As before, each step is pushed as it is done and released when it passes every check.

heading: Plan 0.3: control design › 6. Risks
text: Plan 0.3: control design › 6. Risks. - Linearising at kinks (saturation edges, relays, dead zones) gives a derivative that depends on the side. The engine reports blocks sitting at a kink at the operating point, so a result is never silently wrong. - Live tuning touches the run loop, the most delicate part. Mitigation: only blocks that declare retune can change, changes apply between steps, and the test compares against an equivalent Step. - Trim may not converge on hard models. Mitigation: clear reports of which equations are unmet, starting from the last run's state, and limits on the free inputs.

heading: Plan 0.3: control design › 7. Questions for the user
text: Plan 0.3: control design › 7. Questions for the user. 1. Scope: all of A–E? And should buses and algebraic-loop solving (F) be in this build, or later? 2. Releases: patch releases as each part lands (0.2.1 … 0.2.5, then 0.3.0), as in 0.2? Or one release at the end? 3. Live tuning: sliders for model variables marked as tunable (my proposal: one place, works for every block that uses them)? Or sliders right on any block's parameters too? 4. PID tuning style: is the two-slider design (speed and robustness) what you want, with Ziegler–Nichols and SIMC alongside? Are there other rules you use (for example IMC or lambda tuning, Cohen–Coon)? 5. Motors and drives: should the tuner also offer the usual drive cascade (current loop from motor L and R, then speed loop from inertia), one click for a whole FOC or DC drive? 6. Examples: any plant you want as a worked control-design example? My default would be the DC motor, the tank and a PMSM drive.

heading: Plan 0.3: control design › 8. Automation first (0.2.1, built 2026-11-02)
text: Plan 0.3: control design › 8. Automation first (0.2.1, built 2026-11-02). After the comparison (docs/COMPARISON.md: scripting and batch runs are the one gap every compared tool covers), the user chose "automation first". Built with these defaults: - A command-line program datum-sim-cli (separate from the window, installed next to it): run, sweep, check, info, examples, example, serve. Exit codes 0 done, 1 model errors, 2 wrong command line. - A Python API (import datum_sim, installed with pip from this repository's py/ folder) that drives datum-sim-cli serve over JSON lines: open, set variables and parameters, run (NumPy arrays), sweep, check, save. - Help › Automation in the app with the commands for the open model. - Not in 0.2.1: building models from code (adding blocks and wires), a PyPI release, putting the command line on the PATH. These could follow if wanted.

heading: Datum Sim: plan and roadmap from 0.2.1 › 1. Where we are
text: Datum Sim: plan and roadmap from 0.2.1 › 1. Where we are. - Released: 0.2.1 (2026-11-02), through the in-app updater. It includes the editor, 85 blocks, 14 motor types with LV–HV ratings, discrete control, five solvers, scopes with cursors and run comparison, masks and My blocks, the command line and the Python API. - Strong: ease and install size, motors and drives, public verification, scripting. - Weak: control design is limited to one block at a time. There are no physical (port-based) components, no state machines, no FMU exchange, and the installer is Windows only. - Not verified yet on a real Windows PC: the installed command line, pip install from GitHub, and most features since 0.1.1.

heading: Datum Sim: plan and roadmap from 0.2.1 › 2. How we plan
text: Datum Sim: plan and roadmap from 0.2.1 › 2. How we plan. 1. Small numbered steps, no jumps. Each patch (0.2.2, 0.2.3, …) is one focused piece that works on its own, is released through the updater, and has its tests and a verification record. A minor number (0.3.0, 0.4.0, …) closes a stage. It is a milestone, not a jump. 2. No race to 1.0. 1.0 means "validated and documented for everyday professional use". It comes when the stages below make it true, not on a date. 3. Fixes take the next number. If a bug or a user request comes in, it ships as the next patch, and the planned items move down one number. The order stays; the numbers are only labels. 4. One stage at a time. Each stage gets a short plan with questions before it starts (as PLAN-0.3 does), and the user's answers decide its details. 5. Every step keeps the house rules: engine logic in crates/core with tests against known answers; a UI check for everything visible; a real-app check; CHANGELOG, site.json and MEMORY kept true. 6. The goal (COMPARISON §6): the first free tool people reach for to learn, sketch and check a dynamic system or a drive, working beside the paid tools. Code generation, hardware in the loop and certification are out of scope.

heading: about
text: about. Datum Sim models and simulates dynamic systems. You draw the system as blocks and wires: sources, transfer functions, state space, continuous and discrete PID controllers, lookup tables, and a motor library with DC, induction, synchronous, switched reluctance, BLDC and stepper motors, inverters and transforms. Group blocks into subsystems, give them parameters of their own with a mask, and keep them in your own library. Then press Run and watch the signals on live scopes. Five solvers cover everything from simple fixed-step runs to stiff systems; the variable-step solvers find switching times exactly. Discrete controllers run at their own sample times, and the diagram can colour every block by its rate. Motors come with typical values for low, medium and high voltage ratings. Scopes have measuring cursors, step-response marks and comparison of earlier runs, and a probe reads any wire after a run. Models also run from the command line and from Python, for scripts, batch studies and build servers. Parameter sweeps run in the app's own engine, step-response specifications and Bode plots come from a built-in Python engine, and the solvers, main blocks and motors are checked against known answers.

heading: steps
text: steps. Drag blocks, motors and your own saved blocks from the library, wire them together and set their parameters, or pick a typical rating. Name signals, add notes and colour the blocks. Choose a solver and a stop time, press Run and watch the scopes live. Measure with cursors and step-response marks, compare runs, read any wire with the probe, and sweep parameters to tune the controller.

heading: highlights
text: highlights. text: Verification record: 2026-10-27 (0.1.0 in development) › Hardening (FAMILY §11, crates/core/src/hardening.rs). - Failed edits (13 kinds, including a batch that fails half way) leave the model exactly as it was, with nothing to undo. - 60 random models (2 000 in a longer local run) of random blocks, wires, parameters, groupings, deletions, undos and redos: no panic, invariants hold (unique ids, no dangling wires, one wire per input, ports exist), every compiled model runs, every file round-trips.
