heading: Datum Mesh: project memory › 1. Architecture
text: Datum Mesh: project memory › 1. Architecture. crates/core is the engine (pure Rust, no Tauri): the model and its edits, sections, and (from 0.1.1) elements, meshing, the solver, results and benchmarks. src-tauri is the shell: commands, files, options, recovery and the updater. ui is the window: it draws what the engine returns and sends edits as operations. Units: the engine and the file use SI base units (m, N, Pa, K, W). The window converts for display in one place (ui/src/units.ts): SI shows mm, kN, MPa, °C; US shows in, kip, ksi, °F; frames show coordinates in m (ft), parts in mm (in).

heading: Datum Mesh: project memory › 1. Architecture › The program: the Datum window (0.7.1 on); app/ is the geometry engine
text: Datum Mesh: project memory › 1. Architecture › The program: the Datum window (0.7.1 on); app/ is the geometry engine. 0.7.0 shipped app/ (below) as the program; 0.7.1 withdrew it and went back to the Datum window (ui/ + src-tauri/), which is what the release builds. SolidCraft's crates in app/ stay as the headless geometry engine behind crates/cad, and app/crates/analysis writes the Gmsh scripts. The rest of this section describes 0.7.0's program, kept for reference. 0.9.1 layout of the window: the workflow bar at the far left (Flow, flowSteps, goStep in panels.tsx: the six steps' state, one source for it and the tree), the steps tree (resizable), the model across the middle, the properties card popping up over it (popShown, closePop, popWhat), and the bottom panel (console.tsx: Messages, Solver monitor, Log, Stop). Every message goes through note() in store.ts (kept, written to the Log); edits are described by describeOp. The window people used in 0.7.0 was app/, a fork of SolidCraft (egui + wgpu, Rust 2024; MIT or Apache-2.0, upstream commit f8a98ee), restyled as Datum Mesh. app/AGENTS.md lists what is ours there. It is its own cargo workspace (the root workspace has exclude = ["app"]) and it links crates/core by path.

heading: Datum Mesh: project memory › 1. Architecture › The program: the Datum window (0.7.1 on); app/ is the geometry engine
text: Datum Mesh: project memory › 1. Architecture › The program: the Datum window (0.7.1 on); app/ is the geometry engine. - app/crates/analysis (datum-analysis) holds the study (material, supports and loads on named faces, element size; stored in the design under the metadata key com.edgarmendonca.datummesh.study). It also meshes: STEP out → gmsh mesh.geo -parse_and_exit (OpenCASCADE, fragments, second order, msh 4.1) → tet::read_msh → trace_faces (each mesh face to a model face by nearest surface triangles). Then it builds the model and solves with crates/core. - app/crates/ui-egui/src/sim.rs is the Simulation workspace. Its stage bar has five steps: Material, Supports & Loads, Mesh, Solve, Results. Solves run on a background thread; results are drawn in the viewport scene. Its hooks are in lib.rs (sim::tick), toolbar.rs, context_menu.rs, control.rs (ui.sim for driven tests), viewport.rs and workspace.rs (sync_context leaves the Simulation tab alone). - app/packaging/windows/datum-mesh.nsi is the per-user setup. It installs datum-mesh.exe and gmsh\gmsh.exe, replaces the old Datum Mesh.exe, and associates .dmx files. - Building takes about 25 minutes from scratch: cd app && cargo build --release -p solidcraft --bin datum-mesh. - Gmsh is found through DATUM_GMSH, then gmsh\gmsh.exe beside the program, then PATH. - The 0.6 window (ui/, src-tauri/) stays in the repository as the reference for the analyses still to be brought across. - Driven checks: run datum-mesh --sample --control PORT under Xvfb. The token is in $HOME/.local/share/solidcraft/control/PORT.token. Requests are JSON lines (ui.screenshot, engine.execute, ui.workspace, ui.sim).

heading: Datum Mesh: project memory › 1. Architecture › Release flow
text: Datum Mesh: project memory › 1. Architecture › Release flow. release.yml (windows-latest): checks a pushed tag matches the version, takes the notes from CHANGELOG, runs the engine tests, builds the NSIS installer, writes SHA256SUMS.txt and publishes the GitHub Release. Run it from the Actions tab (tag pushes are blocked from Claude sessions). From 0.7.0 release.yml builds app/ (the version is read from app/Cargo.toml), runs the engine and analysis tests, fetches Gmsh for Windows from gmsh.info on the runner, builds DatumMesh-x.y.z-setup.exe with makensis, and checks it against a 150 MB budget. The updater (app/crates/ui-egui/src/update.rs) reads this repository's releases.

heading: Datum Mesh: project memory › 1. Architecture › How we work
text: Datum Mesh: project memory › 1. Architecture › How we work. 1. The user reviews a release and sends screenshots. 2. Reproduce first. 3. Big asks get a plan file and questions; build after the answers. 4. Engine first (with a test), then the UI. 5. Check every change in the real app (Xvfb screenshots, tests_ui/realapp.sh). 6. Add a UI test for every bug. 7. Run all checks: clippy -D warnings, cargo test (with the hardening tests and benchmarks), the UI type-check and UI tests, cargo deny check. 8. Release. 9. Report in plain language: what changed, what was checked, what is not done.

text: Datum Mesh: project memory › 5. heading: Datum Mesh: project memory › 5. Known limits (0.5.8)
text: Datum Mesh: project memory › 5. Known limits (0.5.8). - Large rotations in 3D frames: not with plates (those stay second order, P-delta); loads keep their directions (no follower loads; end moments are not semi-tangential, which matters only for moments about more than one axis at once); member loads become dead nodal loads with their fixed-end moments on each piece, as for plane frames; elastic only; small strains in each piece; the curve's "turn" is the angle of the node's total rotation vector, kept continuous past a half turn. Forces and tangent by finite differences: about 1e-9 relative accuracy, so very stiff or very large models converge to a looser balance.

heading: Datum Mesh: project memory › 5. Known limits (0.5.5)
text: Datum Mesh: project memory › 5. heading: Datum Mesh: project memory › 5. Known limits (0.5.2)
text: Datum Mesh: project memory › 5. Known limits (0.5.2). - Large deformation: 3D solids only (not plane parts); neo-Hookean only (no Mooney–Rivlin, Ogden or plasticity at large strain); loads dead (pressure does not follow the face); no locking cure for nearly incompressible rubber beyond quadratic wedges (keep ν ≤ 0.49 or refine); load control, so no path past a limit point; load and support markers stay at the undeformed positions in the 3D view.

heading: Datum Mesh: project memory › 5. Known limits (0.5.1)
text: Datum Mesh: project memory › 5. Known limits (0.5.1). - 3D plasticity: swept solids only (wedges; no tetrahedra yet); small strains; load control to collapse as for parts; each tangent is factorised afresh, so large 3D models solve slowly (seconds per iteration past 20 000 unknowns); no thermal loads with yielding.

heading: Datum Mesh: project memory › 5. Known limits (0.5.0)
text: Datum Mesh: project memory › 5. Known limits (0.5.0). - Plasticity: plane and axisymmetric parts only (not 3D solids, frames or plates); small strains and small movements; J2 with linear isotropic hardening (no kinematic hardening, no other yield criteria); load control, so the collapse load is the largest load carried (a lower bound found to about 1/1000 of an increment), with no path past it; results per element (contours a little ragged at the plastic zone's edge); the safety factor is not meaningful once yielded.

heading: Datum Mesh: project memory › 5. Known limits (0.4.5)
text: Datum Mesh: project memory › 5. Known limits (0.4.5). - Member offsets: along the member's own axis only (no offsets across it); rigid zones are 10⁵ times stiffer, so they flex about 10⁻⁵ as much as the member; ignored where a plate runs along the member (it is cut at the plate's nodes instead); truss bars have none.

heading: Datum Mesh: project memory › 5. Known limits (0.4.4)
text: Datum Mesh: project memory › 5. Known limits (0.4.4). - Rigid floors: every height above the lowest is a floor (nodes of a sloping roof at many heights are not tied); a floor is tied by penalty links, accurate to about 10⁻⁷; it does not stiffen plates' membranes beyond the ties at frame nodes; 3D frames only.

heading: Datum Mesh: project memory › 5. Known limits (0.4.3)
text: Datum Mesh: project memory › 5. Known limits (0.4.3). - Tension-only / compression-only: static solves only (large-deflection steps, natural frequencies, buckling and dynamics use every member both ways); judged by a member's mean axial force; a frame left with nothing to resist a push is reported as a mechanism. Settlement: at nodes with supports, in held translations (not rotations), static solves only (left out of large-deflection steps). 3D second order: P-delta with small rotations (no arc length, no large rotations in 3D); plates add no geometric stiffness; hinged pieces' released rotations recovered with the first-order condensation.

heading: Datum Mesh: project memory › 5. Known limits (0.4.2)
text: Datum Mesh: project memory › 5. Known limits (0.4.2). - Dynamics: plane and 3D frames with plates (not solids); linear; one dynamic step on its own (no static loads with it: add by hand); a spectrum's results are unsigned peaks of each quantity separately (no balance, no concurrent forces); one direction of shaking at a time (no 100/30 combination); Rayleigh damping only (from the first two modes); a time history reports the record of one node and the whole model at one time (the time of the largest movement), not an envelope over time; masses lumped at nodes for plates, consistent for members; mass moves with translations only (no rotary inertia of point masses).

heading: Datum Mesh: project memory › 5. Known limits (0.4.1)
text: Datum Mesh: project memory › 5. Known limits (0.4.1). - Plates: thin (Kirchhoff, no transverse shear deformation), elastic, flat triangles (curved shells as facets); one plate per plane region (the last solid shape round a triangle's centre decides its thickness); plates on different planes join only where their meshes share nodes (an edge both have, meshed the same); beams inside a plate (not on its edge) join where its mesh nodes happen to lie on them; no temperature loads, buckling, point loads on a plate face away from a node, or line supports along a plate other than its edges; moving a plate (Move) on a Side or Plan plane is not handled. Nodal stresses averaged from the triangles (contours a little blotchy on coarse meshes).

heading: Datum Mesh: project memory › 5a. Known limits (0.4.0)
text: Datum Mesh: project memory › 5a. Known limits (0.4.0). - Large deflection: plane frames only (3D frames, plates and solids later); elastic only (no yielding); loads keep their directions (no follower pressure); member loads go to the pieces' ends (exact as the pieces get shorter); shear deformation left out (Euler–Bernoulli); linear and large-deflection steps cannot be mixed in one sequence; the pieces of the first step are used for all. Arc length on a mixed vector of movements and rotations (unscaled). The diagrams are drawn along the undeformed members. Load control picks the stable branch at a bifurcation only with an imperfection or a side load to start it off (a perfect straight column stays straight, as it should). - DXF: ASCII only (not binary DXF); blocks (INSERT), splines and ellipses are left out; the drawing's layers are not used to tell part from holes (nesting is). Large 3D solids (about 90 000 unknowns) take 8 to 12 s depending on the machine's load; faster needs a multilevel partitioner or another solver.

heading: Datum Mesh: project memory › 5a. Known limits (0.4.0)
text: Datum Mesh: project memory › 5a. Known limits (0.4.0). - 3D heat: steady only (no transient); no thermal stress in 3D solids yet (temperatures are not passed to a 3D stress solve, and uniform temperature changes are left out with a warning). 3D frequencies: consistent masses, the lowest 30 at most; no point masses. Mode search on large solids is slow (several seconds above 20 000 unknowns). - Frames: combinations are solved one at a time (a few ms each for frames); the envelope is over combinations, or over cases when there are none; no plates or response spectrum yet; P-delta for plane frames only (0.4.0). A 3D hinge releases both bending moments (not one at a time). The tables' J leaves out the root fillets (a little below the tables). Load cases apply to every analysis; combinations to structural ones (not heat). - 3D solids: the solve of large ones (about 90 000 unknowns) takes over 10 s here; the AMD ordering fills in a lot in 3D. No point supports or springs on solids; no thermal loads, pin loads or natural frequencies yet. The cutting plane shows values interpolated linearly inside each element (on corner nodes).

heading: Datum Mesh: project memory › 5a. Known limits (0.4.0)
text: Datum Mesh: project memory › 5a. Known limits (0.4.0). - Sketch tools: corners are rounded or bevelled only between two straight edges; offsets need arcs that meet their neighbours smoothly; a combined result whose arcs came from flattened pieces has its arc ends where the exact curves meet (to about 1e-9 of the part); no canvas picking of corners (by the dialog or the corner table). - 3D frames: buckling by bending only (no flexural-torsional or lateral-torsional buckling: no warping stiffness); utilisation leaves out the shear stress of twisting; an angle bends about its leg axes (the product of inertia is left out); a channel's shear centre is not modelled. - Buckling: frames and trusses only, in their own plane; linear (eigenvalue) buckling of a perfect frame; no lateral-torsional buckling or design-code checks. - Natural frequencies: the six lowest only (up to 30 through the engine), no point masses yet, no damping or forced response. - Axisymmetric loads are round the axis only (no bending of a shaft by a side load: that needs Fourier modes or 3D). - Temperatures for thermal stress come from steady conduction only (no transient heating). - Not yet tried on a clean Windows PC by a person (0.1.5).

heading: Datum Mesh: project memory › 5a. Known limits (0.4.0)
text: Datum Mesh: project memory › 5a. Known limits (0.4.0). - Stresses at the corner where a fixed edge meets a free edge, or at a sharp inside corner, keep rising with mesh refinement (a singularity); the help says so, the app does not mark them. - NAFEMS LE1's error is flat between the first two meshes (0.24 %) before falling to 0.09 %. - A pin load on an edge split in two (a corner added in it) is shared half and half, each half bearing on its own; on a circle hole it is one edge, so this rarely matters. - No copy and paste of geometry. - Overlapping solid shapes join only when meshed (0.1.2); the canvas draws them overlapping.

heading: Datum Mesh 0.1: plan
text: Datum Mesh 0.1: plan. Written 2026-10-28, day 1, from the hub brief (Edgar-Mendonca/Datum/briefs/DATUM-MESH.md). Every decision was made with the user in the hub (session 13), so this plan has no open questions: it records scope, the day plan and the risks, then we build.

heading: Datum Mesh 0.1: plan › 1. Scope
text: Datum Mesh 0.1: plan › 1. Scope. Datum Mesh 0.1 is finite-element analysis in 2D, with its own solver in Rust: - Frames and trusses: nodes and members on a canvas; 2D Euler–Bernoulli beams and truss bars; sections from a library or your own A, I, depth; pinned, roller, fixed and spring supports; point forces and moments, uniform and linearly varying member loads, self-weight. Results: deflected shape, axial, shear and moment diagrams, reactions, stresses and utilisation. - Plane solids: rectangles, circles and polygons (with arcs and holes); plane stress (with thickness), plane strain and steady heat conduction on the same mesh; constrained Delaunay triangles with quality refinement, 6-node triangles by default (3-node as an option); edge and point supports and loads, gravity; temperature, flux and convection. Results: displacement, von Mises, principal and component stresses, safety factor, temperature and flux; contours, deformed shape, probe, min/max, reactions against applied loads (the equilibrium check). - Materials copied from Datum Atlas with their sources (Poisson's ratio added from our own typical values: Atlas has none). - Report printed to PDF, and the verification report generated by the test suite at build time. Not in 0.1: 3D, nonlinear, CFD, DXF import (0.2), modal and buckling (0.2). See the brief §8.

heading: Datum Mesh 0.1: plan › 2. How it is built
text: Datum Mesh 0.1: plan › 2. How it is built. - crates/core (pure Rust, unit-tested): model (the .dmesh document, versioned JSON with repair of damaged files), doc (edits as operations with snapshot undo, as in Plan and Sim), mesh (spade CDT + our refinement → T3/T6), elements (beam, truss, T3/T6 plane and heat), solve (triplets → CSC, supports by elimination, sparse Cholesky from faer), post (recovery, averaging, von Mises, principals, diagrams, reactions), bench (the benchmarks as data and tests), hardening. - src-tauri: the shell from Datum Sim (itself Plan's), without Python: commands, files, options, recovery, recent files, the updater with REPO = "Edgar-Mendonca/Datum-Mesh", a solve thread with progress. - ui: the family window (ribbon Home · Geometry · Mesh · Loads · Solve · Results · View · Help, contextual Format), the canvas (pan, zoom, snap, rulers; SVG for geometry, Canvas 2D for contours), model tree, inspector, legend, ? cards, Options, Print. - Model units are SI base units (m, N, Pa, K) in the file; the window shows mm, kN, MPa (SI) or in, kip, ksi (US).

heading: Datum Mesh 0.2 and 0.3: plan › 0.3: 3D solids for simple problems
text: Datum Mesh 0.2 and 0.3: plan › 0.3: 3D solids for simple problems. Geometry is made from the 2D parts the app already draws: - Extrude a part by a thickness (plates, brackets, lugs, flanges with holes). - Revolve a part about an axis (shafts, vessels, hubs; full turn or a sector with symmetry). - The 2D triangle mesh is swept into layers: 15-node quadratic wedges (or each wedge split into 10-node tetrahedra), so meshing stays robust and needs no new mesher. Release ; Work ; Benchmark ; 0.3.0 ; 3D linear static: extrude, wedge elements, face supports and loads (fixed, roller, pressure, force, gravity), the equilibrium check ; 3D cantilever (beam theory), patch test, Lamé in 3D ; 0.3.1 ; The 3D viewer: orbit, pan, zoom, section plane, contours on faces, deformed shape, probe ; — ; 0.3.2 ; Revolve; symmetry faces ; NAFEMS LE10 (thick plate under pressure), closed-end cylinder ; 0.3.3 ; 3D heat conduction and natural frequencies ; 3D fin; cantilever block modes ; Not in 0.3: arbitrary 3D shapes and STEP import. They need a general tetrahedral mesher and a CAD kernel; the open ones (Gmsh, TetGen, Open CASCADE) are GPL, AGPL or LGPL and could only ever run as separate programs. That is a later step (0.4+).

heading: Datum Mesh 0.2 and 0.3: plan › Risks
text: Datum Mesh 0.2 and 0.3: plan › Risks. - The 3D viewer is as much work as the solver: WebGL with lighting, picking faces and a section plane. - Equation counts: a 3D part of 20 000 quadratic wedges has about 300 000 unknowns; the sparse Cholesky handles it in seconds but needs memory (about 1–2 GB at worst). A conjugate-gradient option may be needed for bigger models. - Eigenvalue solvers (modal, buckling) are new numerics: faer has dense eigen solvers; a sparse shift-invert Lanczos is ours to write and test.

heading: Datum Mesh 0.2 and 0.3: plan › Decisions (the user's answers, 2026-10-29)
text: Datum Mesh 0.2 and 0.3: plan › Decisions (the user's answers, 2026-10-29). 1. 3D geometry: extrude and revolve the 2D parts. STEP and arbitrary shapes later, with an external mesher. 2. Order: analyses first (thermal stress, axisymmetric, natural frequencies, buckling, 3D frames), then 3D solids, then DXF import and Send to Calc/Plot. 3. The 3D viewer: three.js (MIT), recorded in NOTICE. 4. Releases: small numbered releases, each verified and reported. So the order is 0.2.0 thermal stress, 0.2.1 axisymmetric, 0.2.2 natural frequencies, 0.2.3 buckling, 0.2.4 3D frames, 0.3.x 3D solids, then DXF and Calc/Plot. 0.1.5 (first use on Windows) waits for a person to try the app.

heading: Datum Mesh 0.3 and 0.4: plan
text: Datum Mesh 0.3 and 0.4: plan. Superseded from 0.4 on by VISION.md (2026-10-31). The 0.3.x part below was delivered. Written 2026-10-30 after 0.3.0 (extruded 3D solids), from a brainstorm with the user about where Datum Mesh is heading.

heading: Datum Mesh 0.3 and 0.4: plan › Where Datum Mesh sits
text: Datum Mesh 0.3 and 0.4: plan › Where Datum Mesh sits. Datum Mesh is an analysis app, in the spirit of two kinds of commercial tool (named here only; never in public words, FAMILY §13): - Frames and trusses, like the analysis side of a structural program: 2D and 3D frames, reactions, member forces, frequencies and buckling. No building design codes or code load combinations (agreed 2026-10-29). - Parts, like a general finite-element program: linear stress, heat and vibration today; yielding, contact and large deflection (0.4) and heat and flow (0.5) later. It is not a CAD program and not a pre-processor that prepares models for other solvers. One small app does the whole loop (draw, load, solve, read, verify), and proves its answers.

heading: Datum Mesh 0.3 and 0.4: plan › How parts get their shape
text: Datum Mesh 0.3 and 0.4: plan › How parts get their shape. - Simple parts are made in Datum Mesh: a 2D section drawn with sketch tools, then extruded or revolved. This covers most parts engineers check quickly: brackets, plates, lugs, flanges, shafts, hubs, vessels. - Complex parts come from real CAD: the user designs in any CAD program and exports STEP; Datum Mesh meshes it with Gmsh (run as a separate program) and solves it with its own solver. - Full 3D modelling (a feature tree, sketching on faces, edge fillets) is not planned: it is a CAD product of its own, and the open geometry kernels are LGPL (outside the app's licence rule) or not yet mature.

heading: Datum Mesh 0.3 and 0.4: plan › Decisions (the user's answers, 2026-10-30)
text: Datum Mesh 0.3 and 0.4: plan › Decisions (the user's answers, 2026-10-30). 1. Datum Mesh does not become a CAD program or a pre-processor for other solvers; complex 3D shapes come from real CAD through STEP import. 2. Sketch tools come next (0.3.1), before the cutting plane, which moves to 0.3.2 with revolve. 3. Gmsh is bundled in the installer ("don't separate, do a big build"), not a separate download. heading: Datum Mesh 0.3 and 0.4: plan › Risks
text: Datum Mesh 0.3 and 0.4: plan › Risks. - Combining shapes keeps arcs: a union or subtraction of shapes with arcs must keep the arcs as arcs (so supports and loads on them still mean one edge), not cut them into short lines. This is the hardest part of 0.3.1; if exact arc clipping proves too costly, curved results become many short edges and the tools say so. - Tetrahedra from STEP need a new element (10-node tetrahedra) and checks of their own; Gmsh's Windows build and its size need measuring before the installer budget is set.

heading: tagline
text: tagline. One open-source platform for structural and finite-element analysis: frames, plates, solids, heat and vibration, our own solver that proves its answers.

heading: about
text: about. Its purpose: to show any engineer or student how a part or structure carries load, heat and vibration (where it is stressed, how far it moves, how hot it gets) in a free app they can trust because it proves its own answers. From 0.9.1 the window is laid out for the work: the steps down the left (Geometry, Materials, Loads, Mesh, Solve, Results, each ticked when done), the model across the middle, a card that pops up when you pick something, and a terminal along the bottom that keeps every message and follows each solve as it runs (increments, iterations, how far from balance, cut-backs, time left, Stop). It has full sketching and 3D modelling: click a plane and the view turns to it; lines, arcs, circles and rectangles drawn several ways, polygons, slots, ellipses, splines, trim, offset, fillet, mirror, patterns, dimensions and constraints; extrude with the solid changing as you type, revolve, boxes, cylinders, cones and spheres made in one go, solids joined, cut or intersected, sweeps, lofts, drafts and splits, STEP files in and out, holes, fillets, chamfers, shells, press pull, move, mirror and patterns of solids; frames drawn with the same sketch tools, and a history of every feature to edit, suppress, roll back or delete. The solids are then meshed by Gmsh (installed with it)

heading: about
text: about. and analysed by Datum Mesh's own engine, with supports and loads on the faces you click. The geometry comes from SolidCraft's open-source engine, working behind the Datum window. Datum Mesh finds the stresses, deflections and temperatures in parts and structures by the finite-element method. You draw a frame of beams and truss bars, or the outline of a part with its holes, put on the supports and loads, and solve. Frames and trusses give the deflected shape, the moment, shear and axial diagrams, the reactions and member utilisation, by linear analysis or in steps with large deflection and P-delta, followed past the limit load, in 2D and 3D; 3D frames carry plates (slabs, walls) joined to their beams; frames and plates respond to earthquakes by response spectrum or time history. Parts are meshed into triangles and solved in plane stress, plane strain or steady heat conduction, or as 3D solids (extruded or revolved) for stress, vibration and heat, and elastic-plastic (yielding) up to collapse in both; 3D solids also follow large deformation, rubber included (with thermal stress from the temperatures), with contours of stress, displacement, safety factor and temperature, and a probe that reads any point. Every solve ends with an equilibrium check, and Help › Verification solves benchmarks with known answers in front of you (a plate with a

heading: steps
text: steps. Click a plane or a face and the view turns to it; draw with lines, arcs, circles, rectangles, polygons and slots, size them with dimensions and constraints; Finish, and the shape is extruded as you set the distance. Revolve, drill, round and shell; edit any step in the history. Pick the material from the library. Click faces of the solid to hold them (fixed, roller, symmetry) or to load them (force, pressure). Meshed by itself when you need it: Gmsh fills the solids with ten-node tetrahedra; set the element size if you like. Datum Mesh's own engine solves and checks that the reactions balance the loads. Von Mises stress or movement in colour bands on the deformed part, with a legend.

heading: Changelog › 0.6.0 — 2026-11-02
text: Changelog › 0.6.0 — 2026-11-02. More codes, complete. The stage. Since 0.5.1: cold spring with its installed case; a choice of piping code (the process piping code, the power piping code or the European piping standard) with the occasional factor as an input; buried pipe on soil springs that yield at the soil's ultimate resistance; and the European rules for vessel cylinders, spheres, hemispherical heads and cones, with its test pressure. Two new examples show them: boiler steam to a header on the power piping code, and a buried hot water line. Reviewed. Every step with the full checks: 108 benchmark checks, the unit tests by hand, the UI checks and the real app. The random-model test now also runs every piping code and cold springs, and the random vessels both sets of vessel rules. Fixed. Insert Node on a pipe with a cold spring gave both new parts all of it, doubling the cut; it is now shared in proportion. The expansion loop wizard put the cold spring on its bends, which cannot have one, so the edit was refused; it now goes to the loop's last straight. Each has a test. Not yet. The European rules for torispherical and ellipsoidal heads (they keep the default rules, and the results say so).

heading: Changelog › 0.5.5 — 2026-11-02
text: Changelog › 0.5.5 — 2026-11-02. European vessel rules. A choice of rules for each vessel. The Vessels page has Rules for shells and heads: the default thin-shell rules (as before) or the European unfired pressure vessel standard (EN 13445-3). With the European rules, cylinders are calculated using its equation e = P Di / (2 f z − P), spheres and hemispherical heads e = P Di / (4 f z − P), and cones e = P Dk / ((2 f z − P) cos α), with the MAWP from the same equations; the hydrostatic test pressure is the larger of 1.25 Pd × f20/fd and 1.43 Pd, and the test's membrane stress is limited to the yield strength / 1.05. Torispherical and ellipsoidal heads keep the default rules for now, and the results say so. The design stress f is your input from the standard's rules for the material. Verification. A new benchmark: the vertical separator V-101 by the European rules, its shell thickness, MAWP and test pressure by hand (108 checks), and a unit test of each equation.

heading: Changelog › 0.5.5 — 2026-11-02
text: Changelog › 0.5.5 — 2026-11-02. Also in this release: buried pipe (0.5.4). Its own installer could not be published (the release service was down), so it comes with this one: soils for buried pipe under Loads › Soils, Buried in on each element, soil springs that yield at the soil's ultimate resistance, Results › Soil, and the example Buried hot water line. The notes are under 0.5.4 below.

heading: Changelog › 0.5.4 — 2026-11-02
text: Changelog › 0.5.4 — 2026-11-02. Pipe in the ground. Loads › Soils keeps the soils of the model: the depth to the pipe's centre line, unit weight, friction angle, cohesion, the pipe surface's friction and adhesion factors, and the movements at which the soil yields. Choose a soil for any element under Buried in in its Inspector. The analysis then puts soil springs at both ends of every buried segment for half its length: along the pipe, across it, and up and down. Each is elastic up to the soil's ultimate resistance and then yields at it, so a long hot line slides through the soil near its bends and ends and is held fully further in. The resistances come from classical soil mechanics: along, the friction of the earth pressure at rest; across, the Rankine passive and active pressures; up, the soil block above the pipe and the shear on its sides; down, the bearing capacity. You can give your own instead. The soil's force at every buried point, and where it has yielded, is in Results › Soil and counts in the equilibrium check; the soil's stiffness is in the natural modes; buried pipe has no wind; and the 3D view draws buried pipe earth-coloured. Take every soil value from the site's soil report.

heading: Changelog › 0.5.4 — 2026-11-02
text: Changelog › 0.5.4 — 2026-11-02. Example. Buried hot water line: 8" at 90 °C, 60 m in sand rising at a bend to a pump-house wall; the soil yields at 21 of its 30 points when hot. Verification. A new benchmark with two checks: a long buried pipe pushed sideways at its end against Hetényi's beam on an elastic foundation, and a long heated pipe's free end against the classical sliding-friction result F² / (2 EA f) (105 checks). The random-model test now also buries every other element on some models, and every case must still balance.

heading: Changelog › 0.5.3 — 2026-11-02
text: Changelog › 0.5.3 — 2026-11-02. European piping standard. A third piping code. Analysis settings › Piping code now also offers the European piping standard (EN 13480-3). With it the stresses are calculated using its equations: the sustained stress σ1 = p Do / 4en + 0.75 i MA / Z (0.75 i at least 1), the sustained plus occasional stress against k fh (k your input, 1.2 filled in), and the displacement stress range σ3 = i MC / Z against fa = U (1.25 fc + 0.25 fh); with the liberal option, its alternative σ1 + σ3 ≤ fh + fa. The minimum wall uses its equation e = p Do / (2 f z + p). The material's allowable table is the design stress f, your input from the standard's rules for the material; check every factor against the edition you work to. Verification. A new benchmark: a heated L-bend at 10 MPa with the European standard, its design thickness and the alternative range allowable at the anchor by hand (102 checks).

heading: Changelog › 0.5.2 — 2026-11-02
text: Changelog › 0.5.2 — 2026-11-02. Power piping code. A second piping code. Analysis settings has a Piping code choice: the process piping code (ASME B31.3, as before and the default) or the power piping code (ASME B31.1). With the power piping code the stresses are calculated using its equations: the sustained stress P Do / 4t + 0.75 i M / Z (0.75 i at least 1, M the resultant moment with torsion; Datum Pipe also adds the axial force over the area, which the equation's older form leaves out), the occasional stress as the sustained stress plus that of the occasional loads, and the displacement stress range i Mc / Z, with one stress intensification factor at each point (the larger of the in- and out-of-plane values from the same flexibility characteristic). The minimum wall, hoop stress, allowable range and liberal allowance use the same forms in both codes. Allowables stay your inputs. Occasional factor. The factor on the hot allowable for occasional loads is now an input next to the code: 1.33 is usual for process piping, 1.15 or 1.2 for power piping by how long the load acts. Choosing a code fills in its usual value; check it against your code edition. The results, help and report show the factor and name the code in use.

heading: Changelog › 0.5.2 — 2026-11-02
text: Changelog › 0.5.2 — 2026-11-02. Example. Boiler steam to a header: 6" Sch 80 at 300 °C and 40 bar with wind, checked with the power piping code (sustained 0.42, range 0.33, wind 0.44 of their allowables). Verification. A new benchmark: a cantilever with an arm, so the root carries both bending and torsion, under pressure, against the power piping sustained equation by hand, and the new example's equilibrium (100 checks).

heading: Changelog › 0.5.1 — 2026-11-02
text: Changelog › 0.5.1 — 2026-11-02. A pipe made short on purpose. Straight pipe has a new input in the Inspector, Cold spring: the length it is made short by and pulled together at installation. It acts as an imposed shortening of that element. The load cases follow it: a new case COLD is the installed state with the cold spring pulled in (weight, pressure and the cold spring), so its support and nozzle loads are the cold loads; the operating, occasional and hydrotest cases include it; the sustained case does not (its stress is weight and pressure only); and the expansion range is taken from COLD, so the stress range is the same as without it, as the piping codes give no credit for cold spring in the range. The hot loads on anchors and nozzles go down, the cold ones up. Load Cases has a Cold spring column for your own cases; the report lists each element's cold spring. Verification. A new benchmark: a straight pipe between anchors made 3 mm short, installed and hot, against Hooke's law (98 checks). A worked test checks on an L-bend that the hot reactions are those without the cold spring plus the installed ones, and that the stress range does not change.

heading: Changelog › 0.5.0 — 2026-11-01
text: Changelog › 0.5.0 — 2026-11-01. The dynamics stage, complete. Dynamics in Datum Pipe. Since 0.4.1 the analysis can find the piping's natural frequencies and mode shapes, with the mass each mode moves, and draw each mode moving in the 3D view; put a response spectrum on the modes, combined by CQC and checked as an occasional load (OCC SPEC); and give the steady response to a force at a frequency with damping (HARM). The steam rack example shows all three. Reviewed. Every dynamics step with the full checks: 96 benchmark checks (three for dynamics, each against classical theory), the unit tests, the UI checks and the real app. A new test checks that a harmonic load at 0 Hz gives the static deflection whatever the number of modes, that its response grows in step with the load, and that at resonance it stays finite and near 1/(2ζ) of the static; the random-model test now also runs modes, a spectrum and a harmonic load on a quarter of its 80 models. Fixed. The printed report now has the dynamics inputs (modes, damping, spectrum, harmonic load), the natural modes table and HARM's support loads, which were missing.

heading: Changelog › 0.4.4 — 2026-11-01
text: Changelog › 0.4.4 — 2026-11-01. A load at a frequency. Under Dynamics in Analysis settings, Harmonic load takes a force and moment amplitude at one node and a frequency, for a pulsation or a machine's out-of-balance. With the natural modes found, the steady response is the static response plus each mode's dynamic part, u = K⁻¹F + Σ φ (φᵀF) [1/(ω² − Ω² + 2iζωΩ) − 1/ω²], with the damping ratio. The result is the case HARM: the amplitudes of the movements, section forces and support loads. Its values are amplitudes without signs, so equilibrium does not apply to it, and it is not stress-checked (judge its forces and movements against your own vibration limits). If no modes are asked for, a warning says the harmonic load needs them. Fixed. Results › Summary showed an equilibrium figure for OCC SPEC; it now says not applicable, as the Equilibrium table does. A nozzle with allowables is not marked pass or fail in HARM, whose loads are amplitudes. Example. The steam rack example has a 500 N sideways pulsation at the corner 60 at 12 Hz (example values): case HARM moves at most 0.37 mm. Verification. A new benchmark: a heavy mass on a cantilever driven at half its natural frequency, against the one-degree-of-freedom amplitude (96 checks).

heading: Changelog › 0.4.3 — 2026-11-01
text: Changelog › 0.4.3 — 2026-11-01. A spectrum on the modes. Under Dynamics in Analysis settings, Response spectrum takes the acceleration (g) against frequency from the site's seismic study, a factor for X, Y and Z, and the damping ratio. With the natural modes found, each mode's response in each direction is φ Γ Sa(f) / ω², giving its displacements, section forces and support loads; the modes are combined by the complete quadratic combination (CQC) with the damping, the directions by the square root of the sum of squares. The result is the case OCC SPEC, checked as occasional: the sustained stress plus its stress, against 1.33 Sh; its support loads, nozzle loads and displacements are in the results like any case. A combined spectrum has no signs, so the equilibrium check says it does not apply to it. Example. The steam rack example has a horizontal spectrum (example values) on its ten modes: OCC SPEC at 0.46 of its allowable. Verification. A new benchmark: a cantilever's base shear in a flat spectrum with one mode, against the classical 0.6131 of its mass (95 checks).

heading: Changelog › 0.4.2 — 2026-11-01
text: Changelog › 0.4.2 — 2026-11-01. Modes in the 3D view. See each mode move. Results › Modes has a Show button on every mode: the 3D view draws that mode's shape swinging about the still position, with the still centreline dashed, and the legend names the mode and its frequency with a Stop button that goes back to the load case. Colours by stress ratio are off while a mode is shown (a mode's size has no meaning, so it is drawn at a fixed share of the model). Help. Natural modes has the steps.

heading: Changelog › 0.4.1 — 2026-11-01
text: Changelog › 0.4.1 — 2026-11-01. Natural frequencies and mode shapes: the first step of dynamics. Natural modes. Set how many modes to find under Dynamics in Analysis settings and analyze: Results › Modes lists each mode's frequency and period, the share of the moving mass it carries in X, Y and Z, and the running totals. The modes use the analysis's own stiffness with the mass of the pipe, its contents, insulation, rigid parts and expansion joints lumped at the points; one-way rests and gaps are taken as touching and friction is left out. They are found by subspace iteration (one factorisation, the trial vectors kept mass-orthonormal, the small projected problem by Jacobi rotations): 20 modes of a 3 200-point rack take under two seconds. Example. The steam rack example finds its ten lowest modes: the first at 1.38 Hz, the turbine leg swinging sideways. Verification. A new benchmark: the first frequency of a cantilever and of a fixed-fixed span against beam theory, (λ²/2π) √(EI / m L⁴), within 0.6 % (94 checks); a worked test of the modes' order, mass fractions and orthogonality, and a speed gate. Roadmap. Dynamics in small steps: 0.4.2 modes in the 3D view, 0.4.3 response spectrum, 0.4.4 harmonic response, 0.5.0 the milestone.

heading: Changelog › 0.4.0 — 2026-11-01
text: Changelog › 0.4.0 — 2026-11-01. The vessels stage, complete. Pressure vessels in Datum Pipe. Since 0.3.1 the same app designs pressure vessels next to the piping: shells, heads and cones under internal pressure with the liquid's static head (MAWP, MAP, test pressure, weights); nozzles by area replacement; horizontal vessels on two saddles by Zick's method; vertical vessels on a skirt or legs in wind and seismic, with their anchor bolts and base ring; bolted flanges and covers; lifting lugs and trunnions; the piping's loads checked on the vessel's nozzles; and external pressure with stiffening rings. Two worked examples show it: the Vertical separator V-101 with its inlet line, and the Horizontal drum D-201 on saddles at full vacuum. Reviewed. Every vessel step with the full checks: 92 benchmark checks (eight of them for vessels), the unit tests by hand, the UI checks and the real app. A new hardening test checks 200 random vessels of every shape, with nozzles, saddles or skirts or legs, flanges, lifting and vacuum: each is checked with every result a number, or refused with a reason, and every one round-trips through the file.

heading: Changelog › 0.4.0 — 2026-11-01
text: Changelog › 0.4.0 — 2026-11-01. Sources. Every vessel equation is from the open literature or first principles (membrane theory, area replacement, Zick 1951, the bolted flange method of 1937, plate and beam theory, classical shell buckling), with the allowable stresses, joint efficiencies, gasket factors and yield strengths left as your inputs; Help › Sources lists each one. Next. Dynamics (0.5), then more codes (0.6) and more options (0.7); the rest of the plant (hydraulics, valve sizing, tanks, nozzle stresses by our own shell model) waits in the roadmap.

heading: Changelog › 0.3.8 — 2026-11-01
text: Changelog › 0.3.8 — 2026-11-01. External pressure on vessels. Vacuum and external pressure. A vessel takes an external design pressure (full vacuum is 1.013 bar outside), a design factor on collapse (3 by default) and stiffening rings on its shell (spacing and moment of inertia). From classical shell buckling, with no code charts: a cylinder between stiffeners collapses at 2.42 E (t/D)^2.5 / ((1 − ν²)^0.75 (L/D − 0.45 √(t/D))), never below the long-tube 2 E / (1 − ν²) (t/D)³, L the shell between the heads plus a third of each head's depth, or the ring spacing; heads are spheres of their crown radius (0.9 D for a 2:1 head) at 0.1875 E (t/R)², the classical result with a knockdown for imperfections; each is capped by yield and divided by the design factor. A ring needs a moment of inertia of at least the factor × pe R³ Ls / (3 E). Example. D-201 is checked for full vacuum (the steam-out case) with rings every 3 m: the shell at 0.52 of its allowable, the rings at 0.92. Without the rings the 9.4 m shell would fail. Verification. A new benchmark: D-201's allowable external pressure and its rings by hand (92 checks); a unit test of the collapse formulas.

heading: Changelog › 0.3.7 — 2026-11-01
text: Changelog › 0.3.7 — 2026-11-01. Vessels and piping together. The link. A vessel nozzle can be linked to the piping model's nozzle point at its flange (the Piping column of the nozzles table). After the piping analysis, the nozzle's neck is checked under the piping loads of every case: the pressure's P d / 4t, the axial force and the bending on its corroded section, combined with torsion by the maximum shear stress, against 1.5 S. The loads in the nozzle's own axes are listed for the vessel engineer, who checks the local stresses in the vessel wall. Example. V-101 now has its 8" inlet line: 2 m out from N1, 4 m down and 3 m along to an anchor, at 16 bar and 200 °C, with N1 moving 15 mm up and 2 mm out as the vessel grows. The piping and the vessel are in one model; N1's neck passes in every case. Fixed. The 3D view kept each WebGL context when the Model view was left, so switching views many times could run the graphics out of memory and crash the window; it now releases the context and the scene's geometry each time. Verification. A new benchmark: N1's neck stress in operation by hand from its piping loads, and the separator example's equilibrium (90 checks).

heading: Changelog › 0.3.6 — 2026-11-01
text: Changelog › 0.3.6 — 2026-11-01. Lifting lugs, trunnions and legs. Lifting. Plate lifting lugs (number, thickness, width, hole height, metal round the hole, hole and pin diameters, base weld) lifted along a sling at an angle from vertical, and pipe trunnions (diameter, wall, arm), under the empty weight times an impact factor. The lugs are checked for tension across the hole, shear tear-out, pin bearing, tension and bending at the base, and the base fillet welds; the trunnions for bending and shear at the shell. Allowables are fractions of the yield: 0.6 in tension, 0.4 in shear and on the welds, 0.9 in bearing, 0.66 in bending. Legs. A vertical vessel can stand on legs instead of a skirt: each leg carries the weight over the legs plus 4 M / (n D) from the overturning moment of the wind or seismic, checked against Euler buckling of a cantilever leg (K = 2) with a factor of 2 and 0.6 of the yield, with the base shear's bending in the leg and the two combined. Example. V-101 has two 30 mm lifting lugs on its top head, lifted at 30° with an impact factor of 1.5: the highest ratio 0.31, on the base welds. Verification. A new benchmark: V-101's lugs by hand (88 checks); a unit test of the legs.

heading: Changelog › 0.3.5 — 2026-11-01
text: Changelog › 0.3.5 — 2026-11-01. Bolted flanges and covers on vessels. The bolted flange method. A vessel takes bolted flanges and covers at its design pressure: the gasket's effective width b and diameter G from its seating width, the operating bolt load Wm1 = H + Hp (the pressure's end force and the gasket compression m P) and the seating load Wm2 = π b G y, and the bolt area the larger needs against the bolts given. A ring flange (slip-on, lap joint) is checked by its tangential stress Y Mo / (t² B), from the moments of the end force, the face force and the gasket load about the bolt circle, in operation and at gasket seating; a blind cover by its thickness G √(0.3 P/S + 1.9 W hG/(S G³)), in operation and at seating. The gasket factors m and y, the dimensions and the allowables are your inputs. Hubbed weld-neck flanges are not calculated yet. Example. V-101's manway has a bolted cover: 50 mm against 42.9 mm needed in operation and 46.3 mm at gasket seating. Fixed. Picking a nozzle's pipe size in the Vessels view gave dimensions 40 times too small (the library's sizes are already in metres), and the nozzles' schedule boxes did not show their schedule. Both have UI checks now.

heading: Changelog › 0.3.4 — 2026-11-01
text: Changelog › 0.3.4 — 2026-11-01. Vertical vessels: wind, seismic and the skirt. Loads on a vertical vessel. Wind (the site's pressure or profile from Analysis settings, times the shape factor and the outside diameter grown by a factor for ladders, platforms and insulation) and static seismic (a coefficient times the mass at each height) give the shear and moment at every height, the vessel taken as a cantilever from its base. The larger of the two moments is used. The checks. Each shell course at its bottom: pressure plus bending less weight in tension against S E, bending and weight in compression against min(S, 0.0625 E t / R), axial buckling with a knockdown. On a skirt: the skirt at its top and base (no pressure), the anchor bolts (4 M / (N × bolt circle) − empty weight / N, on their root area), the foundation bearing under the base ring (weight over its area plus the moment over its section modulus), and the base ring's thickness (its projection as a cantilever strip, l √(3 σ / S)).

heading: Changelog › 0.3.4 — 2026-11-01
text: Changelog › 0.3.4 — 2026-11-01. On the page. For vertical vessels, a Wind, seismic and skirt section takes the shape factor, the diameter factor, the seismic coefficient, the base elevation, the modulus and the skirt, base ring and bolts; the skirt and base ring are drawn; a table gives every section, the bolts, the bearing and the ring. Example. V-101 now stands on a 2.5 m skirt with twelve M30 anchor bolts, in a 1 kPa wind and 0.15 g of seismic: everything passes, the bolts at 18 MPa. Verification. A new benchmark: V-101's wind and seismic base shears, its anchor bolt stress and base ring thickness by hand (83 checks).

heading: Changelog › 0.3.3 — 2026-11-01
text: Changelog › 0.3.3 — 2026-11-01. Horizontal vessels on saddles. Saddles. A horizontal vessel can sit on two saddles: the distance from each tangent line to its saddle, the contact angle (120° to 180°), the saddle width, welded or not, and stiffening rings. The vessel is checked by Zick's method (1951): a beam on two saddles carrying the heavier of its operating weight and its weight full of water, with the shell at the design pressure, hot and corroded: the longitudinal stress at mid-span and at the saddles (with an unstiffened shell's effective section), the tangential shear in the shell (and in the heads when they stiffen the shell, the saddle within R/2 of the tangent line), the circumferential stress at the saddle horn and the compression at the bottom of the shell. The constants come from their closed forms in the contact angle; at 120° they are the familiar 0.107, 0.192, 1.171, 0.880, 0.760 and 0.0528. Allowables: S for the longitudinal stresses, 0.8 S for shear, 1.25 S at the horn, 0.5 Sy at the bottom. Small openings. A nozzle with a finished opening up to 60.3 mm, or up to 88.9 mm in a wall up to 10 mm, needs no reinforcement calculation (its neck is still checked).

heading: Changelog › 0.3.3 — 2026-11-01
text: Changelog › 0.3.3 — 2026-11-01. On the page. The saddles are drawn under the vessel; a Saddles table gives each stress, its allowable and ratio; the saddle data is under the nozzles for horizontal vessels. On a horizontal vessel a nozzle's angle 0 is on top and 180 underneath. Example. A new worked example, Horizontal drum D-201: 2.4 m × 9 m, 10 bar and 150 °C, on two 120° saddles 600 mm from the tangent lines, with an inlet, an outlet and a vent: every check passes, the highest the mid-span longitudinal stress at 0.46. Verification. A new benchmark: D-201's mid-span moment by statics, and its shear and horn stresses by hand with the published 120° constants (79 checks); a unit test of the constants against the published table.

heading: Changelog › 0.3.2 — 2026-11-01
text: Changelog › 0.3.2 — 2026-11-01. Nozzles on vessels. Each vessel takes nozzles: the part they are on and where, the neck (a pipe size and schedule, its wall counted at 87.5 %, or the diameter and wall of a rolled-plate neck), the outside weld leg, and a reinforcing pad. Reinforcement by area replacement. The metal the opening removes, d × tr (tr the wall the part needs for its pressure with a joint efficiency of 1), must be made up within the reinforcement limit by the shell's excess thickness, the neck's, the welds and the pad (counted up to twice the opening). The neck must be at least the larger of its own pressure thickness and the smaller of the shell's need and 87.5 % of the standard-wall pipe, with corrosion. Large openings are flagged. On the page. Nozzles are edited under the parts, drawn on the vessel, and checked in a Nozzles table with every area; a nozzle that fails turns red and fails the vessel. Example. V-101 has its 8" inlet, 6" gas outlet, 4" liquid outlet and 20" manway, with pads: all pass. Verification. A new benchmark: V-101's inlet by area replacement and its neck's minimum by hand (76 checks); a unit test of the rules (pad past the limit, the neck's minimum).

heading: Changelog › 0.3.1 — 2026-11-01
text: Changelog › 0.3.1 — 2026-11-01. Pressure vessels: shells and heads. A Vessels view. Datum Pipe now designs pressure vessels in the same model as the piping. The new Vessels view (left bar) holds any number of vertical or horizontal vessels: each is its design data (pressure, temperature, allowable stresses hot and cold, yield strength, corrosion allowance, plate under-tolerance, liquid and its level, extra weight) and a row of parts from the bottom (or the left) to the top: 2:1 ellipsoidal, torispherical and hemispherical heads, cylindrical shell courses and cones.

heading: Changelog › 0.3.1 — 2026-11-01
text: Changelog › 0.3.1 — 2026-11-01. What it works out. For every part: the pressure it carries (the design pressure plus the liquid's static head at its lowest point), the thickness that pressure needs and with the corrosion allowance, its MAWP hot and corroded, and its MAP new and cold. For the vessel: the MAWP at the top and the part that sets it, the MAP, the hydrotest pressure (1.3 × MAWP × S cold / S hot) with each part's membrane stress in the test against 0.9 of the yield, the volume, and the weights empty, operating and full of water. Thin-shell membrane equations: cylinder t = P R / (S E − 0.6 P), sphere t = P R / (2 S E − 0.2 P), 2:1 head t = P D / (2 S E − 0.2 P), torispherical head t = P L M / (2 S E − 0.2 P), cone t = P D / (2 cos α (S E − 0.6 P)). The allowable stresses, joint efficiencies and yield are your inputs. Drawing and report. The vessel is drawn to scale with its tangent lines and liquid level; the report prints each vessel.

heading: Changelog › 0.3.1 — 2026-11-01
text: Changelog › 0.3.1 — 2026-11-01. Example. A new worked example, Vertical separator V-101: 1800 mm inside diameter, 6000 mm between tangent lines, 2:1 heads, 16 bar at 200 °C: the shell needs 12.54 mm (15.54 mm with corrosion, 16 mm nominal) and sets the MAWP of 16.59 bar; test pressure 21.57 bar; 6.6 t empty, 11.2 t operating. Fixed. After an edit, the results were not marked out of date when Analyze automatically was off (one of two internal edit hooks replaced the other). Verification. A new benchmark: V-101's shell and head thicknesses, MAWP, test pressure and volume by hand (73 checks).

heading: Changelog › 0.3.0 — 2026-11-01
text: Changelog › 0.3.0 — 2026-11-01. The equipment and flanges stage, complete. Reviewed. Everything in 0.2.1–0.2.9 (ease of use, speed, equipment nozzles, flange leakage, relief valve thrust, nozzle flexibility, expansion joints, wind by height and both directions, .pcf export) was reviewed with the full checks: every benchmark (68), every hand-worked case, every example solving and balancing, the UI checks, and the real app. Sources checked. Every equation and value the app uses was checked against one rule: only what is published openly, or derived from first principles, with code tables left as your inputs. Help › Sources now shows the flange leakage equation's derivation from the statics of the gasket ring. Next. Pressure vessels, in Datum Pipe: shells and heads, nozzles, saddles, vertical vessels, body flanges, lugs and legs, the piping link and external pressure, step by step to 0.4.0.

heading: Changelog › 0.2.9 — 2026-11-01
text: Changelog › 0.2.9 — 2026-11-01. Export a piping component file. File › Export › Export a piping component file writes the model's geometry as a plain-text .pcf file for design tools: pipes, bends as elbows (their ends and corner), tees (run and branch ends at half the run's diameter from the centre), concentric reducers, valves and flanges with their weight, other rigid parts and expansion joints as miscellaneous components, and supports named by their kind. Coordinates are in millimetres with Z up. Materials, schedules, temperatures and pressures are not part of the file. It is also in the command search (Ctrl+K). Checked by reading it back. Every worked example is exported and imported again with the same length of piping, bends, tees, valves, supports by kind and support positions; random models are exported and read back too. Help. The Import topic is now Import and export.

heading: Changelog › 0.2.8 — 2026-11-01
text: Changelog › 0.2.8 — 2026-11-01. Wind by height, and occasional loads in both directions. Wind that changes with height. Occasional loads › Wind by height takes the design wind pressure at a few elevations (Y) from the wind standard for the site. It is interpolated between them and held beyond them, and each element carries its average along its length. Without a profile, one pressure applies everywhere, as before. Both directions. Tick Wind and seismic in both directions for OPE1−WIN and OCC −WIN (and the same for seismic): the loads reversed. With one-way rests, gaps and friction the reversed case can be worse: a rest that carries more load one way lifts off the other way. The load case editor has the reversed options too, and the report says what was used. Example. The steam rack example checks its wind and seismic in both directions. Verification. A new benchmark: a 10 m vertical cantilever under a wind profile, its base shear and moment by statics, and the reversed case (68 checks). A worked test shows a one-way rest lifting off under upward seismic and carrying more under downward.

heading: Changelog › 0.2.7 — 2026-11-01
text: Changelog › 0.2.7 — 2026-11-01. A new component. An element can be a bellows expansion joint, with the maker's spring rates: axial, lateral (a parallel offset with the ends kept parallel), angular and torsional (0 is rigid), its effective area, its weight, and whether it is tied. Datum Pipe makes it a short beam with these rates (EA = ka L, EI = kθ L, GJ = kt L, and the shear flexibility that gives the lateral rate); a lateral rate higher than 12 kθ / L² cannot be modelled that way and is flagged. Pressure thrust. An untied joint cannot hold the pressure: the pressure on its effective area pushes the pipe apart at both its ends in every case with pressure (and the hydrotest), so the main anchors carry it. A tied joint's rods carry the thrust and hold its length. Where to find it. Model › Components › Expansion Joint, or Expansion joint in the table's component column; the rates in the Inspector. The 3D view draws the convolutions (and the tie rods), the isometric a zigzag. The code stresses are checked on the pipe at the joint's ends, not on the bellows.

heading: Changelog › 0.2.7 — 2026-11-01
text: Changelog › 0.2.7 — 2026-11-01. Example. A new worked example, Expansion joint between anchors: 8" steam at 200 °C and 10 bar, 24 m between main anchors, an untied joint in the middle: each main anchor carries 60 kN in operation, mostly the 45 kN pressure thrust. Verification. A new benchmark: a joint's lateral and angular rates, and the pressure thrust shared between the pipe and the joint, by hand, and the new example's equilibrium (65 checks). A worked test covers tied and untied joints, the warning and the stress points.

heading: Changelog › 0.2.6 — 2026-11-01
text: Changelog › 0.2.6 — 2026-11-01. Vessel and tank nozzle flexibility. The wall gives at the nozzle. A nozzle point now has the stiffness of the vessel or tank wall at the nozzle: axial (radial to the shell), shear, torsion, and bending in the longitudinal plane (the plane of the nozzle and the vessel's axis) and in the circumferential plane, with the vessel's axis (vertical by default). With any of them above 0, the anchor at the nozzle's node holds along the nozzle's own axes with these stiffnesses; 0 holds that direction rigidly. The equipment's growth given on the anchor still moves the nozzle, and the nozzle loads are reported as before. Your inputs. The stiffnesses come from the vessel's or tank's maker, or your own calculation; Datum Pipe does not calculate them, and local stresses in the vessel wall are left to the vessel engineer, who gets the nozzle loads in the nozzle's axes. Example. The tank outlet example's nozzle has the tank shell's flexibility (example values). Verification. A new benchmark: a cantilever from a flexible nozzle, the extra tip deflection P L²/kθ + P/ks and the nozzle's rotation by hand, the anchor's moment by statics (61 checks). A worked test covers a skewed nozzle, the nozzle's growth through the flexible wall and a nozzle on a head.

heading: Changelog › 0.2.6 — 2026-11-01
text: Changelog › 0.2.6 — 2026-11-01. Roadmap. 0.2.7 expansion joints, 0.2.8 wind that changes with height and seismic in both directions, 0.2.9 .pcf export, then the 0.3.0 review. Later stages gain load combinations, a sustained case with the operating support states, more operating cases, other pipe size standards and jacketed pipe.

heading: Changelog › 0.2.5 — 2026-10-31
text: Changelog › 0.2.5 — 2026-10-31. Relief valve thrust. The thrust at an open discharge. Loads › Relief Valves puts a relief valve at the open end of its outlet pipe, with its relieving flow, temperature, ratio of specific heats k and molar mass. Datum Pipe calculates the reaction from the conservation of momentum, F = ṁ V + (P − Pa) A, with the gas leaving at sound speed: V = √(2kRT/((k+1)M)) and exit pressure P = (ṁ/A)√(2RT/(k(k+1)M)). This is the same result as the published open-discharge reaction equation of API RP 520 Part II. The force is multiplied by a dynamic load factor (2 by default; check it against your code edition). It pushes the pipe back along the pipe at the open end, or against a direction you give. The exit area is the pipe's bore unless you enter one. Load cases. With relief valves, OPE1+RV (operating case 1 with the thrust) and OCC RV (the thrust's own effect) are added; OCC RV is checked as an occasional load, the sustained stress plus its stress against 1.33 Sh. The load case editor has a Relief thrust option.

heading: Changelog › 0.2.5 — 2026-10-31
text: Changelog › 0.2.5 — 2026-10-31. Results. Results › Relief shows each valve's exit area, velocity, exit pressure, whether the exit is choked, and the thrust before and after the load factor; the report has it too. Where the exit is not choked the pressure term is 0 and the sound speed is kept, which overstates the thrust. Example. A new worked example, Safety valve vent stack: 3 kg/s of steam at 200 °C up a 4" stack, a 3.6 kN thrust with the load factor, OCC RV at 0.14. Units. Mass flows (kg/s, lb/h), flow areas (mm², in²) and velocities (m/s, ft/s). Verification. A new benchmark: a relief valve on an L-shaped outlet, its thrust by hand and the anchor's force and moment by statics, and the new example's equilibrium (58 checks). A unit test checks the thrust against the published form in US units.

heading: Changelog › 0.2.4 — 2026-10-31
text: Changelog › 0.2.4 — 2026-10-31. Equivalent pressure. Loads › Flange Leakage gives a flange pair or a valve's flanged ends a gasket reaction diameter G and a pressure rating at temperature. Each operating and sustained case then checks the joint by the equivalent pressure method: the bending moment M and the axial force F at the joint act on the gasket like an extra pressure P_eq = 16M/(πG³) + 4F/(πG²), and the case's pressure plus P_eq must stay within the rating. Axial compression is counted like tension, on the safe side. The hydrotest is not checked here: it is judged against a test rating. Your inputs. G and the rating come from your flange data; no standard's tables are reproduced. Results. Results › Flanges shows the force, moment, pressure, P_eq, rating and ratio at the joint's most loaded end; the report has it for the operating case. Examples. The pump discharge's gate valve is checked with example values (a 180 mm gasket diameter, a 40 bar rating): 0.84 in operation. Verification. A new benchmark: a flange pair on a cantilever, its moment and axial force by statics and its equivalent pressure by hand (54 checks).

heading: Changelog › 0.2.3 — 2026-10-31
text: Changelog › 0.2.3 — 2026-10-31. Rotating equipment nozzle checks. Equipment. Supports › Equipment Checks groups the nozzle points of a steam turbine, a compressor or a pump. Turbines and compressors are checked against the criteria their standards publish as equations, in the standard's units (lb, ft·lb, inches): - each nozzle: 3F + M ≤ 500·De; - all nozzles, resolved at the reference (exhaust or discharge) nozzle: 2Fc + Mc ≤ 250·Dc, with Dc from the nozzles' combined area, and a limit on each component of the combined loads; - a compressor with a multiplier on every allowable (typically 1.85). Pumps are checked against the allowable loads of the pump standard's table, which you enter for each nozzle (components and resultants, with a multiplier of 1 or 2). Your inputs. Every coefficient, the rules for large nozzles, the component limits, the multipliers and the pump table values are your inputs, filled with typical values: check them against the edition of the standard that applies. No standard's tables are reproduced. Results. Results › Equipment lists each check with its value, allowable and ratio for the chosen case; the report has it for the operating case, and a case with a failing check no longer shows PASS.

heading: Changelog › 0.2.3 — 2026-10-31
text: Changelog › 0.2.3 — 2026-10-31. Examples. The compressor (K-201, factor 1.85) passes; the steam line's turbine (T-301) fails the turbine criteria, as a stiff line near a turbine does: a starting point for adding flexibility. Verification. A new benchmark: a steam turbine with two nozzle lines, its nozzle loads by statics and its criteria by hand (52 checks).

heading: Changelog › 0.2.2 — 2026-10-31
text: Changelog › 0.2.2 — 2026-10-31. Speed on large models. Measured on a rack line of 1441 elements and 1602 supports (one-way rests with friction, guides, line stops): ; Before ; Now ; Analysis (every case settled) ; 16.6 s ; 0.18 s ; Opening the model in the window ; 7.2 s ; 1.8 s ; One edit, drawn again ; 2.4 s ; 0.6–0.75 s ; The window figures are from a test browser drawing in software; a graphics card is faster. Analysis. With more than 64 supports with friction, a sliding force is found from an estimate of the support's flexibility (from the stiffness at its node) instead of an extra solve per support; it settles to the same answer, and the exact method takes over if it has not settled in 40 solves. A test checks Coulomb's law at every support of a large rack. Element table. Only the rows in view are drawn, so a table of thousands of elements opens and scrolls like a short one; a row selected elsewhere is scrolled into view. 3D view. Parts that share a colour are drawn as one object (a click still finds the element, node or support), straight pipe is drawn as a cylinder, and large models use fewer facets.

heading: Changelog › 0.2.1 — 2026-10-31
text: Changelog › 0.2.1 — 2026-10-31. Ease of use: the first step of the third stage. Where a model is free. When the piping can move without resistance, Analyze names the node and the direction nothing holds ("at node 30, turning about X") and shows that node. Analyze automatically. Every edit is analysed again a moment later, and a model is analysed when it opens, so the stress colours, tables and support loads follow what you type. It stays quiet unless something is wrong. File › Options turns it off. Values with units. Any number field, and the element table, takes a value with its unit: 20 ft, 3' 6", 1 ft 6 in, 150 mm, 3.5 bar, 300 °F. A unit of the wrong kind is refused with the reason. Right-click in the 3D view. A node offers its supports, a nozzle point and a load; an element its component, Insert Node, Add an Element After, the expansion loop and Delete; empty space Fit and Analyze. A click within a few pixels of a node picks the node. Roadmap. The third stage (equipment and flanges) is split into 0.2.1–0.2.6, with 0.3.0 as its milestone (File › Roadmap).

heading: Changelog › 0.2.0 — 2026-10-30
text: Changelog › 0.2.0 — 2026-10-30. The milestone that closes the second stage: nonlinear supports, occasional loads, spring hangers and import (0.1.5–0.1.11), reviewed. No new features. Fixes from an independent review of the engine. - Two one-way or gapped supports touching on the same direction at one node now share its load equally, with a warning; each reported the whole load, so the equilibrium check failed. - A bend whose radius is half its pipe's diameter or less is refused (its bend factor turned negative and the wall check passed); the wall check of such a bend fails. - A spring hanger whose attachment moves in operating case 1 is sized on the pipe's movement relative to the attachment, so it carries its hot load in operation. - Importing a piping component file joins an olet's branch to its run pipe (the run was not split there, leaving the branch unconnected). Each with a regression test. The verification record (48 checks), the screenshots, the README and the site describe everything up to this release.

heading: Changelog › 0.1.11 — 2026-10-30
text: Changelog › 0.1.11 — 2026-10-30. Import of piping component files. Import. File › Export › Import a piping component file opens a plain-text .pcf file from a design tool as a new model: - pipes; elbows and bends at their corner, with the radius from their tangent length; tees and olets; concentric and eccentric reducers (as concentric); valves, flanges and other in-line items as rigid parts with their weight; - supports as one-way rests, or anchors, guides and line stops when their name says so; - millimetres or inches; coordinates turned from Z up to Datum Pipe's Y up; - pipes at the library's nominal sizes with Std wall, and the default material and line conditions: set them for the line. Anything it cannot read is listed when the model opens. A sample file is in docs/examples/6-P-101.pcf. Roadmap. The public piping benchmark problems published by nuclear regulators are dynamic problems (natural frequencies and response spectra), so they move to 0.4 with dynamics, where they can be checked. The next release is 0.2.0, which closes this stage.

heading: Changelog › 0.1.10 — 2026-10-30
text: Changelog › 0.1.10 — 2026-10-30. Spring hanger selection. Spring hangers. Supports › Spring Hanger puts a hanger on a node, and Analyze sizes it: - the hot load H: the operating weight it carries with the pipe held level there; - the travel Δ: its movement in operating case 1 with the hanger carrying H; - the spring: the first size in the spring table whose working range takes both H and the cold load C = H + k Δ, with the load variation ; k Δ ; / H within the limit (25 % unless you change it). Every load case is then solved with the chosen springs, each set to its cold load. A hanger no spring fits becomes a constant-force support carrying H, with a warning. Spring table. Supports › Spring Table: the sizes hangers are chosen from, in order, with the load variation allowed. It starts with a generic table (three series with 25, 50 and 100 mm of working travel, twenty sizes each), not any maker's catalogue: replace it with your supplier's sizes. Results. Results › Hangers lists each hanger's size, rate, hot load, travel, cold load, load variation and working range; the report has the same table. Examples. The tank outlet's first support is a spring hanger sized by Analyze.

heading: Changelog › 0.1.9 — 2026-10-30
text: Changelog › 0.1.9 — 2026-10-30. Wind and static seismic loads, and the occasional stress check. Wind. A design wind pressure, a shape factor Cd and the direction the wind blows, in the Inspector's Occasional loads (or Loads › Wind). Each element carries q × Cd × D per metre, with D over its insulation and cladding, from the part of the wind that blows across it: wind along a pipe puts no load on it. Static seismic. Factors of g along X, Y and Z (Loads › Static Seismic); each element carries its operating weight per metre times them. Load cases. With wind, OPE1+WIN (operating case 1 with the wind) and OCC WIN (the wind's own effect, OPE1+WIN − OPE1) are added; the same for seismic. The Load Cases dialog has an Occasional column for your own cases. Occasional check. An occasional case's stress at each point is the sustained stress plus the stress of the occasional loads (the same expression, without pressure), against 1.33 Sh. Your inputs. The wind pressure and the seismic factors come from the standards for the site; Datum Pipe reproduces none of their tables. Help › Sources lists the new equations. Examples. The steam line on the rack has 0.8 kPa of wind from the south and 0.15 g of static seismic sideways.

heading: Changelog › 0.1.8 — 2026-10-30
text: Changelog › 0.1.8 — 2026-10-30. Friction at rests and guides. Friction. Rests, guides, line stops and restraints can have a friction coefficient μ (0.3 is typical for steel on steel, 0.1 for PTFE slide plates). It acts across the support's direction: a rest resists the pipe sliding horizontally, a guide resists it moving along the pipe. Sticking and sliding. In each load case a support with friction holds the pipe while the force that needs is within μ × the load pressing the support; beyond that the pipe slides, and the support pushes back with exactly μ × its load against the movement, in whatever direction the pipe moves across it. A rest that lifts off has no friction. This is solved in the same iteration as one-way rests and gaps; sliding forces are found exactly from the support's own flexibility, one support after another, so supports at one node settle together. Results. Support Loads shows each support with friction as sticking or sliding, with its friction force, which is part of the support's load and of the equilibrium check. Examples. The steam line's rests and guides have μ = 0.3. Verification. A new benchmark: friction at a heated rest, sliding (μ P, and the movement ε L − μ P L / EA) and sticking (E A ε) (38 checks).

heading: Changelog › 0.1.7 — 2026-10-29
text: Changelog › 0.1.7 — 2026-10-29. One-way rests and gaps. One-way rests. A rest can let the pipe lift off: it pushes the pipe up but never pulls it down. New rests are one-way; the Inspector switches it. Rests in files from earlier versions stay two-way, so their results do not change. Gaps. Rests, guides, line stops and restraints can have a gap: below the pipe for a rest, on each side for the others. The support takes no load until the pipe has moved across it. How it is solved. With one-way rests or gaps, each load case is solved again until every such support has settled as touching or open: a touching support must push the pipe, not pull it, and an open one must not be passed. The expansion range is still the difference of the operating and sustained results. If only open gaps hold the piping in some direction, they keep a light stiffness (1 N/mm) so the case can be solved, with a warning. Results. Support Loads shows each one-way or gapped support as touching, open or lifted off, with the pipe's movement and the gap, and how many solves the case took. Examples. The examples' rests are one-way, and the steam line's guides have 3 mm gaps.

heading: Changelog › 0.1.5 — 2026-10-29
text: Changelog › 0.1.5 — 2026-10-29. Code check fixes, and where every equation comes from. - A bend is also checked at its intrados, where the wall needs most metal: the design thickness uses the bend factor I = (4R/D − 1)/(4R/D − 2). - A pressure design thickness of D/6 or more now fails, with a warning: the thin-wall equation does not apply there. - A reducer is checked at both ends, each with its own pipe (diameter, wall, corrosion and mill tolerance); it was checked at its large end only. Tees. The branch of a tee uses the effective section modulus Ze = π r₂² Ts, with Ts the lesser of the run's wall and ii × the branch's wall. Analysis Settings can turn it off for code editions that use the branch pipe's own section modulus. Pressure elongation. Straight pipe can grow with its pressure in the operating cases (ε = (σL − ν σh)/E). Off unless you choose it in Analysis Settings; the sustained case never includes it. Shared supports. Two rigid supports holding the same direction at one node now share its load equally, with a warning; the first one took it all.

heading: Changelog › 0.1.5 — 2026-10-29
text: Changelog › 0.1.5 — 2026-10-29. Sources. The README, NOTICE and report say that Datum Pipe contains none of the code's text, tables or figures and is not affiliated with or endorsed by ASME. Verification. heading: Changelog › 0.1.4 — 2026-10-28
text: Changelog › 0.1.4 — 2026-10-28. Polish: the build to start with. Every example analyzes, draws its isometric and prints its report. Fixes from an independent review of the engine. - An expansion range between two operating cases now takes the hot allowable Sh at the hotter of the two cases; it took the second case's even when the first was hotter, which was on the unsafe side. - Guides and line stops at a tee act along the run; the branch was averaged into the pipe's direction, so a line stop could take loads across the pipe. At a corner, where there is no single direction, Datum Pipe now says so. - A tee drawn as the end of its branch takes its stress intensification from the run pipe, and a tee without a straight run gets its plane from its legs (with a warning). - Bends' stress intensification factors use the lowest operating pressure for the pressure correction (on the safe side in every case); their flexibility still uses the highest. - A flexible anchor's stiffness applies to its three movements; its rotations are held. - A reducer's small end uses its own pipe's corrosion allowance in the sustained stress. Isometric. The sheet fills the window at the proportions of a landscape page, with its title block the same width.

heading: Changelog › 0.1.4 — 2026-10-28

Code stresses are listed in table order, element by element, with each bend after its straight part; Worst first still sorts them by ratio. Examples. The turbine nozzle of the steam line points the right way (from the turbine into the pipe). Checked. heading: Changelog › 0.1.3 — 2026-10-28
text: Changelog › 0.1.3 — 2026-10-28. Editing tools, smoother typing in the table, and a tidier report and isometric. Expansion loop wizard. Select a straight element and choose Model › Expansion Loop: give the loop's width and height, sideways or upwards, and the element becomes a loop in its middle with four long-radius bends, drawn to scale before you make it. Copy and mirror a section. Model › Copy Section copies a range of table rows, with their components and supports, onto any node; Mirror Section does the same mirrored across X, Y or Z. Typing in the table. Tab and Enter keep the keyboard in the table after every edit (before, an edit rebuilt the rows and the cursor was lost), and Enter in the last row adds the element and stays there for the next one. Report and isometric. Report pages keep their content inside the header and footer, headings print in plain type, the isometric shows one stress ratio tag per element (bends showed two), and the 3D view fits the model more closely.
