heading: Datum Schema 0.1: plan
text: Datum Schema 0.1: plan. Written before building, from the brief (Edgar-Mendonca/Datum › briefs/DATUM-SCHEMA.md, hub session 22). Every product decision was made in the brief; this file says how the build is cut and where the risks are. Choices the brief left open are in docs/MEMORY.md › Decisions.

heading: Datum Schema 0.1: plan › Scope (brief §2)
text: Datum Schema 0.1: plan › Scope (brief §2). Intelligent P&IDs and process flow diagrams: draw the plant with real symbols; every symbol and line carries its data and knows what it is connected to. From that, Datum Schema writes the line list, equipment list, instrument index and valve list, checks the drawing as you work (13 rules), and sizes every line (velocity and pressure drop against limits). Printing to PDF, SVG per sheet, DXF (R12, our own writer). Three examples plus "Find the faults" for the exhibition.

heading: Datum Schema 0.1: plan › How it is built
text: Datum Schema 0.1: plan › How it is built. - Engine first (crates/core): the model (project, sheets, items, lines, notes), operations with undo, the symbol library as data (one drawing per symbol in a small primitive language, turned into SVG for the window and blocks for DXF), connectivity (graph), tags, checks, hydraulics, lists, the sheet frame (border, zones, title block, revision table) and DXF. The window draws what the engine returns: routed line paths with hops and flow arrows, symbol placements, badges. - The canvas is Datum Sim's block canvas (pan, zoom, snap, marquee, drag) with Sim's orthogonal router extended to ports facing any of four directions. - Units from Datum Calc's table (by way of Datum Pipe): SI and US display, SI in the file. - Pipe sizes from Datum Pipe's library (½"–24", every schedule) for inside diameters. - Shell from Datum Plan (guarded commands, crash.log, atomic saves, checksummed updater), Excel export with Plan's writer (rust_xlsxwriter).

heading: Datum Schema 0.1: plan › Day plan (brief §6)
text: Datum Schema 0.1: plan › Day plan (brief §6). Step ; Work ; Release ; 1 ; Read; skeleton from Plan (renamed, magenta, logo, publisher "Datum", updater, CI, release); a blank sheet with border and title block saves and opens ; 0.1.0 ; 2 ; Engine: model, graph, tags, units, pipe library, undo; tests ; — ; 3 ; Canvas from Sim: sheets, placing symbols, lines with ports, split by in-line items, off-page connectors; the inspector ; 0.1.1 ; 4 ; All ~80 symbols and line types; data on everything; automatic numbering; legend sheet ; — ; 5 ; Checks (13) and the Checks panel; hydraulics with badges; the four lists with CSV/Excel ; 0.1.2 ; 6 ; Print to PDF, SVG, DXF; the three examples and "Find the faults"; ? cards ; 0.1.3 ; 7 ; Polish, 500-item performance, screenshots, README, site.json; final check ; 0.1.4 ; Cut order if time runs short (brief): the Hold cloud, line hops, ANSI sheet sizes, the less common symbols. Never cut connectivity, checks, lists, hydraulics, printing or DXF.

heading: Datum Schema 0.1: plan › Risks
text: Datum Schema 0.1: plan › Risks. - Size of the job in one run. Mitigation: the engine carries everything the window and DXF share (symbols, frame, routes), so each feature is written once; the examples are built in code and double as tests. - Routing quality with ports on four sides and many lines: Sim's sparse-grid router is proven; user bend points override it. - Releases from a cloud session: tag pushes are blocked, so each release runs release.yml by workflow_dispatch on Windows; the CI on Linux checks the same code first. - No Windows machine here: the window is checked in Chromium with a mocked bridge (Playwright) and the real shell is built on Linux (WebKitGTK) for compile checks; the installer is built only by the release workflow.

heading: Datum Schema 0.1: plan › Course change (after 0.1.3)
text: Datum Schema 0.1: plan › Course change (after 0.1.3). The user set the long-term direction: an object-based plant engineering tool for whole projects, not a drawing tool. Objects are the master and a symbol is only a view of one; every object sits in a plant hierarchy (project › plant › unit › area); classes and their attributes are data (a JSON class library; users add attributes); the project is one SQLite database with a history of every change; names follow DEXPI. 0.1 shipped on the drawing-centred core (0.1.0–0.1.3; 0.1.4 held). The object core is the 0.2 stage, proposed in docs/PLAN-0.2.md and to be agreed with the user before it is built. If it costs time, cut from the brief's cut list, never from connectivity, checks, lists, hydraulics, printing or DXF.

heading: Datum Schema: the object core (agreed; releases 0.1.5 onwards)
text: Datum Schema: the object core (agreed; releases 0.1.5 onwards). Written after 0.1.3, when the user changed course (session 1). Nothing here is built yet; the questions at the end are for the user. It describes Datum Schema's own goals (FAMILY §13).

heading: Datum Schema: the object core (agreed; releases 0.1.5 onwards) › 1. Feedback
text: Datum Schema: the object core (agreed; releases 0.1.5 onwards) › 1. Feedback. Datum Schema must not stay a drawing tool that knows its connections. The aim is an open-source, object-based plant engineering application: easy, reliable, efficient, robust, for students, researchers and engineers, written from scratch in Rust with no proprietary content. The user's five points:

heading: Datum Schema: the object core (agreed; releases 0.1.5 onwards) › 1. Feedback
text: Datum Schema: the object core (agreed; releases 0.1.5 onwards) › 1. Feedback. 1. Objects are the master. Every equipment item, line, valve and instrument is an object with a unique id; a symbol on a sheet is only a view of it. An object can appear on several sheets, in lists and in datasheets. Deleting a symbol asks: delete the object, or only remove it from this sheet? 2. Plant hierarchy. Every object sits in a tree: project › plant › unit › area, with defaults so it can be ignored at first. A "Plant" panel beside the palette; lists group by it. 3. Class library. Object types are data, not code. Each class (centrifugal pump, control valve, pressure transmitter…) defines its attributes (name, unit, allowed values, required or not) and its default symbol. Built-in classes ship as a JSON library; users add attributes in Options. Checks and lists read attributes through the classes. 4. One file, a database inside. The .dschema file becomes one SQLite database: objects, attributes, classes, hierarchy, sheets, views, and a history table recording every change (who, when, old value, new value). The base for revisions and, later, several people working on one plant. 5. DEXPI names. Name classes and attributes after the open P&ID data standard (DEXPI) where it costs nothing, so import and export is a mapping, not a rewrite.

heading: Datum Schema: the object core (agreed; releases 0.1.5 onwards) › 2. What object-based plant engineering needs (public documentation and open standards)
text: Datum Schema: the object core (agreed; releases 0.1.5 onwards) › 2. What object-based plant engineering needs (public documentation and open standards). - One object database for the whole plant life. Each component is one object holding all its data; drawings, lists, datasheets and documents are views linked to it. Library ("base") objects are templates; each plant object takes its defaults from one, and classes group them. - A classified library. A tree of base objects and classes (unit, location, device…) carries attributes and symbols; administration adds attributes and rules without code. - Rules. Consistency is checked in real time against company rules, inconsistencies are marked on the drawing and listed; rules also propagate values (a line's size to its valves). A task list tracks what must be updated when shared data changes. - Many people, one plant. Items are claimed by a project; work areas or working layers let people change a copy of the plant data and release it to the baseline, compare layers, and keep a project history. - Revisions and versions of objects and documents, compared visually and as reports. - Integration with instrumentation, electrical and 3D design: the logical P&ID is compared with the physical 3D model and isometrics (connections, valve sequence, attributes).

heading: Datum Schema: the object core (agreed; releases 0.1.5 onwards) › 3. Diagnosis: where 0.1 stands
text: Datum Schema: the object core (agreed; releases 0.1.5 onwards) › 3. Diagnosis: where 0.1 stands. What 0.1 already has that carries over: the symbol drawings, routing, the frame, the 13 checks, hydraulics, lists, print, DXF, the examples and the test harness (engine tests, hardening, UI checks against the real engine). What must change underneath: - An item is its symbol (one Item per placement); a line is its drawn piece. Pipelines (runs) are inferred from matching line numbers, which caused the review's run bugs. - Attributes are a free data map; the fields per category are Rust code (fields.rs); the checks read hard-coded keys. - No hierarchy, no history beyond undo, a JSON file.

heading: Datum Schema: the object core (agreed; releases 0.1.5 onwards) › 4. Proposal › 4.1 The model (DEXPI-aligned names)
text: Datum Schema: the object core (agreed; releases 0.1.5 onwards) › 4. Proposal › 4.1 The model (DEXPI-aligned names). - A line number becomes a real object (PipingNetworkSystem) instead of something inferred: renaming it renames every piece; a valve dropped on a line becomes a component of its segment. The run logic and its bugs go away. - Topology (what connects to what) is separate from geometry (where it is drawn), so the same object can be on two sheets and the checks never depend on the drawing. - Ids are UUIDs, so two copies of a project can later be merged.

heading: Datum Schema: the object core (agreed; releases 0.1.5 onwards) › 4. Proposal › 4.2 The class library
text: Datum Schema: the object core (agreed; releases 0.1.5 onwards) › 4. Proposal › 4.2 The class library. - classes.json, built in: about 80 classes for today's symbols, with inheritance (Pump › CentrifugalPump), each with DEXPI class name, display name, default symbol, tag prefix, nozzles, and attributes { name (DEXPI where one exists), label, quantity/unit, type (number, text, choice, boolean), choices, required, default }. - Company classes and attributes added in Options are stored in the project (and can be saved as a company template). - fields.rs disappears; the Inspector, lists and checks read the classes. Check 6 (missing data) reads "required".

heading: Datum Schema: the object core (agreed; releases 0.1.5 onwards) › 4. Proposal › 4.3 The file: SQLite
text: Datum Schema: the object core (agreed; releases 0.1.5 onwards) › 4. Proposal › 4.3 The file: SQLite. - rusqlite with SQLite bundled (both permissive licences; to confirm with cargo deny). One file, opened in WAL mode, saved by the same atomic rule (a copy is written and renamed) or kept open with transactions — to decide (question 4). - Tables: meta (format, units), classes, attributes (class attributes), nodes (hierarchy), objects, values (object, attribute, value, unit-free SI), connections, sheets, views, routes, notes, settings, history (seq, time, user, operation, object, attribute, old, new). - Undo and redo come from the history table; revisions are named points in the history ("Rev A issued"). - 0.1 .dschema JSON files are read and converted on open (the examples too).

heading: Datum Schema: the object core (agreed; releases 0.1.5 onwards) › 4. Proposal › 4.4 The window
text: Datum Schema: the object core (agreed; releases 0.1.5 onwards) › 4. Proposal › 4.4 The window. - A Plant tab beside the palette: the hierarchy tree with every object (drag to move between units), filter, "show on sheet". - Deleting a symbol asks: remove from this sheet, or delete the object everywhere. Objects not on any sheet are listed in the Plant tab ("not drawn"). - Lists group by plant, unit or area; the line list is one row per PipingNetworkSystem. - Options › Classes: browse classes, add attributes.

heading: Datum Schema: the object core (agreed; releases 0.1.5 onwards) › 4. Proposal › 4.5 What stays the same
text: Datum Schema: the object core (agreed; releases 0.1.5 onwards) › 4. Proposal › 4.5 What stays the same. Symbols, routing, the frame, print, DXF, hydraulics, the checks (re-written over the object model, same 13 rules and tests), the examples, the shell, the updater, the tests.

heading: Datum Schema: the object core (agreed; releases 0.1.5 onwards) › 5. Size and order
text: Datum Schema: the object core (agreed; releases 0.1.5 onwards) › 5. Size and order. This replaces the core under the window, so it is the 0.2 stage, in small releases (FAMILY §9): Release ; Content ; 0.2.0 ; The object model and SQLite file; objects ≠ views; line numbers as objects; 0.1 files converted; every 0.1 test passes on the new core ; 0.2.1 ; The class library (JSON, inheritance, DEXPI names); Inspector, lists and checks read it; user attributes in Options ; 0.2.2 ; Plant hierarchy and the Plant panel; delete from sheet or object; an object on several sheets; lists grouped by plant/unit/area ; 0.2.3 ; History: every change recorded (who, when, old, new), undo from history, named revisions, compare two revisions as a report ; 0.2.4 ; DEXPI (Proteus XML) export, then import ; The old 0.2–0.5 roadmap (links to Pipe and Sim, PFD, instrument documents, templates) moves after this stage.

heading: Datum Schema: the object core (agreed; releases 0.1.5 onwards) › 6. Questions for the user
text: Datum Schema: the object core (agreed; releases 0.1.5 onwards) › 6. Questions for the user. 1. 0.1.4. Release it as the exhibition build on today's core (it is ready and tested), or hold it and show 0.2 when the object core is done? 2. Scope of the stage. Is 0.2.0–0.2.4 the right order, or should DEXPI export come earlier (it proves the object model against an outside standard)? 3. Who works on a project. Is "one person per file, with history and revisions" enough for the 0.2 stage, with several people on one plant (claims, working copies merged back) planned for later? Or should multi-user shape 0.2 now (a server, not a file)? 4. The file. Keep the familiar save button (the database is written as a whole on Save, recovery as now), or let the database save every change as it happens (no Save, like a database application)? 5. Disciplines. Beyond P&ID: is the next discipline instrumentation (index, loop diagrams, datasheets), electrical (motor lists, cable schedules), or the link to 3D (Datum Pipe)? 6. Hierarchy names. Project › Plant › Unit › Area, or your company's breakdown (site, plant, unit, system, area…)? Fixed levels or user-defined? 7. Users and history. "Who" in the history: the Windows user name, or a name typed in Options?

heading: Datum Schema: the object core (agreed; releases 0.1.5 onwards) › 7. Agreed with the user (session 1, after 0.1.3)
text: Datum Schema: the object core (agreed; releases 0.1.5 onwards) › 7. Agreed with the user (session 1, after 0.1.3). - Versions stay consecutive: 0.1.4 (the held exhibition build) is released, then 0.1.5, 0.1.6, 0.1.7… — no jump to 0.2.0. The table in §5 is renumbered: Release ; Content ; 0.1.5 ; Objects and views: every equipment item, valve and instrument is an object with its tag and data; symbols are views of it; a line number is an object (PipingNetworkSystem) owning its drawn pieces; plant hierarchy node on every object (defaults); the project file is one SQLite database with a history table; 0.1 JSON files open and convert ; 0.1.6 ; The class library as JSON (DEXPI names, inheritance, attributes with units, choices, required); Inspector, lists and checks read it; user attributes in Options ; 0.1.7 ; The Plant panel (hierarchy tree), delete from sheet or object, objects not drawn, lists grouped by plant/unit/area ; 0.1.8 ; Instrument datasheets generated from the class attributes: one per instrument, editable, printable, exportable — the user's daily pain point in the oil and gas work ; next ; History and revisions, DEXPI export and import, further datasheets (valves, equipment), loop diagrams ; - The user's aim: a flexible, free, open-source plant engineering tool for students and engineers, free to use; datasheets and every document from one place. Built from scratch in Rust in the Datum way; open-source libraries only where needed (SQLite).

heading: Datum Schema: the object core (agreed; releases 0.1.5 onwards) › 7. Agreed with the user (session 1, after 0.1.3)
text: Datum Schema: the object core (agreed; releases 0.1.5 onwards) › 7. Agreed with the user (session 1, after 0.1.3). - No reverse engineering of other software (the user suggested a reverse-engineering toolkit; it is not used on proprietary software). Only public documentation and open standards. - Defaults chosen for the open questions (to revisit with the user): Save button kept (the database is written as a whole on Save, atomically; recovery as now); hierarchy levels Plant › Unit › Area with names the user edits; "who" in the history is the name in Options (default: the computer's user name); one person per file for now, with UUIDs and history so merging can come later.

heading: about
text: about. Datum Schema draws piping and instrument diagrams where every symbol and line carries its data and knows what it is connected to. You place real symbols (vessels, pumps, exchangers, valves, instruments) and join them with lines that route themselves; drop a valve on a line and it goes into it, carry a line to another sheet with a pair of off-page connectors. Because the drawing knows its connections, Datum Schema writes the line list, the equipment list, the instrument index and the valve list for you, always in step with the drawing; it checks the drawing as you work (duplicate tags, open ends, size changes without a reducer, pumps without check valves and more); and it sizes every line, with its velocity and pressure drop against limits for its service. Hydraulic results are a sizing aid, checked by the engineer. Every symbol is a view of a plant object (equipment, valve, instrument, line number) in a plant › unit › area hierarchy, defined by a class library you can extend with your company's attributes. Every change is recorded in the project file, and every piece of equipment, instrument, control valve and relief device has a datasheet whose process conditions come straight from the P&ID. Process flow diagrams sit beside the P&IDs: streams with their flows and conditions, a stream table

heading: about
text: about. on the sheet, and heat and mass balance checks. A client's legend sheet (DXF) becomes a symbol library to draw a project to their standard; an old drawing can sit behind a sheet to trace over; issued sheets are compared and the changes clouded. Lines go to Datum Pipe for stress analysis and control loops to Datum Sim for tuning.

heading: steps
text: steps. Drag symbols from the palette and draw lines port to port. In-line valves and fittings split the line they are dropped on; off-page connectors carry lines between sheets. Check it as you go Twenty-seven rules run on every change: duplicate tags, open ends, size and class changes, check valves, relief paths, control loops, velocities and pressure drops, heat, mass and component balances on process flow diagrams, instrument ranges, loop wiring pipe specs, instrument wiring and your company's own rules. Click an issue to go to it, or choose one of its fixes. Print the drawings and lists Print the sheets to PDF with their border and title block, export DXF for any CAD program, and the line list, equipment list, instrument index and valve list to Excel or CSV.

heading: What's new in Datum Layout › 0.1.4 — 2026-11-03
text: What's new in Datum Layout › 0.1.4 — 2026-11-03. Datum Layout 0.1 is complete: the examples, printing, help and pictures, checked end to end. Examples. File › Examples opens the pump suction and discharge, the exchanger hook-up and the small pipe rack run with no clashes and no errors, and "Find the clashes" with exactly its three planted problems. Every line of every example is read and solved by Datum Pipe. Print. File › Print (Ctrl+P) puts the 3D view as it is on screen on its own page with a title block, then the line list, the equipment list with nozzles and the material take-off, on any paper, with a header and footer; Save as PDF in the print window makes a PDF. Help. Every ribbon group and panel has its ? card; Help › Getting Started walks through placing equipment, routing lines and handing over; the glossary explains the plant-design words; Help › Sources lists where every catalogue table comes from. Pictures. New screenshots of the pump example, a valve being dropped onto the header, the clash list and the line list.

heading: What's new in Datum Layout › 0.1.3 — 2026-11-03
text: What's new in Datum Layout › 0.1.3 — 2026-11-03. The hand-over to Datum Pipe, proved. Datum Pipe reads every line. Every line of every example is exported as a piping component file and read by Datum Pipe's own engine, which then solves it: the same nodes, bends, tees, valves, flanges and reducers. The record is in docs/verification/0.1.3.md, and the check now runs on every change. glTF checked. Every example's 3D model passes the Khronos glTF validator with no errors and no warnings. Checks. Every check has a failing and a passing case in the tests. A component a class does not allow is now named properly ("a 16\" ball valve is not allowed by class CS1"). Lists. The material take-off is tested against what example 1 holds: valves, tees, reducers, flanges, one gasket and one bolt set per flanged joint, and the pipe length of each line.

heading: What's new in Datum Layout › 0.1.2 — 2026-11-03
text: What's new in Datum Layout › 0.1.2 — 2026-11-03. Dropping and moving fittings, and branches, made exact. See where it snaps. While you drag a valve or fitting over a pipe, the marker shows exactly where it will land (the nearest free straight length between elbows, flanges and other components), or turns red and says why it cannot go there. Slide a component along its run. Select a valve, strainer, tee or reducer and drag its amber arrow; it moves to the nearest free place, or onto another run of the line. Branches. Dropping a tee starts routing its branch at once; double-click (or right-click) ends the branch at a free point, or click a nozzle. Fixed: a double-click did not end a route. Resizing. A line's reducers keep the size after them when the line is resized, and a branch larger than its run is reported as a mismatch at the tee.

heading: What's new in Datum Layout › 0.1.1 — 2026-11-03
text: What's new in Datum Layout › 0.1.1 — 2026-11-03. Lines now follow the equipment they connect to. Move equipment, keep the lines. When you move a vessel, pump or exchanger, each line on its nozzles follows: the move passes along the line's runs, each run stretching along its own direction, so the route stays square and its corners stay where they can. A run too short for its fittings moves whole instead. Branches follow their tees, and components slide along their run when it gets shorter. Route Again. Turning equipment, or a move no run can take, leaves a line skewed: it is reported ("route it again"), and Piping › Route Again (or the button in the Inspector) routes it square between its ends through its corners, keeping its components on their runs. A new check. A line that no longer leaves its nozzle or tee square to it is reported, even when it has no turn.

heading: What's new in Datum Layout › 0.1.0 — 2026-11-03
text: What's new in Datum Layout › 0.1.0 — 2026-11-03. The first release: lay out a plant in 3D, route its pipes, check them and hand each line to Datum Pipe. The plot. A site grid with east and north coordinates, the plant north arrow, the ground and areas. Grid spacing, extent, north and ground are set in the Inspector. Equipment from its datasheet. Six types: vertical vessel, horizontal drum, storage tank, column, centrifugal pump with motor and baseplate, and shell-and-tube exchanger. Drag one from the catalogue onto the plot, then set its tag, position, rotation, sizes, nozzles (size, rating, facing, position, direction) and datasheet lines. Drag its arrows to move it. Routing. Piping › Route Line: click a nozzle, the corners and the other nozzle. Long-radius elbows appear at every turn (short radius by choice), a reducer where the nozzle and line sizes differ, and a weld-neck flange, gasket and bolt set at each flanged nozzle. Turns that are not 90° or 45°, and turns too tight for their elbow, are reported and not drawn. Drag and drop fittings. Gate, globe, check and ball valves, strainers, flange pairs, tees and reducers snap onto the pipe, take the line's size and class, and split the pipe. A tee starts a branch. Change a line's size and every component re-sizes; move a straight run and the elbows follow; undo everything.

heading: What's new in Datum Layout › 0.1.0 — 2026-11-03
text: What's new in Datum Layout › 0.1.0 — 2026-11-03. Checks. Clashes between pipes, pipes and equipment, and pipes and the ground, with a 25 mm clearance; open ends; size, rating and end mismatches; components the line's class does not allow; lines without a number. Click a finding to go to it. Lists and exports. The line list, the equipment list with nozzles and the material take-off per line, each to CSV. A piping component file (.pcf) per line or for the whole plant that Datum Pipe reads; glTF 2.0 for any 3D viewer; print or save as PDF. A catalogue of generated parts. Pipe ½" to 24", 90° and 45° elbows, equal and reducing tees, concentric reducers, caps, weld-neck and blind flanges in class 150 and 300, gaskets and bolt sets, and four valve types, each from a table whose rows name their source. One pipe class (carbon steel). Plug-in packs add your company's classes and parts. Examples. A pump suction and discharge, an exchanger hook-up with a bypass, a small pipe rack run, and "Find the clashes" with three planted problems.

heading: Datum Layout: notes for Claude
text: Datum Layout: notes for Claude. Read docs/MEMORY.md first. It is the project's memory: architecture, decisions, roadmap, and a log of every session. The family design guide is FAMILY.md in Edgar-Mendonca/Datum (read-only from here; docs/FAMILY.md links to it). The brief this app started from is briefs/DATUM-LAYOUT.md in the same hub repo. At the end of every session that changes anything, update docs/MEMORY.md: - tick the roadmap - add a session-log entry - record any new decisions - refresh the architecture section if files moved - Rust and Tauri 2, small and efficient code, Windows first. The same look, ribbon, help, printing and updater as every Datum app (FAMILY §2–9); copy from the reference apps rather than reinventing: Datum Plan (shell), Datum Pipe (3D view, pipe library, PCF, units), Datum Mesh (3D techniques, verification pattern), Datum Schema (object model, plant package). Every copy becomes Layout's own code; never link shared code. - Ship in small numbered releases (0.1.0, 0.1.1, …). Every release appears in the in-app updater. - All geometry and rules belong in crates/core (pure Rust, unit-tested), not in the UI. The window only draws what the engine sends and sends edits back as operations (doc::Op). - The UI is SolidJS + Vite in ui/src/*.tsx (built to ui/dist). State lives in ui/src/store.ts. The 3D view uses three.js (MIT).

heading: Datum Layout: notes for Claude
text: Datum Layout: notes for Claude. - The engine and the .dlayout file use metres with X east, Y north, Z up. The engine sends the display units (SI and US) from its unit table (crates/core/src/units.rs); ui/src/units.ts only applies them. - Parts are generated, never downloaded or bundled: a shape rule in code + a dimension table in catalogue/ (every row with its source) + ports. Never copy a standard's tables or text, or any other program's parts library. - Public words (README, CHANGELOG, site.json, help, commits, comments): never name, compare with, or say the app copies or replaces any commercial plant-design, CAD or 3D product (FAMILY §13). Standards and file formats may be named (PCF, glTF, IFC, STEP). The UI test fails if a product name appears in the window (names kept only as hashes in tests_ui/run.cjs). - Datum Layout models geometry; it never simulates the process. - Licences: MIT/BSD/Apache/MPL only. Record every dependency in NOTICE. Checks before pushing: - cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings - cargo test --workspace (geometry, routing, exchange with Datum Pipe's reader, examples, hardening) - npm run check:ui, then npm run test:ui (builds the window and the engine bridge crates/core/examples/bridge.rs, then drives the window with the real engine behind it; set NODE_PATH=$(npm root -g) if Playwright is installed globally) - cargo deny check (licences, advisories, sources; CI runs it)

heading: Contributing › How the code is laid out
text: Contributing › How the code is laid out. - crates/core: the engine in pure Rust: the plant model and its edits, the catalogue (tables and pipe classes), part shapes and ports, the six equipment types, routing, the checks (clashes with parry3d), lists, and the PCF and glTF exports. All geometry and rules live here, with tests. - catalogue/: the dimension tables and the pipe class, as plain CSV and JSON with a source on every row (catalogue/SOURCES.md). - src-tauri: the desktop shell (commands, files, options, recovery, plug-in packs, the updater). - ui/src: the window (SolidJS + TypeScript, three.js for the 3D view). It draws what the engine computes and sends edits back as operations. - docs/MEMORY.md: architecture, decisions, roadmap and a log of every session. Read it first.

heading: Contributing › Before you send a change
text: Contributing › Before you send a change. Keep code compact and in the style around it. A new part or rule comes with a test against its table; a new window feature with a UI test where it can. Never copy a standard's tables or text, or any other program's parts library. Never link GPL, LGPL or AGPL code into the app. By contributing you agree your work is released under the MIT licence.

3D plant layout and piping: place equipment, route lines, check and hand over. Place equipment from its datasheet sizes, route pipes between nozzles, and the elbows, tees, flanges and valves appear and size themselves from the line's size and pipe class. Drag a valve onto a pipe and it snaps into place. Then check for clashes, list every line and its materials, and send each line to Datum Pipe for its isometric and stress analysis. It is for piping and layout designers, mechanical and process engineers, and students learning plant design. It is free and open source (MIT), Windows first, installs in seconds and updates itself. More on the family site: edgar-mendonca.github.io/Datum/apps/layout.

heading: What it does
text: What it does. - Place the equipment. Vertical vessels, horizontal drums, storage tanks, columns, centrifugal pumps with motor and baseplate, and shell-and-tube exchangers, drawn from a few datasheet sizes, each with its nozzles (size, rating, facing, position, direction). - Route the lines. Click from nozzle to nozzle with orthogonal guides: spec elbows at every turn (long or short radius), reducers where sizes change, weld-neck flanges, gaskets and bolt sets at flanged nozzles. - Drop the fittings. Valves, strainers, flange pairs, tees and reducers snap onto the pipe by their ports, take the line's size and class, and split the pipe. A tee starts a branch. Resize a line and everything on it re-sizes. - Check. Clashes (pipe–pipe, pipe–equipment, pipe–ground) with a clearance, open ends, mismatches, class rules and missing line numbers, each one a click away. - Hand over. Line list, equipment and nozzle list, material take-off (CSV); a piping component file (.pcf) per line for Datum Pipe; glTF 2.0 for any 3D viewer; print to PDF. Every part is generated from a dimension table and a shape rule, never downloaded: each table row names its source (catalogue/SOURCES.md), and plug-in packs add your company's pipe classes and parts. Check dimensions against your supplier's data before ordering or building.

heading: Datum Layout: project memory › 1. Architecture
text: Datum Layout: project memory › 1. Architecture. crates/core is the engine (pure Rust, no Tauri). The model holds only what the designer decides (equipment with sizes and nozzles; lines with a path of corner points and components placed on a segment at a distance); route::build derives every part with its shapes and ports from it, so resizing, moving and undo never leave stale geometry. src-tauri is the shell: commands, files, options, recovery, plug-in packs, the updater. ui is the window: it draws what the engine sends and sends edits as operations. Coordinates: metres, X east, Y north, Z up, in the engine, the file and PCF; the 3D view turns its group so Z is up in three.js's Y-up world. Units: the engine's display table (units::shown) gives every quantity in SI (m, mm, bar, °C) or US (ft, in, psi, °F).

heading: Datum Layout: project memory › 5. Known limits
text: Datum Layout: project memory › 5. Known limits. - Eccentric reducers and the walk view are not in 0.1 (cut list). - Plug-in packs are folders only (no zip yet). - Turning equipment, or a move no run can take (a sideways move of a single straight leg), leaves its line skewed and reported until Route Again; Route Again does not yet look for clashes. - Dimension tables are typical catalogue values; they are checked against their sources before 1.0. - Datum Pipe's PCF reader has no 22" bore (reads it as 20") and no cap (reads a short pipe): noted for Datum Pipe's chat. - Not yet run on a real Windows PC by the user; the 3D view was checked in Chromium's software renderer. - Hub task: add Datum Layout to apps.json (id layout, accent #3A5A78), copy docs/brand/datum-layout-icon.svg to the hub's brand/, and the rest of the hub's list (AppGlyph, phrases, nine-app hero, FAMILY §1, Datum Home's list, brain).

heading: Datum Layout: project memory › 6. How we work
text: Datum Layout: project memory › 6. How we work. 1. The user reviews a release and sends screenshots. 2. Reproduce first. 3. Big asks get a plan file and questions; build after the answers. 4. Engine first (with a test), then the UI. 5. Check every change in the window (SHOTS=dir node tests_ui/run.cjs). 6. Add a UI test for every bug. 7. Run all checks: clippy -D warnings, cargo test (with the geometry, exchange and hardening tests), the UI type-check and UI tests, cargo deny check. 8. Release. 9. heading: Datum Layout 0.1: plan › Feedback → diagnosis
text: Datum Layout 0.1: plan › Feedback → diagnosis. - The family's plant workflow is four apps: Schema (P&ID, plant package) → Layout (3D layout of one plant) → Pipe (isometrics, stress) and Sim (dynamics). Layout models geometry only. - Open parts libraries are GPL/LGPL or licensed per asset, and vendor models cannot be redistributed, so every part is generated from a dimension table and a shape rule.

text: Datum Layout 0.1: plan › Proposal. 1. Engine first (crates/core): units (from Pipe/Calc), catalogue (CSV/JSON tables with sources, plug-in packs), parts (shapes → meshes, ports), the six equipment types, the model (objects with ids and uids after Schema, .dlayout with format and repair), edits as operations with undo, routing (path → straights + spec elbows with exact cut-backs, reducers, end flanges; drop components by snapping to the nearest free place; branch tees), checks (parry3d clashes, open ends, mismatches, class rules, numbers), lists and take-off, PCF (writer, plus Pipe's reader for the tests) and glTF. 2. Tests: parts against their tables, ports coincide and face each other, no gaps or overlaps, lengths add up, 90°/45°/too-tight turns, resizing; each example's PCF read by Pipe's reader; glTF verified; hardening (failed edits, random edits, damaged files, 2,000-part speed gate); UI tests driving the real engine through a bridge.

heading: tagline
text: tagline. 3D plant layout and piping: place equipment, route lines, check and hand over.

heading: for
text: for. Piping and layout designers, mechanical and process engineers, and students learning plant design.

heading: about
text: about. Datum Layout lays out one plant in 3D. You place equipment from its datasheet sizes, route pipes between nozzles, and the elbows, tees, flanges and valves appear and size themselves from the line's size and pipe class. Every part is generated from a dimension table and a shape rule, so nothing is downloaded and every dimension has a source. Then it checks the model for clashes, open ends and spec problems, lists every line, the equipment with its nozzles and the material take-off, and hands each line to Datum Pipe as a piping component file for its isometric and stress analysis.

heading: steps
text: steps. Drag vessels, drums, tanks, columns, pumps and exchangers onto the plot and set their sizes and nozzles from the datasheet. Click from nozzle to nozzle: spec elbows, reducers and flanges appear by themselves. Drag valves and tees onto a pipe and they snap, size themselves and split it. Check and hand over Find clashes, open ends and class problems, export the line list and material take-off, and send each line to Datum Pipe.

heading: highlights
text: highlights. Six parametric equipment types with nozzles: vertical vessel, horizontal drum, storage tank, column, centrifugal pump with motor and baseplate, shell-and-tube exchanger Routing with orthogonal guides: long- or short-radius elbows at every turn, reducers where sizes change, weld-neck flanges, gaskets and bolt sets at flanged nozzles Drag and drop valves, strainers, flange pairs, tees and reducers that snap onto the pipe by their ports; a tee starts a branch Change a line's size and every component re-sizes; move a run and the elbows follow; undo everything Clash check (pipe–pipe, pipe–equipment, pipe–ground) with a clearance, plus open ends, mismatches, class rules and missing line numbers Line list, equipment and nozzle list, and material take-off per line, all to CSV PCF export that Datum Pipe reads unchanged, and glTF 2.0 for any 3D viewer A catalogue of generated parts (½" to 24") with every row's source, and plug-in packs for company pipe classes

CentriForge is an open-source compressor engineering suite, a Windows desktop app (or browser app) for the preliminary design, selection, simulation and technical evaluation of industrial centrifugal compressors. Every module works on one shared engineering model, so a change to the gas, an operating case, the shaft or a bearing propagates through thermodynamics, aerodynamics, mechanics, rotordynamics and verification in a single run. [!IMPORTANT] Results support preliminary engineering, design studies and comparisons. The suite does not certify compliance with API 617, API 614, API 692, ISO 15156 or any other standard. Acceptance criteria are configurable and must be checked against the edition that applies to your job. Detailed design and safety-critical conclusions require review by a qualified engineer.

heading: Contents › Quick start › Windows: install the app (recommended)
text: Contents › Quick start › Windows: install the app (recommended). 1. Open the latest release and download CentriForge-Setup-x.y.z.exe. 2. Run it. It installs for your user only (no administrator rights) and adds Start-menu and desktop shortcuts. Windows SmartScreen may warn because the installer is not code-signed: choose *More info → Run anyway*. 3. Start CentriForge. It opens in its own window on the launcher page. No Python, Node.js or command line needed. Updates: the launcher checks GitHub Releases when it opens. When a newer version exists, click UPDATE TO x.y.z: it downloads the installer, installs silently and restarts CentriForge. Projects are stored in Documents\CentriForge and are never touched by updates or uninstalling.

heading: 3. Start › How it works
text: 3. Start › How it works. - One data model. backend/compsuite/core/model.py defines every input. The API publishes it as a JSON schema and the browser forms are generated from it, so a new input field shows up in the UI automatically. - Traceability. Every result carries the method, engine, software version, input hash, assumptions, references and warnings. Reports print them; saved runs keep the project revision and input hash. - Adapters, not lock-in. Built-in methods always work; external engines (CoolProp, ROSS, CalculiX, CadQuery) are used when installed and are compared against the built-in methods in the tests. Technology: Python, NumPy, SciPy, pandas, pydantic, FastAPI, SQLite, matplotlib; React, TypeScript, Vite, Plotly, Three.js.

heading: Architecture › Shared engineering data model
text: Architecture › Shared engineering data model. core/model.py defines one Project (pydantic) containing every input: gas, operating cases, design basis, shaft, bearings, seals, train, lube, piping, criteria and materials. Units are part of the field names (suction_pressure_bara, journal_diameter_mm). Optional fields set to None are estimated by the owning module and the estimate is reported. The same model drives the API (/api/schema publishes it as JSON Schema) and the frontend forms, so adding a field to the model makes it editable in the UI.

heading: Architecture › Workflow
text: Architecture › Workflow. core/workflow.run_project(project, level) runs the modules in dependency order so a change to any input propagates to every result: Multi-casing designs are handled per casing for the mechanical and lateral analyses. level="fast" (used inside optimisation loops) uses coarser bearing tables and skips unbalance sweeps and maps.

heading: Architecture › Traceability
text: Architecture › Traceability. Every module returns a CalcRecord (core/trace.py) with: module, method, engine (built-in, CoolProp, …), software version, a hash of the inputs it used, assumptions, references and warnings. Reports print these records, the checklist cites the module behind each check, and stored runs keep the project revision, input hash and software version (core/storage.py).

heading: Architecture › Numerical notes
text: Architecture › Numerical notes. * Lateral FE: 4 DOF per node (x, φx, y, φy), consistent mass with rotary inertia, Timoshenko shear factor, skew gyroscopic matrix. Repeated solves (Campbell, unbalance sweeps, stability search) are done on a 40-mode Ritz basis built from the undamped system with symmetrised bearing stiffness; this is checked against the full model in the tests. * Bearing coefficients are finite differences of the integrated fluid force about the static equilibrium, in the same coordinate frame as the rotor model. This avoids frame/sign errors that arise when transcribing closed-form coefficient tables. * Off-design maps use stage stacking on the real-gas model, so density changes, intercooling and stage mismatching appear in the overall map.

heading: Architecture › Extending
text: Architecture › Extending. * New compressor types (API 618, screw): add a sizing/performance module that produces the same sizing-like dictionary (speed, power, stages or cylinders) and a rotor/crankshaft builder; the torsional, lube, piping, materials, reporting and checklist modules are reusable. * New engines: add an adapter next to the built-in method (see thermo/backends.py, rotordynamics/ross_adapter.py, structural/calculix.py) and a validation test comparing the two. * Criteria editions: Criteria in the model carries the edition label and numeric limits; keep one JSON per edition under version control and load it into the project.

heading: SHPB Analysis Tool › Explanation for Stress-Strain Calculation in SHPB Experiment
text: SHPB Analysis Tool › Explanation for Stress-Strain Calculation in SHPB Experiment. In the Split Hopkinson Pressure Bar (SHPB) experiment, the characteristic relations associated with one-dimensional elastic wave propagation in the bar provide the basis for calculating stress and strain in the specimen. 1. Particle Velocity at Specimen/Input-Bar and Specimen/Output-Bar Interface: - The particle velocity $ v_1(t) $ at the specimen/input-bar interface is given by: $ v_1(t) = c_b(\varepsilon_I - \varepsilon_R) $ - Here, $ c_b = \sqrt{\frac{E_b}{\rho_b}} $ represents the bar wave speed, with $ E_b $ denoting the Young's modulus and $ \rho_b $ the density of the bar material. - The particle velocity $ v_2(t) $ at the specimen/output-bar interface is given by: $ v_2(t) = c_b \varepsilon_T $ 2. Mean Axial Strain Rate in the Specimen: - The mean axial strain rate $ \dot{e}_s $ in the specimen is calculated as: $ \dot{e}_s = \frac{c_b}{l_0} (\varepsilon_I - \varepsilon_R - \varepsilon_T) = \frac{v_1 - v_2}{l_0} $ - Here, $ l_0 $ represents the initial specimen length. 3. Calculation of Bar Stresses and Normal Forces: - The stresses and normal forces at the specimen/bar interfaces are computed as follows: - $ P_1 = E_b (\varepsilon_I + \varepsilon_R) A_b $ at the specimen/input-bar interface. - $ P_2 = E_b \varepsilon_T A_b $ at the specimen/output-bar interface. - Here, $ A_b $ denotes the cross-sectional area of the bars.

heading: SHPB Analysis Tool › Explanation for Stress-Strain Calculation in SHPB Experiment
text: SHPB Analysis Tool › Explanation for Stress-Strain Calculation in SHPB Experiment. 4. Mean Axial Stress in the Specimen: - The mean axial stress $ \bar{S}_s(t) $ in the specimen is given by: $ \bar{S}_s(t) = \frac{(P_1 + P_2)}{2} \left( \frac{1}{A_s} \right) $ - Here, $ A_s $ represents the initial cross-sectional area of the specimen. 5. Stress-Strain Relationship: - Assuming stress equilibrium, uniaxial stress conditions in the specimen, and one-dimensional elastic stress wave propagation without dispersion in the bars, the nominal strain rate $ \dot{e}_s $, nominal strain $ e_s $, and nominal stress $ S_s $ in the specimen are estimated using: - $ \dot{e}_s(t) = \frac{2c_b}{l_0} \varepsilon_R(t) $ - $ e_s(t) = \int_0^t \dot{e}_s(\tau) d\tau $ - $ S_s(t) = \frac{E_b A_b}{A_s} \varepsilon_T(t) $ 6. True Stress-Strain: - True strain $\varepsilon_s(t)$ in the specimen is given by: - $\varepsilon_s(t) = -\ln(1 - e_s(t))$ Here, $e_s(t)$ represents the engineering strain in the specimen. - The true strain rate $\dot{\varepsilon}_s(t)$ in the specimen is calculated as: - $\dot{\varepsilon}_s(t) = \frac{\dot{e}_s(t)}{1 - e_s(t)}$ - The true stress $\sigma_s(t)$ in the specimen is obtained as: - $\sigma_s(t) = S_s(t) \cdot (1 - e_s(t))$ Here, $S_s(t)$ represents the nominal stress in the specimen.

heading: Split Hopkinson Pressure Bar: design, testing and data analysis
text: Split Hopkinson Pressure Bar: design, testing and data analysis. A Kolsky bar built from scratch for testing materials at strain rates of 10² to 10⁴ s⁻¹: the frame and bars, the gas gun, the velocity gate, the strain-gauge amplifiers, and the software that turns the signals into stress–strain curves.

heading: Split Hopkinson Pressure Bar: design, testing and data analysis › Overview
text: Split Hopkinson Pressure Bar: design, testing and data analysis › Overview. The Split Hopkinson Pressure Bar (SHPB), or Kolsky bar, measures how materials behave when they are deformed very quickly: the conditions of a crash, a blast or a ballistic impact. A short specimen sits between two long elastic bars. A striker hits the first bar, a stress pulse runs down it into the specimen, and strain gauges on both bars record what goes in, what is reflected and what passes through. From those three signals, one-dimensional wave theory gives the specimen's stress, strain and strain rate over time. I led the project end to end: design and CAD of the frame and bars, manufacture, the compressed-air striker launcher, an infrared velocity gate, a two-channel strain-gauge amplifier, testing, and the MATLAB and Python software that reduces the data. Figure: The SHPB as built, annotated. Figure: CAD model of the bar on its frame.

heading: Split Hopkinson Pressure Bar: design, testing and data analysis › The method
text: Split Hopkinson Pressure Bar: design, testing and data analysis › The method. The input (incident) and output (transmitted) bars stay elastic throughout the test; only the specimen deforms plastically. The bars are high-strength steel, and the striker is the same material as the bars. When the striker hits the input bar, a compressive pulse travels to the specimen. Part of it is reflected back into the input bar and part is transmitted through the specimen into the output bar. The gauges are placed so the incident and reflected pulses do not overlap. - Incident pulse : generated by the striker impact. - Reflected pulse : from the input bar / specimen interface; it carries the specimen's strain rate. - Transmitted pulse : through the specimen into the output bar; it carries the specimen's stress. Figure: Two-dimensional layout of the SHPB. Figure: Lagrangian (time–distance) diagram of the stress waves in the bars. The SHPB covers the high strain-rate range, 10² to 10⁴ s⁻¹, above what servo-hydraulic machines and drop towers can reach and below plate-impact tests. Figure: Experimental techniques by strain-rate range.

heading: Split Hopkinson Pressure Bar: design, testing and data analysis › The method › Where it is used
text: Split Hopkinson Pressure Bar: design, testing and data analysis › The method › Where it is used. - Dynamic strength of metals, ceramics, composites and polymers for armour, pipelines, pressure vessels and offshore structures. - Crashworthiness of aerospace and automotive materials, and the impact response of protective gear. - Effects of temperature, strain rate, loading history and microstructure on flow stress.

heading: Split Hopkinson Pressure Bar: design, testing and data analysis › Design of the bar
text: Split Hopkinson Pressure Bar: design, testing and data analysis › Design of the bar. The whole apparatus sits on an I-beam, the backbone that carries the gas gun and the holders for the incident and transmitted bars. The holders are machined so the gun barrel and both bars share one centreline. A 4 m ladder frame raises the beam to working height, five A-frames stiffen the structure, and levelling screws on every leg let the line be aligned precisely.

heading: Split Hopkinson Pressure Bar: design, testing and data analysis › Design of the bar › Design rules
text: Split Hopkinson Pressure Bar: design, testing and data analysis › Design of the bar › Design rules. - Ratios : bar length to diameter L/D ≈ 100; bar to specimen diameter D/d₀ = 2–4; specimen length to diameter l₀/d₀ = 0.6–1. - Bar length : long enough that incident and reflected pulses do not overlap at the gauge. - Alignment : bars and specimen on one axis, to keep the stress uniaxial and the tests repeatable. - Specimen : flat, parallel, lubricated faces to limit friction and stress concentrations. - Acquisition : high-speed, synchronised recording of both bars and the striker velocity. Figure: Outline of the SHPB set-up. Figure: The bar line on its frame. Figure: Bar supports and alignment. Figure: Gas gun and striker end. Drawings: assembly (PDF) · parts (PDF) .

heading: Split Hopkinson Pressure Bar: design, testing and data analysis › Striker launch system
text: Split Hopkinson Pressure Bar: design, testing and data analysis › Striker launch system. A compressed-air gas gun fires the striker into the incident bar. The launch pressure sets the striker speed, and so the energy of the impact and the strain rate in the specimen. - An air compressor fills a storage cylinder. - A flow controller, filter and ball valve feed a reservoir tank through a non-return valve; the reservoir is charged to the exact pressure for the speed wanted. - A 3/8 in, 180 bar hydraulic hose links the reservoir to the barrel. - A 3/4 in normally closed diaphragm solenoid valve (220 V AC) sits at the barrel; pressing the button opens it and the air drives the striker down the barrel. Figure: Outline of the striker launch system. The launch velocity follows from the reservoir pressure , the barrel area , the striker mass and its travel in the barrel (an upper bound, since it ignores friction and expansion of the air):

heading: Split Hopkinson Pressure Bar: design, testing and data analysis › Velocity measurement
text: Split Hopkinson Pressure Bar: design, testing and data analysis › Velocity measurement. Two infrared sensors 50 mm apart sit at the barrel exit. An Arduino Uno records the moments each beam is broken, in microseconds, and a 16×2 LCD shows the transit time and the striker velocity: Figure: Circuit of the velocity measurement system. Control code: Control-code-for-Velocity-Measurement-system on GitHub.

heading: Split Hopkinson Pressure Bar: design, testing and data analysis › Strain gauges and amplifier
text: Split Hopkinson Pressure Bar: design, testing and data analysis › Strain gauges and amplifier. Each bar carries a full Wheatstone bridge at its centre: two gauges along the axis ( ) and two around the circumference ( ), all on one centreline. Under load the bridge goes out of balance and gives a small voltage: Figure: Full-bridge strain gauges mounted on a bar. Figure: Strain gauges in a Wheatstone bridge. The bridge signal is amplified by a two-channel instrumentation amplifier, one channel per bar. The INA128 (or the faster FET-input INA111) runs at a gain of ×100, set by a 500 Ω resistor between pins 1 and 8; an OPA227 stage and a trimmer remove the DC offset at rest. Figure: Two-channel strain-gauge amplifier circuit. Figure: The amplifier board as built. Figure: Amplifier wiring colour scheme. Figure: Gain against frequency for the INA111 and INA128.

heading: Split Hopkinson Pressure Bar: design, testing and data analysis › Strain gauges and amplifier › From voltage to strain

text: Split Hopkinson Pressure Bar: design, testing and data analysis › Theory › Designing a test: the response diagram. The incident strain is set by the striker velocity, . Combining this with the relations above gives the line every test on a given bar, specimen and velocity must lie on: The test runs where this line crosses the material's own flow-stress curve. The two ends of the line are the limits: for a material with no strength, and for one that does not flow. So the same set-up drives a strong material at a lower strain rate than a soft one; to reach a chosen point, change the specimen size or the striker velocity. heading: Split Hopkinson Pressure Bar: design, testing and data analysis › Validity checks
text: Split Hopkinson Pressure Bar: design, testing and data analysis › Validity checks. - Stress equilibrium : the loading must last much longer than the specimen transit time ; checked by comparing the forces on both faces. - Friction : friction at the faces stiffens the result, more so at small ; keep between 0.5 and 1 and lubricate with MoS₂ or lithium grease. - Dispersion : short, sharp pulses spread out along the bars and add oscillations; a pulse shaper between striker and bar lengthens the rise time. - Inertia : axial and radial inertia add an error to the flow stress that grows with the square of the strain rate:

heading: Split Hopkinson Pressure Bar: design, testing and data analysis › Data reduction and results
text: Split Hopkinson Pressure Bar: design, testing and data analysis › Data reduction and results. - Crop the recorded voltage–time traces and line up the incident, reflected and transmitted pulses. - Smooth them with a Savitzky–Golay filter. - Convert voltage to strain with the bridge relation. - Compute particle velocities and the specimen strain rate; integrate it for strain. - Compute specimen stress from the transmitted pulse, then true stress and true strain. heading: Stress waves in solids
text: Stress waves in solids. Impact tests on long bars to watch stress pulses travel, reflect and change at a step in section, and a non-destructive way to measure Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio from them.

heading: Stress waves in solids › Overview
text: Stress waves in solids › Overview. When a load is applied slowly, the whole body adjusts together. When it is applied suddenly (an impact, a blast, an earthquake), the far parts of the body do not feel it at first: the disturbance travels through the material as a stress wave, at a finite speed, reflecting at every free end and change of section. Designing parts that survive impact means knowing how fast these waves travel, how they reflect and how they decay. This study pairs Hertz contact theory with impact experiments on long steel bars: a ball striking a bar, a bar striking a bar, and a ball striking bars that step up or down in section.

heading: Stress waves in solids › Body and surface waves
text: Stress waves in solids › Body and surface waves. P-waves (primary, compressional) push and pull the material along the direction of travel and are the fastest. S-waves (secondary, shear) move it across the direction of travel and only pass through solids. Along a free surface travel Rayleigh waves , with an elliptical particle motion, and Love waves , with horizontal shear. Figure: A P-wave: compression and dilatation along the direction of travel. Figure: An S-wave: shear across the direction of travel. Figure: A Rayleigh wave: elliptical motion at the surface. Figure: A Love wave: horizontal shear at the surface.

heading: Stress waves in solids › Ball-on-bar impact
text: Stress waves in solids › Ball-on-bar impact. The contact between the ball and the end of the bar follows Hertz: the contact force grows with the 3/2 power of the approach of ball and bar, The ball (mass ) is slowed by , while the bar end moves away at . Together these give the equation for the approach during contact, and the stress pulse sent into the bar: Figure: Ball-on-bar impact: schematic and notation.

heading: Stress waves in solids › Stepped bars
text: Stress waves in solids › Stepped bars. At a change of section from to , force balance and continuity of velocity split the incident pulse into a transmitted and a reflected part: A step down in section amplifies the transmitted stress; a step up reduces it.

heading: Stress waves in solids › Expected pulses
text: Stress waves in solids › Expected pulses. A ball sends a compressive pulse down the bar; it reflects from the free far end as tension. A spherical wave starts at the contact point and becomes a plane wave within a few bar diameters. The contact time is the pulse width , and one round trip takes the characteristic time . The axial pulse comes with a lateral pulse through the Poisson effect; their ratio is Poisson's ratio. A bar striking a bar gives a rectangular pulse. With a free far end it returns as tension; with a fixed end it returns as compression, and it keeps re-reflecting until damping removes it. Figure: Ideal stress–time record of a ball-on-bar impact. Figure: Ideal longitudinal and lateral strain records. Figure: Ideal stress–time record of a bar-on-bar impact. Figure: Bar-on-bar impact with the far end fixed.

heading: Stress waves in solids › Experiment
text: Stress waves in solids › Experiment. A steel bar, 20 mm in diameter and 1.2 m long, hangs level from nylon threads. A 30 mm steel ball hangs as a pendulum, just touching the centre of the bar end. A 0/90° strain-gauge rosette (3 mm gauge length, 350 Ω, gauge factor 2.16) at mid-length senses axial and circumferential strain; each gauge is one arm of its own quarter bridge, fed by a two-channel amplifier and recorded on a digital storage oscilloscope. The ball is pulled back to angle on a string of length and released, so it strikes at Figure: Ball-on-bar experimental set-up.

heading: Stress waves in solids › Tests
text: Stress waves in solids › Tests. Figure: Ball on bar: a wave started from a single point. Figure: Bar on bar: a wave started over the whole face. Figure: Ball on a stepped bar, larger to smaller section. Figure: Ball on a stepped bar, smaller to larger section. Figure: Axial and lateral strain from the 0/90° rosette. The recorded traces matched the expected pulse shapes: separate incident and reflected pulses on the long bar, the change in amplitude at each step, and a lateral pulse in phase with the axial one.

heading: Stress waves in solids › Material properties from the waves
text: Stress waves in solids › Material properties from the waves. The same test is a non-destructive way to characterise an elastic material. Poisson's ratio is the ratio of the peak lateral to the peak axial strain; the wave speed comes from the round-trip time read off the strain record, and with the density gives Young's modulus:

heading: Lateral compression of thin-walled tubes
text: Lateral compression of thin-walled tubes. Ring compression of aluminium 6063 tubes between flat plates: yield stress, elastic modulus and hardening modulus from one quasi-static test, checked against the Reid–Reddy theory.

heading: Lateral compression of thin-walled tubes › Overview
text: Lateral compression of thin-walled tubes › Overview. Thin-walled tubes are used as energy absorbers in vehicles, aircraft and structures. In the ring (lateral) compression test a tube lies on its side between two rigid flat plates and is squashed across its diameter. Seen along the load, it takes a saddle shape. The test is simple, and its load–deflection curve carries enough information to back out the material's yield stress, elastic modulus and strain hardening. This was part of a wider study of aluminium tube deformation and impact energy absorption, with experiments, analytical models and finite-element models compared side by side. Figure: Lateral compression of a tube between two plates. Figure: Finite-element models of tube crushing.

heading: Lateral compression of thin-walled tubes › Load–deflection response
text: Lateral compression of thin-walled tubes › Load–deflection response. The curve has three phases: - Elastic : load rises linearly and the tube springs back if unloaded. - Yield : plastic hinges form and the load levels off at the collapse load . - Hardening : the slope rises again as the material strain-hardens and the geometry stiffens. Figure: Ideal load–displacement response of the ring compression test. Figure: The elastic and yield region in detail.

heading: Lateral compression of thin-walled tubes › Experiment
text: Lateral compression of thin-walled tubes › Experiment. An aluminium 6063 tube, 50 mm long, 50 mm in diameter and 1.6 mm thick, was compressed at a constant 4 mm/min. The load–displacement record was taken together with photographs of each stage of the collapse. The collapse load, read where the tangents to the elastic and plastic parts meet, was 0.94 kN . Figure: Stages of the tube collapsing under lateral compression.

text: Lateral compression of thin-walled tubes › Properties from the test. Yield stress from the limit load (with for short rings, , and for long tubes, ), and elastic modulus from the elastic load and deflection (DeRuntz and Hodge; in plane stress, in plane strain): With kN, kN, mm, mm, mm and mm: Yield stress 183.6 MPa Young's modulus ≈ 68 GPa Hardening modulus 1.08 GPa

heading: Lateral compression of thin-walled tubes › Theory and fit
text: Lateral compression of thin-walled tubes › Theory and fit. Reid and Reddy describe the hardening response with one non-dimensional parameter, which sets the shape of the load–deflection curve: The test curve is made non-dimensional (load over collapse load, , against deflection over radius, ) and laid over the theoretical curves for a range of . The best fit was , which gives the average hardening modulus: Figure: Theoretical non-dimensional load–deflection curves for several mR. Figure: Experiment against theory: best fit at mR = 4. The code that draws the theoretical curves and fits them to a test record is on GitHub .
